3846: The petitioner, a woman, filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for maintenance and for interim relief. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the petitioner was not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the special leave petitions, this Court HELD: 1. The presumption is rebuttable, a heavy burden lies on him who seeks to deprive the relationship of legal origin. Law leans in favour of legitimacy and frowns upon bastardy. In this view, the contention of the petitioner deserves no consideration. [880C] 2. The presumption arises in favour of wedlock between the two, by the petitioner in this case, has been negatived by the High Court. A strong presumption arises in favor of legitimacy or frownatio n upon bastardse. In this case, the petitioner has failed to prove her marriage with the respondent. [881D E] 3. The presumption arising from the facts of this case is rebuttabe. The petitioner cannot be allowed to take advantage of the presumptions arising from other circumstances. [882E] 4. The presumption can only be rebutted if it is shown that the evidence led by the parties before the court is such as would disentitle the party against whom the presumption is sought to be drawn. If the evidence is such that it would have been impossible for the party to adduce it to establish the factum of marriage, then the presumption may well be rebutted. [883F G] 5. The presumption does not arise merely because the evidence is not sufficient to rebut the presumption. It is open to the party aggrieved to rely on the presumption to disprove it. [884A B] 6. The presumption must be rebutted by adducing evidence. [885B]

The High court has rightly held that the award is vitiated because of nonconsideration of relevant documents. [642C] 2.1. The award does not indicate that all relevant documents have been taken into account. The parties participated in the arbitration without demur. In 1981, the award was made. No objection was taken at that time that the award had been passed. No objection raised at that time, that the award should be set aside. The matter is pending for a long time. 886: The appellant was the owner of a piece of land in village Mohammadpur Munirka. He purchased it from one Smt. Sethi and her husband, who were the owners of the land. After the purchase, the appellant filed a complaint against the vendor and his wife alleging that they had committed offences under sections 420, 109 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate ordered that the case be adjourned to enable the complainant to file a further report on the basis of which he directed that the case should stand adjourned. The appellant moved the High Court under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings initiated by the First Information Report lodged by him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no case had been made out for quashing the proceeding initiated by the first informant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in dismissing the petition. [504 C] (ii) The High court was wrong in its view that the allegations made against the accused person did constitute an offence alleged but there was either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. [505 D] (iii) The High Courts power to quash criminal proceedings is not intended to stifle prosecutions. It is used only to preventandalise the Civil Courts and to scuttle them where the offender appears to be prima facie guilty of serious offences. [506 E] (iv) The High courts power to quash proceedings is not meant to encourage or advance the prosecution. [507 F] (v) The High has jurisdiction to quash criminal cases as a matter of course subject to such exceptions as may be found necessary to bring home the charges. But at the same time the High Court has also to keep in mind the nature of accusations and the manner in which they are sought to be proved or assumed. [508 G H]
2023: The assessee was a resident of India and was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51 in respect of two years. He claimed exemption from taxation under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that he had not been assessed to income-tax for the said two years. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the assessee 's income was exempt from tax under the International Law. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On further appeals by the assessee, the Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that as the assessee ceased to be a sovereign during the accounting year, his income did not accrue to him but only to the Government of India. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee enjoyed immunity from taxation under International Law. [302 B] (ii) The assessee was not liable to tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 in respect of any part of his income. His income up to that date was not liable for tax. [303 C D] (iii) The assessee could not claim exemption under International Law in respect of the assessment for the year 1950 51 on the ground of being exempt from taxation under international law. [304 E]

2079: The appellants were convicted under section 353, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for one year. The High Court set aside the conviction on the ground that the two offences being fundamentally distinct in nature could be separately taken cognizance of. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the two sections being separate offences, the trial of the appellants should have been separated from the other offences and not the offence under section 186, Indian Penal code. HELD : (i) Section 195, Criminal Procedure Code does not bar the trial of an accused person for the distinct offence under section 352, Indian Penal Court. [880 E] (ii) The two offences being a fundamentally different in nature, could be separately tried under section 186 of the Indian Penal Code. [881 C D] (iii) The two sections being distinct in character cannot be separately tried. [882 A B] (iv) The two provisions being mutually exclusive are not mutually exclusive. [883 C] (v) The two acts being fundamentally distinct in nature can be separately tried both under section 186 and section 186 of Indian Penal Code, though they may be substantially different. [884 D]
1076: The assessees were carrying on business principally in dyes and chemicals. In the course of their business they sold some of the goods manufactured by them and paid commission to the agents. The sales tax authorities charged the commission at the rate of 12 1/2% of the net profits of the company for each year and deducted the amount of commission from the gross profit of the company. The I.T.O., however, disallowed the amount of the commission paid to the agent. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order which allowed the amount of remuneration to the agent but reduced it to 10% on the ground that the commission was not payable to the agent as the turnover had been sold to him. The Tribunal held that the commission paid was not deductible under Rule 12 of Schedule 1 of the Excess Profits Tax Act and that the assessee was entitled to deduct the same from the gross profits. On reference the High Court answered the question against the assessee. It is a payment to an employee who has no fixed or definite right to do so. It is merely a payment to the employee. [605 E] (iii)The payment must be actual payment to the assessee. The payment may be voluntary or implied. It is not necessary that there should be actual payment. It is enough if there is a payment in consideration of past services rendered by the employee. It is also sufficient if there is payment in consideration for past services rendered. 2366: The appellant was convicted under section 5 (3) (a) of the Explosives Act, 1884 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and also to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000 in default to undergo rigorous imprison ment for six months. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the State Government and convicted the appellant under section 5(3)(a) of that Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous im prisonment for one year and also to payment a fine of Rupees 2,000. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the three minor boys were employed in the manufacture of fireworks; (ii) the four minors were employed in any event as labourers and (iii) the appellant could not be held guilty under section 304A IPC because the four minves were not used in the manufacture. HELD : (1) The definition of "fireworks" in section 3(2) of the , is wide enough to include all such operations which may take place on the premises licensed under the Rules or in contravention of the provisions of the Explosive Rules. [657 D E] (2) The definition is wide enough so as to cover every activity which might take place on any premises licensed under these rules. It cannot be definitely inferred from the evidence that the four minions were actually employed in the manufacturing process of fireworks. [658 F G] (3) The appellant was not employed in any activity other than the manufacture of explosives on April 28, 1960. He was not employed on that date. Therefore, he was not liable to be punished under section 304 A IPC. [659 C]
6753: The appellant, a Sagar Mahila Vidyalaya was incorporated by giving donations and was duly registered under the Societies Registration Act. On 17th November, 1933 one Govind Rao Harshe mortgaged some agricultural land and house known as `Harshewada ' to Lakshmi Chand and Duli Chand Modi. The mortgage was created by a deed of mortgage dated 17th November 1933 in favour of the appellant. The mortgage deed recited that the mortgage had been redeemed on 10th April, 1943. The appellant applied for the revival of the execution proceedings on the ground that the judgment debtor had defaulted in carrying out the directions of the revisional court and as such the order passed by the Debt Relief Court granting instalments had ceased to exist and the whole amount had become payable in lumpsum. The executing court dismissed the application but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the condition of the sale certificate having ceased to exist, the decree holders were entitled to execute the sale certificate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the condition could not be imposed by the executing court as it was not a condition which could be prescribed by the D.I.T. and that the executing court had no jurisdiction to pass the final decree. HELD : (1) The condition can only be imposed by a court or authority exercising its powers under the Code of Civil Procedure. [864 E] (2) It is well settled that an executing court cannot go behind the decree; nor can it add to or subtract from the decree. [865 A B] (3) The executing court has power to add to or enlarge the decree. But the executing court cannot add to or substitute the decree except by passing necessary orders after hearing the parties. [866 C] (4) The executing Court cannot travel outside the decree. The executing Court can always modify the decree. If the executing Court finds that the decree suffers from any infirmity it can correct the same. [867 D] (5) The executing courts are not competent to vary the terms of the decree. They have no jurisdiction to do so. [868 F] (6) The executing Courts are not competent even to modify the decree merely because they find that there is some error

It does not apply where the officer in charge is not a police officer within the meaning of section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act. [616 D E] (ii) The provisions of section 25 are not intended to make any difference between an officer who is empowered to investigate an offence and an officer who may be authorized to investigate an offense. The word "officer" in section25 means a person who is actually in charge of the police station. He can be said to have been authorised to investigate an Offence under the Act. [602 F G] (iv) The expression "any person ' in section 25 includes a person who has been arrested or detained without warrant by a Magistrate. [603 H] (v) The word "person" in section 26 of the Indian Police Act, 1861, means a person whose duty it is to enforce the law and which is competent to do so. [604 D] (vi) The word 'officer ' in section 26 is not confined to an officer who exercises powers under the Criminal Procedure Code. 5339: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1960 61, it had borrowed money from its mother and her two sons. The Income tax Officer found that out of the loans advanced by the assessee, the amount of interest paid to Barivallabndas Kalidas Estate on loans taken by her, was of a sum of Rs. 1250 only. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal before the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the expenditure under the head 'income from other sources ' could not be allowed as revenue expenditure because the assessee had not made any contribution towards the loan. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that the expenditure was not an admissible deduction under section 57(iii) of the Act. In further appeals before this Court, the assessee contended that the expenditure incurred in connection with the investment of the assessee was not an allowable deduction under section 5 of the Act, but was a personal one and payment thereof cannot at all be said to be expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of earning income. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 12(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922 is not applicable to the case of the assessee. [547E] 2. The expression "any expenditure" in section 57(ii) of the 1922 Act has been used in the context of the provisions of section 12(1)(b) of the 1961 Act. The expression 'any expenditure ' in section 57 (iii) of that Act means 'any expenditure or allowance which the assessee may have made if he were entitled thereto. [548F G] 3. The expression, 'any expenditure' in section 57 of the 1922 is not defined in the Act. It is a term of art and includes every kind of financial assistance given to meet existing liabilities. The expression is not defined either in the 1922 Act or in the 1961 Act, but is defined in section 2(6) of the Indian Income tax Act. The definition of expenditure in section 2 (6) of that section is not exhaustive. The expression has been used to denote any expenditure or allowance granted to meet existing liability. [549G H; 553A B
5892: The petitioner in W.P.(C) No. 961 of 1988 was a candidate for admission to MBBS/BDS Course in the State of Haryana. She applied for the same and was allotted a seat in the Medical College, Chandigarh. On the basis of information received by the Director General of Health Services, she was allocated a seat in PG NO 909 the Medical College. In order to decide the criteria to be adopted for allocation of vacant seats as a result of drop outs in the number of candidates who had been allocated MBBS/BD Courses, a meeting was held under the chairmanship of the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India on 25.3.1988. The Committee took a decision regarding the allocation of seats in the MBBS/BDC courses. After hearing the learned Counsel of the petitioners in these writ petitions, the Court directed that the following guidelines should be followed for the purpose of filling up the said seats in the medical colleges for admission to the MBBS/ BDS course: (i) The first preference given to the candidates who have already been admitted in the MBBS or BDS Course shall be made within a period of three weeks from today. (ii) The second preference given to those candidates who have not joined in all the courses and have been admitted in other medical colleges shall be made before the third preference is given to those who are still in service. (iii) The third preference given to candidates who have been admitted against available vacant seats in order of merit shall be given to them also at the time of final selection. (iv) The third preferences given to those students who have been allotted MBBS/BED seats in various medical colleges shall also be given to those applicants who have not been allotted MBBS /BDS seats in any other medical college. (v) The third option given to those persons who have been allocated MBBS /BD seats in various Medical Colleges shall also be made before final selection. The petitioner Amanjit Singh Gill in Writ Petition (Civil) No.961 of 1988 is a resident of Punjab. He has since joined the said college. No particulars have, however, been given by her as to in which medical college in Delhi, the two seats were lying vacant. Be that as it

The appellant denied the allegations and pleaded that the delay in filing the present application should be condoned because joint representation of both the parties was made before the Payment of wages Authority, Bombay. Section 72 lays down that nothing in the Act shall apply in relation to an establishment belonging to, or under the management of, a Railway Company. 2406: The respondent, a widow of a tenant in the land in question, executed two mortgage deeds in favour of her husband, one for Rs. 10,000 and another for Rs. 5,000. In the year 1928, the proprietary rights of the respondent were purchased by her husband from the appellants. In the years 1939, the proprietary right of the respondent was acquired by the appellants under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. On the death of the respondent, the respondent became the owner of the land. The respondent filed an application to the Revenue Court under sections 12 and 13 of the Central Provinces Tenancy Act, 1920 for restoration of possession of her occupancy rights in this plot. The appellants contended that the respondent had become the ex proprietor occupancy tenant of this plot on the basis of the mortgage decree passed in terms of the award and, therefore, she was not entitled to claim actual possession from the mortgagors. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not entitled for possession from the appellants as the respondent had no title to the land. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent could only be evicted from the land if she had transferred her interest in the land to the appellants. The appellants then appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) Section 12 of the Central C.P. and Berar Tenancy Act, 1908 is applicable to the case. Under section 12(1), the proprietary rights in the land are transferable. If the land is transferred by sale or otherwise, the transferees are entitled to possession thereof from the transferor. [274 A] (ii) The respondent had become an occupancy tenant of the land in the year 1895. The respondent had been dispossessed from this land in pursuance of the mortgage decrees passed in terms with the award. The respondent was not in possession of the land at any time during the period of the mortgage. The respondent could not have been dispossessed without the intervention of the Court. [276 B D] (iii) The respondent was entitled to remain in possession till the mortgage was redeemed. The respondent did not acquire any right over the land. [277 E]
7115: The appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. It was a subsidiary of the respondent company. The appellant company had its registered office at Ernakulam in Kerala and its main office is at Kottayam. The appellant was holding company 's share capital. The appellant filed a petition before the High Court for winding up of the respondent Company on the ground that it was not liable to pay the amount due to it as a result whereof the holding company could sell the land and other assets of the appellant company. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the holding company was not liable for payment of the amount due from the appellant to the subscribers. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The holding company shall deposit with the official Receiver or Assignee concerned a sum equivalent to the deposited sum on which the High Court was pleased to direct sale deed to be executed in favour of the creditors association together with 25% interest minus the interest, if any earned by the deposit made, calculated on the deposited amount from the date of deposit till 31st July, 1993 within a period of three months from today. [5G] 1.2 The holding company has no liability to make payment of the amounts due to it. The holding company cannot be said to be liable for payment because the holding company has not paid the entire amount payable to it. [6A B] 2.1 The High Court rightly held that the holding Company is not liable to make payment to the subscribers who were members of creditors association on the date when their claim applications were decided by the Kerala High Court. [6C D] 3.1 The question whether the holding company is liable for payment to the subscriber is one of fact. The holding Company is a body of creditors. The holding of the holding Company consists of persons who are interested in the affairs of the company. The holding is not merely a matter of formality but also a matter of substance. The holding itself is an asset of the company and the holding company can be said to have been discharged only after the decision of the High Court. The holding does not necessarily involve the discharge of the liabilities of the subscribers. The holding may consist of several persons who may be interested in
1257: The appellant was convicted under section 307, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The condition of acute emaciation in which Bimla Devi was found on 5th June, 1956, was not due to any calculated starvation but it was on account of prolonged illness, the nature of which was not known to the accused till Dr. It follows therefore that a person committed an offence under section 308, Indian Penal code. [701 D] (2) The first is Queen Empress vs Nidha (1), and the second is Queens 's case (2). The facts are different from those of the present case. [702 C D] (3) There is no evidence to show that the appellant had intention to commit murder. The mere fact that he did not intend to commit murder does not necessarily lead to the inference that he intended to commit murder of the deceased. [703 E F] (4) The first circumstance against him was that he had an intention to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The other circumstances were also not sufficient to prove that he intended the act of committing murder. [704 A] (5) The second circumstance against him is that he had knowledge that the act of the appellant was likely to cause death or cause such bodily injury as would be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [705 G]
4865: The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court set aside the acquittal of the appellant but set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. The High 'Court, however, set aside the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence; (ii) the High 'Court 's appreciation of the evidence is vitiated because the High Court had failed to consider the reasons given by the trial Court in support of its conclusion; (iii) the High court 's approach was erroneous as the High Court did not take into consideration the evidence of the witnesses who were interested in the prosecution; (iv) the High Courts ' attention should be drawn to the fact that the accused persons were acquitted by the Sessions Judge and the High Court; and (v) the High. Court 's judgment was perverse. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in setting aside the acquittal and convicting the appellant. [862 B] (2) The High ' Court was wrong in holding that the evidence of P.W. 2 was not corroborated by the recovery of blood stained baniyan and knife from the appellant. The High. Court was wrong also in holding that there was no motive for the murder. [863 C D] (3) The High.Court was wrong in acquitting the appellant relying on the evidence of a witness who was not independent. The High,Court could have taken into consideration the other evidence which was available before it. [864 E] (4) The High court was wrong in taking into consideration the fact that P.W 2 was an independent witness. The High court could have taken the evidence of another witness if he was present at the time of the incident. [865 F] (5) The High, Court was wrong when it came to the conclusion that the evidence was not reliable. [866 A] (6) The High Courts' attention was not drawn to the evidence of two independent witnesses who were not independent witnesses. The High Courts ' findings are based on the evidence and cannot be said to be perverse. [867 B]
6063: The appellants were manufacturers of 'Supercem Water proof Cement Paint '. They entered into an agreement with Gillanders for sale of 'Appliances ' and other allied products in their factory at Madras. The agreement provided that the selling agents would sell the goods to the appellants on a price determined by the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, New Delhi. The appellants were required to pay excise duty on the goods sold at the rate of Rs. 1.25 per litre. The appellants had also agreed to accept the price fixed by the Government. The appellants paid excise duty on goods manufactured by them. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of the said agreement. The Assistant Collector rejected the contention of the appellants and held that the assessable value was the price at which Gillands sold the goods. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the true character of the agreement was that it was an agreement for sole selling agency and not an agreement for sale. The Tribunal also referred to the expression 'a related person ' in the definition given by Sec. 4(4)(c) of the Act and held that it was abundantly clear from the conditions that the title to and the owner ship in the goods consigned to Gillandars was not to pass to them. The Tribunal further referred to the meaning of the word 'agent ' as defined in the Act and concluded that the appellants were liable to pay excise duties on the goods purchased by them. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The agreement between the parties clearly stated that the selling agent had agreed to purchase the goods at the price fixed under the agreement. The appellants did not have any right to sell the goods at a higher price than the price fixed in the agreement. [790C] (2) The appellants were not entitled to the benefits of the agreement because they were not the owners of the goods. [791A] (3) The appellants are not entitled to get the benefit of Section 5 of the Act. [792B] (4) The appellants had no right to sell goods at a lower price than the one fixed under the contract. The appellants could not be asked to pay excise revenue on the goods imported by them
3786: The appellant was appointed as a Subordinate Judge in 1935. He joined the erstwhile State of Manipur as a junior clerk in 1935. After the Government of India took over the administration of Manipur, he was served with a notice dated 30 June 1966 that he was required to retire from Government service with effect from 1 October 1966 in pursuance of the direc tions of the President in Paragraph 6 of the Government of Indi a Decision No. 23 noted below Fundamental Rule 56. The appellant did not earn good reports from superior officers. The appellant was served with notice dated 30th June 1966 that his services were terminated with effect from the date of expiry of three months from the date on which it was intended to be terminated. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of compulsory retirement and prayed for quashing the same. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The power conferred on the appointing authority is an executive power. It is a plenary power. It has been conferred upon the appropriate authority. It must be exercised bona fide and in public interest. If the exercise of power is based solely on extraneous considerations or merely on con fusion of some oblique motive it would be violative of the constitutional mandate. [701 B C] (2) The power under F.R. 56 can be exercised only if there is a validating provision giving such finality to the action taken. In the instant case, the impugned order of compulsory ret irement was passed after the Government had considered the matter in its entirety and had come to the conclusion that the appellant was not fit to continue in service. [702 D E] (3) The power to compulsorily retire a government servant is a discretionary power vested in the appropriate authority and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or mala fide. [703 G H]
891: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain properties in Ahmedabad. The assessee was a partner in a firm which had its registered office at Ahmedabad. The firm was dissolved on November 11, 1947. The assessee claimed that the income from the firm should be assessed in his hands in the status of an association of persons and not as an " association of persons ". The Income tax Officer issued notices to the legal heirs of the deceased, and after considering the objections raised by the assessee, passed orders for assessment of the income of the firm. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire estate of the deceased was inherited by the three widows as joint tenants and its income was liable to be assessed in their hands in the hands of the three widows. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the income of a Hindu undivided Hindu family was liable to tax under section 9(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the department. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the entire property of the deceased should be assessed as an association of person with regard to the income which they earned as heirs of their deceased husband. [947E] (2) The Tribunal rightly held that the shares of the three wives were definite and determinable and section 9(4) was applicable. [948F] (3) The Tribunal has correctly held that the three wifes were separate entities. The fact that the three widows were separate entities does not make them separate entities. [949A] (4) The Tribunal is correct in holding that in the case of a Hindu Undivided Family, the income from property must be assessed in the hands or in the hands and under the personal law of the individual concerned. [950B]
4967: The respondent company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling coal. It had been levying cess for the year 1958 59 a sum of Rs 42,073.00, which amount was entered in its profit and loss account as miscellaneous income. The respondent company claimed exemption from the assessment of cess in respect of the sale price of coal received by it for the year 1959 60 a sum of money equivalent to the cost of collection of the cess levied under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880. The respondent contended that the cess levied was not contrary to the provisions of the Bengal Cess (Amendment) Act, 1930, and that the cess was not liable to be assessed as such. Held: (i) The cess levied is not contrary to any provision of the Bengal Act and the rules of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941, and the rules made thereunder. (ii)The cess levied is neither unreasonable nor excessive. The cess levied was neither unreasonable nor unjustified. [355 D] (iii)The cess imposed is not in excess of the net profits earned by the colliery but is in excess of what is actually spent by the collieries. The cess is not unreasonable or excessive. [356 B C] (iv)The cess is not exigible to tax. The cess cannot be said to be unreasonable merely because the cess has been levied for some other purpose. [357 E] (v)The cess being a levy of a special character, it is not open to the authorities to impose it without any basis whatsoever. [358 F] (vi)In the present case, the cess levied is nothing more than a fee. The cess was not exigible as a component of the gross receipts of the colliery. [359 A B]
1135: The respondent, a State Government Company, was carrying on the business of mining coal. In 1944, the respondent issued notices to the appellants calling upon them to pay coal tax for the coal manufactured at the mines sold by rail or sold otherwise than for export by rail within the jurisdiction of the original Independent Mining Board for the area in question. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to continue the levy and recover the tax in question. They also claimed that the tax should be levied on coal as it was being produced from the coal mine. The respondent contended that the appellants ' claims were barred by res judicata by reason of the earlier decision of this Court in the case of Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd., and that the appellants had no locus standi to file these petitions. Held, that the appellants could not maintain the petition under article 32 of the Constitution because the appellants did not have any right to claim the benefit of the decision of this court in the case referred to above. The appellants had no right to claim exemption from payment of tax in respect of coal which was being produced outside the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellants were not entitled to claim exemption in respect of the coal which was produced outside the territory of India. The appellants could not claim exemption in view of the decision in the case. The appellants having failed to establish that they were not entitled either to exemption or to claim exemption, the High Court rightly refused to grant relief to the appellants.

6051: The assessee is a co operative society constituted under the Cooperative Societies ACt. The assessee owns a ginning and pressing factory to cater to the needs of its members. For rendering the services of ginning and plucking, ginns and presses the assessee charged the members a certain amount by way of ginning charges. In the course of assessment for the assessment years 1961 62 to 1963 64 the assessee claimed that the receipts from the ginning and press activities were exempt under section 81(i)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 as it stood prior to its amendment on 1st April, 1968. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the orders of the Income tax Officer. In second appeal the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that having regard to the circumstance that the receipts were from members only, that there was a general market for ginning and selling cotton with the aid of power, and even if those activities were regarded as an integral part of the marketing activity, they would not come within the category of exempted activities in view of the proviso to section 81(1)(c). The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing cotton and ginnas and that the receipts could be treated as income of the assessee 's business. HELD: (1) The assessee carried on ginning and filing cotton with the help of power. It had no control over the working of the cotton. The assessee was not engaged in the manufacture or production of cotton. The cotton was manufactured out of ginning, pressing, cotton seeding and ginning. There was no evidence to show that the cotton was sold to the outside world. [766 D E] (2) The assessee was a co operative Society registered under the Co operative Societies ACt, and the assessee was a member of the Society. The assessee had been carrying on the business of selling cotton and ginning and processing cotton. The profits and gains of the business were exempt under Section 81(i) (c) of Income Tax Act. 6421: The appellants were recruited as Assistant Engineers in the Bihar Engineering Service, Class II. In the new set up, the cadre of District Engineers was created by the erstwhile State Boards under the 1948 Rules. The re cruitment and conditions of service of the said cadre were governed by the 1948 Rules which were framed under the 1948 Act. Under the 1948 Rules, the cadre was divided into two categories, namely, (i) Assistant Engineer, (ii) Executive Engineer, (iii) Assistant Engineer (iv) Executive Engineer. The cadre of Assistant Engineers was a part of the said re cruitment. The cadre was created by a notification dated February 18, 1977. The re gular cadre of District Engineer was created under the 1948 Rule. The re spondents were appointed as Assistant Engineers on ad hoc basis for a period of six months from January 1, 1973 to March 31, 1974. On the other hand, the cadre created by the 1948 Rule was not disturbed. The respondents challenged the merger order before the Patna High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The re fixation of cadre of District Enginee r is not arbitrary or unreasonable. [880C] 2. The restructuring of the cadres has been done with the object of providing better career opportunities to the employees. The re re fixation of the cadre of the District Engineer is not arbitrary nor it can be said to be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [881D E] 3. The re designated cadre of District Engineering Officers is a part of a re constituting the cadre of Executive Engineers of Public Works Department. The re designation of District Engineer is a part and parcel of the re constituting the cadres of Executive Engineers. The re designations are made on the basis of the cadre strength of the respective cadres. [882F G] 4. The redesignation of District Engineer as Assistant Engineer is not based on any intelligible differentia but on the basis that the cadre of Assistant Engineer is a separate cadre. [883A C] 5. The re-designated District Engineer is an entirely new cadre. The re scale of District Engineer has been introduced by the 1948 Act and the
6116: The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of the property mortgaged to him by the respondent, filed a suit for redemption on 28.12.1913, contending that he had been put into possession of the mortgaged property on 1.11.19 13 and that the sale deed contained an acknowledgment of the right of the mortgagor to redeem the property. On the other hand, for the respond ents, it is contended and this contention was accepted by the High Court that the recitals mentioned above do not serve as an acknowledgement. 1597: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a factory at Bombay and its factory is situated in Bombay. The Company was running a textile mill at Bombay. In the year 1958 it took over the business of the Company. On December 1, 1959, the Company made an application to the Industrial Court for referring certain disputes to arbitration. The Industrial Court by its award dated December 4, 1959 directed payment of gratuity to the employees at the rate of 1 month 's average wage to be calculated for the period December 1, 1 958 to November 30, 1960 to every 515 employee who had to his credit uninterrupted service of not less than five years on termination of his service, except by dismissal on account of misconduct. The Company challenged this order before the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of section 7(1) of the Act were not attracted because the Company was not in a position to pay the amount of gratuity to its employees as they were not in receipt of any gratuity. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The provision for gratuity scheme is not based on any statutory enactment but has been evolved by industrial adjudication as a step to achieve social justice. In doing so, industrial adjudication has proceeded on the basis that only a small percentage of workmen retire in any particular year and so the provision for paying gratuity to retiring workmen would ordinarily be not an unreasonable burden for the employer to be asked to bear. [519 B C] (ii)The provision for payment of gratuity scheme is also based on an assurance that the Company will be closed down and the Company will not be able to continue with its business. The provision for payment to the employees of the Company is not based upon any statutory enactment nor has been evolved for the benefit of the employees. Therefore, the provision for payment is not based merely on an assurance or assurance that the employer will be closed. [520 D E] (iii)The provision of payment of gratuity is not dependent on the existence of an agreement between the employer and the workman concerned. The provision of payment is not dependant on the existence or non existence of an existing agreement. The provision is made for the benefit and protection of the workmen. The provision does not depend on the existence
6094: The appellants are manufacturers of beer and gunnies. They were assessed to sales tax under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 on the value of packing material at the rate of 10 paise in the rupee at every point of sale other than at the point of last sale at which the goods were sold at the time of or before delivery of the goods and any other sums charged by the dealer for anything done in respect of goods sold at the rate specified therein. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the assessments made under the Andhra Pepsu General Sales Tax Rules, 1956 on the value o f packing material at 5 paise in the rupees at every point. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the consideration paid by the purchaser to the dealer consists not only of the price of the contents, namely, beer or cement but also includes the price of containers, that is the bottles and the cartons in the case of beer and the gunnies in the caseof gunnies and that the price of each of them is separately mentioned in the Schedule to the Act and therefore the turnover of the goods covered by the Schedule to that Act cannot be taxed at the hands of the dealer. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts' decision in the cases of goods mentioned in the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh Act, is correct. [308C] 2. The High court has rightly held that the consideration received by the appellant for the packing material is liable to tax at the rate applicable to the sale or purchase of the product. [309D] 3. The High courts' decision in these cases does not call for interference. [310E] 4. The High Cour ts have no power to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Tribunal. [311A] 5. The High 'Court was right in dismissing the writ petitions. [312B]
6141: The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, is engaged in the manufacture of Ossein and Gelatine. It has been granted an application for registration to establish an undertaking for the manufacture of Oceanic Oil. The application was rejected by the C.G. on 20th September, 1988. The appeal against that order was also dismissed by the Central Government on 20th Sept., 1988. In the writ petition filed by the appellant, the High Court held that the order dated 20th September 1988 was vitiated as it merely set out the bald conclusion of the officer concerned. The High Court further held that the C.C. had not given any reasons in support of its conclusions. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principles of natural justice are applicable where quasi judicial authorities exercise administrative or quasi judicial powers. [550F] 2.1. The principles which govern the making of decisions by administrative bodies are well settled. The said principles have been reiterated in several cases. [552A] 3.1. In the instant case, the C.D. has made a clear grievance about the non-supply of copies of documents at the personal hearing. The appellant has no opportunity of meeting the new case. [553B] 3.2. The appellant 's contention that the impugned order is bald, unreasoned or cryptic and definitely does not disclose any reason for rejecting the same. [554E] 3.3. The appellant had no opportunity of explaining the grounds for rejection of its application for registration. The appellant could not be heard to say that the CCC had failed to pass a reasoned order. Rule 22(a) provides that every application for registration shall be accompanied by a fee of Rs. 10/- and a copy of the application. 199: The Mysore Income tax Act, 1950, was enacted by the Indian Legislature to provide for the levy and collection of income tax and super tax in respect of any period not included in the previous year for the purposes of assessment under the Indian Income tax Act. Section 13 of the Act provided that the income tax and the super tax shall be levied and collected in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Mysore Income Tax Act, 1950 was passed by the Mysore Legislature on April 1, 1950, and it came into force from April 1, 1951. The Mysore Act was repealed by the Indian Income Tax Act. The Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950. was passed by Parliament on April 1. 1950. The Mysore High Court held that the Mysore Act did not apply to the Mysore State and that the Mysore Income tax Ordinance, 1949, applied to the Mysore state. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Mysore Act is a law made by Parliament within the meaning of article 245(2). [539 B] The Mysore Act does not purport to regulate the levy and collect of income tax or super tax but only provides for the levy of income tax. The Mysore legislature has no power to legislate on the subject of income tax which is being lawfully levied by the Government of Mysore after the commencement of the Constitution until provision to the contrary is made by Parliament by law. [540 C D] The Mysore Income 'tax Act, 1950 is a law relating to income tax and is not an independent law. It is not a law relating exclusively to income tax. It is a law imposing a charge on income. [541 E] The Mysore High Courts decision in [The State of Mysore vs The State of Mysore], ; , followed.

On a proper construction of Rule 125A of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, the order taking over the management of the Sugar Mills under the said rule was invalid as on the date of the order the Sugar Mili was closed and the appellant had no intention of re opening the same. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Mill had ceased to be an undertaking within the meaning of Rule 125 A and the order passed under Rule 125A must be held to have been passed at the time when the Mill was lying closed and the Mill had not ceased to be engaged in production, generation, supply, distribution or provision of water, transport, fuel, light, electricity or other power or any other thing or service which is notified by the Government as essential to the life of the community, because the Mill had been closed with intent of not reopening the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Mill was not an undertaking within section 2(g) of the Act. The Mill could not be said to have been closed down because the Mill was not working properly. The Mill has been running its own business for more then 20 years. [538D E] 3.2 The Mill was entitled to take over the management and control of the affairs of the Mill from the date of its closure. The Mill cannot be said to carry on the business of running its business without the permission of the Central Government. 4302: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain shares in Mitra Prakashan Pvt. Ltd., and was also a benamidar thereof. In Maya Press Pvt. Ltd. 's case (supra) the question for determination was whether the shares allotted to the wife of the deceased as his nominee or as benami were, as from the commencement of the holding of the deceased, property which passed on his death. The High Court answered both the questions against the accountable person and in favour of the Controller of Estate Duty. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court erred in answering the two questions against the accountsable person and the Controller of Estates. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the two sections are mutually exclusive and they have independent fields of operation. The High Courts had no power to decide questions of law arising out of the decisions of the courts below. [801 G] The High Court rightly held that the two provisions were mutually exclusive and could not be regarded as subject to such refinement. [802 A B] The High Courts were wrong in holding that there was no difference between the two sections. [803 C D]

At a meeting held on May 25, 1946, the board of directors of the Company allotted shares to Goverjabai, and 1000 shares to Jivanbai, against three separate applications for shares signed by them. In view of section 277(1) Of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, the company was unable to carry on business unless the subscribed capital was not less than half the authorised capital. In order to comply with the requirements of section 276(2), the directors decided that they or their nominees would subscribe for a large number of shares. [881D] (iii) The directors have acted in accordance with law and there is no reason to interfere with the decision taken by the directors. 894: The respondent, a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the Punjab Legislative Council, filed an election petition in the High Court of Punjab under section 81(1) (c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, challenging the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(3) of the Act. The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of sections 117 and 117 were not complied with. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : The order dismissing the petition was wrong because the terms of section 117 did not apply to it as there was no appeal provided against it. Section 117 does not provide that an appeal lay to the High Court. It is only when an appeal lies to the Supreme Court that the order of the High Court can be challenged. [520 B C] The order of the Tribunal dismissing the petition must be set aside. The order of dismissal passed by the Tribunal was not made under section 98 but was made under section 90(3). The order of rejection of the petition was made under sections 117 and 118 of the Act and the order of dismissal was not made in accordance with section 81. [521 D E]
6373: The appellant along with two others were convicted for murdering Kumari Mangala in furtherance of their common intention and causing disappearance of evidence of the offence. They were sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life under the first count and to pay a fine of Rs.2,500 each with a default clause and directed both the substantive sentences to run concurrently. The High Court confirmed the conviction of all the convicts but reduced the sentence to seven years rigorous imprisonment. The State appealed against the said order of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the High Court enjoys the power of revision under section 397 read with Section 401 Cr. P.C. subject to the provisos (1) and (2) to Section 386(c) of the Code. [780B] 1.2 The High Court enjoy the power of enhancement of sentence under Section 377 Cr. P C. [781A B] 1.3 The High Court exercises its revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 read with Sec. 401 Cr.P.C. and not suo motu or on an application by any person aggrieved by the same. [782D E] 1.4 Under Section 377(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, the State Government in any case of conviction on a trial held by any Court other than the High Court is empowered to direct the public prosecutor to present an appeal to the High Court against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy. However, the High court notwithstanding of the exer cise of its powers under the appellate jurisdiction under Section 37 Cr. P., the High Court although has inherent power to enhance the sentence, it must be exercised sparingly and only when there is some prima facie case established against the accused. [783E F] Nadir Khan vs The State, [1975] 2 SCC 406, referred to.
1049: The petitioners were carrying on the business of slaughtering animals in Uttar Pradesh. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The High Court held that the Act was not applicable to the petitioners as they had been carrying on the trade or business of slaughtered animals within the State of Uttar Pradesh, and that the Act did not apply to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Act applied only to those persons who carried on the business and not to others who carried on their business. HELD: (1) The Act does not apply to the petitioners. It is not necessary that the person carrying on the activity should be a citizen of India. [857 C] (2) The Act applies to all persons carrying on the same business. Section 3 of the Act provides for imposing disproportionate restrictions on the right of the petitioners. The Act does no more than prescribe the maximum limit of slaughter and the maximum period of slaughter has been prescribed by the Act. The Act is intended to regulate the slaughter of animals and to provide for the regulation of the slaughter of such animals. The Act also prescribes the maximum limit which may be imposed by the Government. The Act therefore cannot apply to the petitioner. [858 E F] (3) The Act is not applicable to a person carrying on a business or profession. The Act applies only to persons carrying on a trade or business. [859 A B] (4) The Act makes no distinction between a person carrying out a business and a person carrying any other business. The Act deals with the subject matter of the business of the petitioner. The Act lays down the maximum limit for slaughter of animals. The maximum limit is fixed by the Act itself. The Act thus provides for the regulation and control of the slaughter and the slaughter of bulls and bullocks. The Act provides for the imposition of reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the section. [860 D E]
1882: The appellant was convicted in Sessions Trial No. 35 of 1961 by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Ujjain for offences under section 467 read with section 471 and section 477A I.P.C. He was sentenced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment under section 409 I.P,.C. by Shri Dube, First Additional Sessions Judge. Ujjain, on July 20, 1963. The sentences were directed to run concurrently with the sentence imposed in the other case. In the fourth appeal, the High Court held that the various acts of criminal breach of trust committed by the appellant in the four cases were not so simple as to constitute a distinct offence under section 409 IPC and a sentence of four years' rigorous imprisonment could be considered excessive. In the fifth appeal, the appellant was sentenced to 3 years ' rigorous imprisonments. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The convictions of the appellant in these two cases are not illegal because they do not fall within the scope of section 222 Cr. P. C. [360 D E] (2) The appellant was tried in four cases for committing criminal breach of the trust. The charge against him was one of misappropriation of the amount entrusted to him in the first two cases. The trial of the other two cases was completed in the third case. The sentences awarded in the third and fourth cases were directed to be run concurrently with each of them. [306 B C] (3) The appellant had been rightly convicted for the offence under section 467 I.P.,C. and he was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. [305 A B]

On 1st October, 1957, the respondent opted for the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of Government with effect from 1st October 1957. In the year 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promotion Regulations in the exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948. The Single Judge who heard the petition dismissed it and the Division Bench allowed the appeal. It is also not possible to assume that the allottees arc exempted from passing S.A..S. Examination. The only reason therefore on which the order of promotion was challenged by the respondent was that the respondent was exempted from passing that examination. [820 B C] 2.2. There is nothing in the Regulation or the Resolution

2301: The appellants were the owners of a plot of land in the State of Andhra Pradesh. On the question whether the acquisition proceedings were mala fide and in fraud of the Act and whether the Government was entitled to an injunction against the Government taking possession of the land, HELD : (1) The notification under sec. 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was issued on November 15, 1956 and the notification under sec 4 was issued on December 22, 1957. The Government had not made any declaration under sec.6 of the Act within the prescribed period. The notification under section 6 was issued only after the amendment of sec. 6 by Act 38 of 1923. [683 F] (2) The Government could not be said to have satisfied itself that the land was needed for a public purpose or for a company. It is not necessary that the Government should make a declaration before it can take possession of the property. [684 A B] (3) The Government has no power to issue a notification under secs. 4 and 6 of the Act without making a declaration. The Government cannot go behind the notification and issue a notification. [685 C D] (4) The Government must be satisfied with respect to the purpose for which the land is required and the need for the acquisition. If the Government does not satisfy the requirements of the statute, the notification would be void. [686 E]
4878: The assessee was a company in liquidation. In the assessment year, 1960 60, the Income tax Officer took over the assets and liabilities of the company on the ground that the company had gone into liquidation and that the amount of Rs. 1,00,000 which was paid up share capital was not liable to be deducted from its profits under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but the Tribunal held that the amount paid up share Capital was not liable for deduction under section 10 (2)(x) of the Act. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the revenue. Dismissing the appeal by the Revenue, HELD: The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that after a company has gone into liquidation there cannot be any amount that can be distinctly designated as paid up sharecapital of the company or as 'reserve ' with respect to which the capital of the company is to be worked out as provided in Second Schedule to the Act for calculation of the 'standard deduction' under section 10 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. [675 B C]
5825: The respondents were charged with the offence of murdering Gulam Rabbani and injure others. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and sentenced them to death. The High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the charge framed against the respondents was not in accordance with law; (2) the judgment of the High Court was vitiated because it failed to consider the evidence adduced by the prosecution in support of its findings; (3) the judgment was vitiated because the High Court had not considered the evidence separately under different heads of charges framed against each of the accused persons; (4) the judgment did not discuss the evidence separately as required by section 340 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; (5) the judgment had not discussed the evidence separately and (6) the judgment could not be said to have dealt with the evidence separately. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment of the trial court cannot be sustained. [874B] 2. The judgment does not deal with the evidence independently. It is a rolled up one. It is, therefore, clear that while arriving at the aforesaid finding, the learned trial Judge has not discussed about the common object or the unlawful assembly being to murder Gulam Rabani and injuring others. [875A B] 3. The judgment is vitiated because it fails to consider the relevant evidence and the conclusions drawn therefrom. [876E] 4. The judgment cannot be sustained because the High court has not considered the entire evidence in detail. [877F] 5. The judgment, therefore, cannot be sustained and is set aside. [878G]
3872: The appellant was a tenant of the disputed lands in accordance with the Bhopal Land Revenue Act, 1932. He became an occupancy tenant under section 185(1)(i) (iv)(b). On his coming into force of the Act of 1932, he became a Bhumiswami under clause (c) of section 158 and the respondent became an occupancy tenants under section 185 (1)(i)(iv)(b) of the Act. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that he was not an occupant within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Bhopal Act of 1932 and that he was entitled to conferment of Bhumiswary rights on him under section 490 of the Bhopal Land Reforms Act, 1952. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it. In appeal by certificate, HELD: 1. The appellant was an occupant within meaning of section2(15) and the respondent was a sub tenant under section 184 of the Bhopal Tenancy Act, 1932 and was therefore entitled to conferment under section 491 of the Bhopal. [584C] 2. The appellant could not be said to have been an occupant within section 2(14) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959. The respondent was a tenant under the Bhopal Act and was therefore not entitled to conferment on him under the Bhopal Land Reform Act, 1952, as he was not a Shikmi under the Bhopal Tenancy law. [585D E] 3. The respondent had no right to the land in question. The respondent could not claim any right to the grant of Bhumiswami rights under section 185 of the Bhopal State Land Reforms Act. [586E] 4. The respondent did not dispute that if the appellant was an occupancy tenant, the first respondent would be a Shikmidar under section 185 and the respondent would be entitled to conferment the Bhumiswami rights. [587F]
5255: The appellant was a public servant and was holding a post in the State of Andhra Pradesh. He filed a complaint against him alleging that he had committed offences under sections 409, 465, 468, 471, 477A, 120B, 201, 420, 467, 468, 479, 472, 473, 474, 476, 477, 478, 479 and 470 of the Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process to the appellant. The appellant raised objection before the Metropolitan Magistrate that the sanction for prosecution was not necessary as the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Magistrate rejected the said objection and held that section 197 is attracted only when a public servant is not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government. The appellant challenged the order of the Magistrate before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Magistrate who can remove the appellant from service by virtue of regulation No. 1 of the Regulations framed under the Act has no power to remove the appellant except by or with sanction of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The regulations framed by the Central Government are not statutory regulations nor do they confer any power on the Central Government to remove the public servant from his office. [471C] 2. Section 197 of the Cr. P. C. does not apply to the facts of the present case. It is not disputed that the appellant was a Public servant. He was holding a civil post. He was not holding a post where he could not be removed from service except by or without the sanction of Government. Therefore, the view taken by the Courts below is not correct. [472D E] 3. The appellant cannot be removed from his service by merely giving notice to the Government. [473E]
418: The respondent was charged with having committed an offence under section 7 of the East Punjab Essential Services (Maintenance) Act, 1947. He pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The Magistrate convicted him and sentenced him to 15 days ' rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the conviction was bad because the respondent had been absent from duty as a foot constable in the Police Lines, Dharamsala, from 9 p.m. to 1 1 p.m., and, secondly, that on the same date he had refused to obey the lawful orders given by a superior officer who had assigned him duty as such foot constable. Held, that the conviction could be set aside only if the prosecution evidence showed that the respondent had disobeyed the lawful orders of his superior officer. The fact that the respondent did not return to duty after the expiry of the period of absence would not make the respondent liable for the offence. The respondent was not entitled to any relief. The order of acquittal passed against him was proper and no interference was called for.
1886: The appellant company was a private limited company and the Government of India acquired land belonging to it under the Defence of India Rules. The Government of India, however, took possession of the land in pursuance of an order made by the Government on February 18, 1944. The land was divided into plots by the Government during the war and the appellant entered into contracts with the Government for the purchase of plots from them. The Government paid Rs. 202/ by way of earnest money. The appellant contended that the contract was not discharged because of the fact that its performance was rendered unlawful as a result of the requisitioning orders made by the government which were sought to be raised before this Court in that case. Held, that the contract could not be said to have been discharged because of its being rendered unlawful either for a determinate period of time or for an indeterminate period of Time. The contract was one which was made by the State Government and the Government had no power to terminate it at any time. The contract did not come within the mischief of section 9 of the Indian Contract Act. The contract, therefore, was not a contract of service but a contract for the purpose of carrying out the terms of the contract.
4291: The assessee was a firm of M/s. The original assessment for the assessment year 1955 46 was completed long back, but it seems that some information was received by the Income Tax Officer that a sum of Rs. 1,07,350 was remitted by two telegraphic transfers through Punjab National Bank Limited and the Income Tax Department. This letter of the Manager of the Punjab National Bank Ltd., addressed to the assessee made inquiries about this remittance and did not disclose it to the assessee nor did he make any reference to it in the letters dated 24th February 1955 and 4th March 1955. On these facts the Income Tax officer issued notice under section 34(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, calling upon the assessee to show cause why an order should not be passed against him on the basis of the said letter. The assessee replied to the notice stating that the letter had been written by him without disclosing the fact that the amount was remitted by him to the bank and that the receipt thereof was not supported by any evidence. The Income Tax Officer held that the letter was not genuine and that the income from the account of the assessee was assessable to tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax authorities. In appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the Income Tax Officers were justified in holding that the letter of the manager of the Punjab Nirmal Bank Ltd. was a forged one and that the letter must be treated as having been written by the assessee with his own knowledge and belief. Held: (i) The letter of the Bank cannot be regarded as a letter of authority by the assessee to the Bank. It is only when the Bank has acted honestly and bona fide in carrying out its statutory obligations that the letter can be regarded as an instrument of trust or agency. [857 D] (ii)The letter of the bank cannot be regarded merely as a letter signed by the assessee. The letter must be read along with the letter of title and the letter must have been written by a person who was not authorised to do so. [858 E] (iii)The letter must be construed as a letter which was written by the appellant to the Bank and not by the assessee himself. The letter was not intended to be used as evidence of the
6761: The appellant, a manufacturer of wagons, supplied the wagon to the Railway Board. The wagons were manufactured by the appellant and were ultimately supplied to the Railway board. The railway authorities charged the price of the wagon charged by the appellant from the Railway Board without charging any price. The appellant challenged the show cause notices by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Calcutta High Court which was heard by a learned Single Judge who allowed the writ petition and quashed the demand raised by the central excise authorities. The Division Bench allowed the appeal in the following words: "The value of the wagons as a whole has not been mentioned in the agreement and we feel that the cost of normal price should include cost of construction and furthermore, when sale is the charge and the same under charging section of the said Act would mean actual price of the goods viz. wagon as a whole, so the value of the goods cannot be calculated after adding back the price of components supplied free of cost by the Railway Board." The appellant appealed against the judgment of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 4(1)(a) of the , does not apply in this case because the cost of the wago as a whole had not been mentioned therein. [962B] 2. The cost of the goods as a whole means actual price of goods viz. the wagon as part of the relevant and necessary assessable value under section 4 of the , as the manufacturing cost of a complete wagon cannot be conceived of without taking into account or consideration the cost of free supply items. [963C D] 3. The cost for the wagon is not taken into consideration in fixing the price of wagons sold by the appellant. The cost is also not taken into account in determining the assessable value under Section 4 of the Act. [964E F] 4. The cost includes cost of construction, and furthermore it is not possible to say that the cost will include cost of installation and commissioning of the wags. [965A B] 5. The cost can include cost of maintenance of the wagos and other materials used in the manufacture of the wagON. [966D] 6. The cost must
4107: The appellant was a displaced person in respect of certain house property. He filed an application under section 16(1) of the Displaced Persons Act, 1950 for restoration of the house to him. The Central Government passed an order on 18 3 1957 restoring the house to the appellant. On 27 10 1956 the Central Government ordered that it had revised its order dated 11 11 1960 and the petitioner was entitled to compensation only under section 20A of the Act. The appellant filed an application before the Custodian General under section 16 of the Act for restoration of his house. The Custodian General rejected the application holding that the house was not evacuee property as defined by section 2(2) of the Act and that the house could be restored to the appellant subject to payment of compensation. The appellant came to know later that the Central Government had revised its earlier order dated 11 10 1960 and the petition was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Central Government having reviewed its earlier order, the order dated 11 12 1960 was illegal; (ii) the Central Govt. had no power to review its earlier order and (iii) the order dated 18 3 1957 was invalid because the Central Government did not have the power to review the earlier order. HELD : (i) The Central Government had power to revise its earlier order. The Central Govt. has power to review it if it is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do in the public interest. [997 E] (ii) The Central Govt.'s power to review an earlier order is not limited to cases where the previous order is either erroneous or prejudicial to some party. It can review the earlier decision even without the previous order being pointed out to the Central Government. [996 F G] (iii) The Central Govern ment cannot review its earlier decision unless it is shown that there is a mistake apparent from the record. [995 D] (iv) The Central Gov ernment has no power to revise the earlier order and the Central Govt., in exercise of its power under section 20 A of the Act, can review its earlier orders. 2018: The respondents filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that they were the legal heirs of Raj Kaur and that they had been in continuous possession of the property from before. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the suit was governed by article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908, as held by the High Court, the suit was within time. HELD : (i) Article 142 of the Limitation act is not applicable to suits under article 134 of the Limitation. Article 144 provides that where a person suing as a pauper has obtained a decree against his father or other family member, the period of limitation shall be computed according to the law applicable to the suit. [851 C] (ii) Article 142 applies only when the right to sue accrues. It does not apply when the right is claimed by the plaintiff himself. [852 D] (iii) Article 142 is not applicable because the suit was instituted after the death of the appellant 's father. The suit was filed by the respondent on the basis of a will executed by her father. The will was probated and the appellant could not have any grievance if he had any grievance with the will. [853 E] (iv) Article 142 does not apply to suits under articles 134 and 134 of the Act. Article 144 applies only when a person sues in a civil court and the suit is based on title. [854 F] (v) Article 142 deals with cases where the person suing is a pauer, and not a party to the suit, and the suit must therefore be regarded as barred by time. [855 G]
4192: The appellant was declared as an evacuee and the Custodian of Evacuee Property, Deoria. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice under section 7 and the subsequent proceedings based on it. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (1) The notice issued by the Assistant Custodian General, Evacuee Property, U.P., to the appellant and his brother Bashir Ahmad is invalid. [880 E] (2) The notice does not contain any particulars about the property which the appellant claims to be evacuee property. It merely states that the information in possession of the Custodian is that they are evacuees under clause (iii) of section 2(d). The notice does mention only what the form contains and that is as follows: " Acquisition of any rights to interest in or benefit from any evacuee or abandoned property in Pakistan, otherwise than by way of purchase or exchange." [881 F G] (3) The notice in question appears to be merely a copy of the prescribed form without particulars. The notice in this case appears to be simply a copy of a form without particulars but there is no reason why the notice should have been issued more than one month before the date of the notice. [881 H; 892 A B] (4) The notice is not a mere copy of the form but is a copy of all the material facts necessary for the decision of the case. [882 D E] (5) The notice must be read as a whole and not in isolation. If the notice is read as a composite notice it would be clear that the notice is intended to be a complete one. The notice must also state that the information required by the notice is that the person claiming to be an evacuee has been declared as evacueee. [883 C D] (6) The notice cannot be construed as a mere reproduction of the original form. The notice may be vague or indefinite but the notice must be such as to enable the person making the statement to know the nature of the information he had given.
