4919: The petitioners in these petitions filed under Article 32 of the Constitution are various companies engaged in the business of editing, printing and publishing newspapers, periodicals, magazines etc. Some of them are trusts or other kinds of establishments carrying on the same kind of business. The petitioners contended that the imposition of customs duty on news print which had enjoyed total exemption from its payment till March 1, 1981, as the foreign exchange position was quite comfortable, was arbitrary and discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. It was also contended that there was no need to impose customs duty on newspaper circulating at the rate of 15% ad valorem. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners have a fundamental right to carry on their trade and business guaranteed by article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and they cannot be denied the same except according to procedure established by law. [825C] 2. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief. [826D] 3. The petitioners do not fall within the category of persons who can claim the benefit of the exception. They are not entitled for the benefit of section 5 of the Act. [827E] 4. The petitioners cannot claim the benefit under section 5 of Act 51 of 1975. [828F] 5. Section 5 of the is not ultra vires Article 14 of the constitution. [829A] 6. The petitioners will be entitled to the benefit of Section 5 of Act 52 of 1962. [830B]
1604: The appellant, who was the son of his brother, executed a will on January 14, 1895 in favour of his mother. Subbarao died on May 5, having executed a will in favour of the appellant. Subbaratha, the daughter of his brother Pitchayya, took only 4 acres of land and the rest of the property being divided between the four sons by metes and bounds. Subbarama Rao, the daughter, filed a suit for partition claiming that the properties were joint family properties and that the appellant had no right to claim partition. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Will was not proved as required under section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and that the Will did not constitute a partition in status. On appeal, the High Court held that the Will could not be said to have been executed by Subbaraopa Rao, father of the appellant, and that it was not proved that Subbaraosa Rao had signed the Will in his presence or that he had read over the contents of the Will to Subba Rao. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question whether the recitals in the will themselves constituted a partition in Status could not be allowed to be raised as that point was raised only for the first time in the High Court. The question whether Subbaraoca Rao had knowledge of the execution of the will was a mixed question of law and fact which could be decided only after evidence was adduced before the trial court. [901 E F] (2) The question about the validity of the will would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the will is found to be genuine and duly executed, then the question of its validity would arise. If the testator has given his intention to divide by metes, and bounds, then the intention of the testator would be to divide by means of a registered instrument. [902 C D] (3) The question as to whether the recital in the will itself constitutes a partition in a status could not be permitted to be raised at all. [903 A B] (4) The question regarding the validity of a will can be raised only during the course of trial

951: The appellants were assessed to income tax and super tax on the total income of their respective assessees. They filed a return under the Income Tax Act showing a net profit of Rs. 4,78,5945 0 as assessable income, and they were assessed to tax and supertax by the Income Tax Officer on that return. The Income Tax Officer held that the net profit was Rs. 1,35,736 8 0 and that the tax payable was Rs. 2,00,000. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer but the High Court in appeal set aside the order of assessment and remanded the case for fresh disposal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Income Tax authorities had no power to assess or reassess the income of the appellants without issuing notice to them; (ii) the Income tax Officer could not proceed to assess or reassessment the income of a person who was not a citizen of India; (iii) the Income-tax Officer could not initiate proceedings against the appellants without giving them an opportunity of being heard; (iv) the Income 'tax Officer could only proceed to assess the income of an assessee if he was a citizen of Indian State; (v) the Income, tax Officer could only assess the income which was disclosed by the appellant before him and not the income which had escaped assessment; and (vi) the Income. tax Officer could take action only after the appellant had been given an opportunity of hearing. If the Income tax officer is satisfied that there has been a failure to comply with the requirements of section 5(2) of the Act, then the Income tax authority must proceed to assess and reassess the appellant. [447 C D] (ii) The Income Tax Officers are invested with the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure to investigate into matters which fall within their jurisdiction. The Income tax Officers are not entitled to act as a court of appeal over the orders passed by the Income tax Officers. [448 E F] (iii) The Income-tax Officers are not bound to follow the procedure laid
3187: The State of Uttar Pradesh enacted the Uttar Pradesh Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1963. Section 68D(2) of the Act provided that no person other than the State Government or a local authority shall be entitled to operate any motor vehicle on any inter state route except under and in accordance with the conditions of a permit granted by the Regional Transport Authority of the State in which such route is included. The State Government issued a notification dated March 16, 1964 for the purpose of granting permits to private operators including those who had been granted permits by the Regional Tractor Transport Authorities of Rajasthan. The appellants, who were operating their stage carriages on inter state routes, challenged the validity of the scheme on the ground that it was ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature. The High Court held that the scheme was not sanctioned by the State Government and the State Government could not issue a notification under section 68D(1) of the , as the State Government had no power to issue a notification in respect of an inter state route. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme was approved by the State Transport Authority of Rajasthan and the State Transport Appellate Tribunal. The State Transport Appellate Committee had no power under section 68C of the Act to issue a direction to the Regional Transport Authorities of the State of Rajasthan to grant permits to private operator including the appellants. [174 D E] (ii) The State Government had the power to issue directions under section 68F(2). The State Government could issue such directions only if it was satisfied that the scheme involved a substantial public interest. [175 C] (iii) The State Transport Undertaking had no power or jurisdiction to issue a circular or a direction to a private operator to ply his stage carriage on inter state route unless the scheme itself was approved by a State Government. The State Road Transport Corporation had no power, nor could it issue a direction under section 68E(2) to the private operator to operate his stage carriage service on inter state portion of inter state route without the approval of the State Government. [176 B C]

T.A. had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals under section 64(a) and (3) of the , and dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The R. T..A. had power to decide whether a proposed route should be opened or not. The RT.A.'s decision was final and could not be reviewed under section 47(3). [424 B] The R. C. T. A. had no power to decide the question as to whether a proposed scheme should be opened. The Rt. R.A. is entitled to decide whether the proposed route should have been opened or not, and the RT. A. cannot review its decision under section 47 (3), if it chooses to do so. [425 E F]

The Collector of Central Excises, Bombay, however, rejected the contention of the appellant that the products are 'containments ' falling under Entry 17(4), as 'article of paper and paper Board ' and not under Item 17, as 'ar Articles of paper and Paper Board '. 1506: The appellants were charged under section 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed the murder of one Gurcharan Singh. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons but convicted them of the offence under section 302 read with section 149 and sentenced each of them to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the charge under section 302 had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt and so, according to him, the prosecution case under section 148 had not been established beyond a reasonable suspicion. HELD : (i) It is well settled that in a criminal proceeding, the onus of proving the guilt of an accused person rests heavily upon the prosecution. But if the prosecution fails to prove its case beyond a reasonable shadow of doubt, the failure of the prosecution to discharge the burden cast on it under section 106 of the Evidence Act may be held to have vitiated the conviction. [880 B C] (ii)The evidence of the eye witnesses examined by the prosecution has to be scrutinised carefully and independently without being influenced by any extraneous consideration. If the prosecution succeeds in establishing its case beyond reasonable doubt, the accused cannot escape penalty merely because the prosecution fails in proving its case beyond the reasonable doubt. [881 D E] (iii)It is well settled by several decisions of this Court that where the prosecution fails both in proving the guilt as well as the evidence adduced in support of the same, the accused can be convicted solely on the basis of such proof. [882 F] (iv)In a criminal proceeding the standard of proof required is that of preponderance of probabilities and not proof beyond reasonable doubt. The standard of proof so requires only in a civil suit. [883 G H; 894 A] (v)If the prosecution fails or fails to establish its case beyond any reasonable doubt, and the accused is acquitted, the courts will usually take a different view. [884 B C]
3351: The respondent was a dealer in foreign goods. He purchased the goods from Ram Avtar and gave them to him on the following day. The goods were sent by Ram Avtars to Ram Avtari for delivery at Ram Avtary. Ram Avtaria, who was the appellant before the High Court, was arrested by the police after he had been apprehended. The respondent filed a revision petition against his order of arrest which was allowed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in quashing the charges against the respondent on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him. HELD: (1) There is no cogent ground for interfering with the judgment of the High Court in a revision petition under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The report lodged by Ram Arota was not only an informatory report but also a statement of facts contained therein. It was therefore not necessary for the High Court to examine the correctness or otherwise of the report. [279 C D] (2) The High Court was right in its view that the charge against the respondent was not proved. [280 E] (3) The High court was wrong in quashing the charge against him. The High Court could have taken into consideration all the circumstances of the case including the fact that the respondent was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought washer plates in a taxi. The evidence of Ram Avtarwala was not sufficient to prove that the respondent had knowledge of the fact that he was present along With Shanker Lal. [281 F H]
7070: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission issued a notification on May 28, 1984 inviting applications for the posts of munsifs and requested the Government to initiate appropriate steps for selection of candidates. The Commission sent three select lists, one containing twenty candidates, the other containing three scheduled castes candidates and a waiting list of ten candidates. The Government did not approve of the names in view of a number of vacancies and the waiting list was kept pending without being approved as required by Rule 39 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Services (Judicial) Recruitment Rules, 1967. On March 11, 1985 the High Court intimated the Government that the Government had decided to constitute a fresh selection committee for selecting candidates. The government wrote to the public service commission on December 27, 1986 requesting the Government to recommend names in order of merit. The Government, however, declined to approve the names in spite of the fact that the names of twenty candidates were included in the select list. The Government filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the selection process. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Government could not alter or temper with the order of merit determined by the commission but it was open to the government to stop at a particular point where it feels that a particular candidate is not likely to be selected. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The Government cannot alter or tempered with the order passed by the High Court. [880C] 1.2. The Government has been empowered under Rule 39 of Jammu and Kashmir Judicial Service Recruitment Rules, 1987 to approve and publish the list recommended by the Public Service Commission. The Government can do so only after approval of the list. [881D E] 1.3. The Government may have to consider the matter afresh from the point of view of the candidates who are eligible for appointment as munsiffs. But the Government cannot change or modify the list already prepared by the Public service commission. [882E F] 1.4. The Government should not interfere with the recommendations made by the Public services commission. [887F] 1.5. The Government must take into consideration the recommendation made by the High court while approving the list submitted by the Public Services Commission. [886G
2362: The respondent was a tenant of the appellant under a rent note executed on February 27, 1947. He fell into arrears of payment of rent and the tenancy was to be for a period of one year from 22nd February, 1947. On April 18, 1947, the respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on March 15, 1951. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (i) the respondent had disputed the municipal taxes and permitted increases; (ii) the conditions under section 12(3)(a) were not present; (iii) the appellant had no right to continue as a tenant under the respondent; and (iv) the respondent was entitled to protection of the Act. HELD: (1) Section 12(3) (a) of the Transfer of Property Act is applicable only if there is a dispute as to the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act. The condition necessary for the applicability of section 12(2) (a), therefore, is not satisfied. [880 E] (2) The provisions of section 12 (3) (b) are not attracted because the respondent did not dispute the municipal taxes or permitted increases. The conditions mentioned in section 12(4) (a)) are not present. [881 C D] (3) The conditions under section12(3)(b) are also not present. The conditions under sections 12(3), (a) and (b) have been fulfilled. [882 B] (4) The conditions mentioned under section 12 (4) (c) are not present in section 12 (2). [883 A B] (5) The conditions referred to in section 12 are not present when the parties entered into a compromise. The terms of the compromise are not present at the time of the compromise. [884 C] (6) The conditions of section 12 are also not satisfied. The conditions are not present, as they are not present before the Court. [885 D] (7) The conditions in section 12 do not apply where there is a question as to the standard rent or permissible increases recoverable under the Act. [886 F]

3607: The appellant was employed as a peon in the respondent 's establishment. He claimed that he had been working for more than 240 days in a year and that he had worked for more than 180 days in a calendar year. The State Government issued a notification under section 27 declaring its intention to add employment in potteries industry with an explanation to the Schedule to the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The appellant contended that the Explanation to item 22 of the Schedule to which it is not necessary to refer to articles of pottery included in the Schedule was not applicable to the industry of the appellant and that the Act was not applicable in his case. Held: (i) The Explanation indicates that potteries industries are intended to cover all possible articles of potnaras. The object of the Explanation is to enlarge the meaning of potteries Industry in any way. The object is to include articles of potment within the meaning of the Act. [901 G] (ii)The Explanation does not indicate that pottery industry includes articles of potmancy. It merely provides that the items mentioned therein are included in the definition of "potteries industry". The Explanation only clarifies that potterise industry includes articles or of potmental labour. The Explanation does not contemplate that potteris must be excluded from the definition of the word "potters" in the Act. The Explanation is intended to enlarge the scope of potterism in any way and does not exclude articles of potterious labour. [902 B C]
8: The appellant, a Hindu, was the adopted son of Gnanambal. He died on 25th April 1905 leaving behind him as his near relations, his widow and two daughters. The adoption deed recites that the appellant 's mother had given an authority to her daughter to adopt a son after the death of the testator 's wife, and that she would be the adopted son in respect of the properties mentioned therein. The appellant 's father executed a will on 13th March, 1905, bequeathing the properties to the appellant ' s wife and two daughters, who were the sons of the testator. The will recited that the properties were given to the appellant " for life time" and that he should take the children of his second daughter, and that if the children did not take the children, they would be given to the grandson of the testator "after his death". The appellant ' 's mother died on 3rd January, 1905. On the death of his mother, the appellant ' 'his mother became a widow and the properties vested in the appellant as the adopted son. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for possession of certain properties which included the properties described in paragraph 5 of the plaint. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the adoption deed was valid and that the appellant was entitled to succeed to the properties described therein. The High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the adoption deed recited that it was made under the authority of the widow 's husband and that the widow ' 's husband had no right to make any disposition of the properties after the death; (ii) the adoption was invalid because the widow ' had not taken the property after the death and (iii) the adoption having been made under the instructions of the widow, the appellant could not claim title to the properties. HELD: (i) The adoption is valid and the appellant has not acquired any interest in the properties. [866 D] (ii) The adoption was valid and the adoption was valid. [867 E] (iii) The adoption must be held to have been made under authority of the guardian of the minor child
2608: The Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Ordinance, 1962 was promulgated by the President of India on April 27, 1962. The Act came into force on December 20, 1961. The Act was passed to enable effect to be given to the International Conventions in 1949. The Act received the assent of the President on March 26, 1962. On April 27, 1963, the Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1962 was enacted and was deemed to have come into force on March 1, 1963. The Act is now extended to Goa, Daman & Diu. The Act has been amended from time to time. The Act provides for the establishment of a Commission to investigate offences committed under the Act. Section 2(a) defines "Commission" as meaning an investigation directed by law or order made by any authority empowered by law to make such investigation. Section 3 provides that the Commission shall investigate any offence alleged to have been committed by any person punishable under the Act before it was established. Section 4 provides that the commission of an act which is done by any person who is reasonably suspected of having committed an offence under the Act shall not be taken cognizance of except with the previous sanction of the Central Government. Section 5 provides that the provisions of the Act shall apply to all offences committed under this Act after the commencement of the Act. The Act, therefore, became applicable to Goa, and the Act was brought into force on January 1, 1962. In the meantime, the Goa, Daman And Diu (Administration), Ordinance, 1962, was promulgated on April 27. 1962. The Goa, Mumbai Area Development Act, 1962, came into force from December 20, 1962. By section 3 of the Act, the Act was repealed and replaced by the Goa, Bombay Area Development Act. 1962. Section 2 of the Act provided that the Act shall cease to apply to the whole of Goa, Damanand Diu and the rest of the Dadra and Nagar Haveli and the rest were to be deemed to be laws in force in Goa immediately before the appointed day. The Act thus became applicable to the Goa, Mumbai area and the rest. The Act also applied to Goa, Mumbai and the rest, but the Act was not extended to Goa. 4946: The appellant was a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926. It represents employees in the Chambal Hydel Irrigation Scheme under the Department of Chambal Project of Government of Madhya Pradesh in Gwalior Division. The Union raised three demands and served notices on the Deputy Chief Engineer, Major Project, Chambal, Bhopal. The demands were: (1) Cumulative effect of strike by the workmen; (2) Payment of dearness allowance equal to that of Central Government employees; and (3) Wages for the period of strike lasting days in the year 1966. Copies of these notices were sent to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, Indore and Secretary, Government of Madhya Bharat, the first respondent in the appeal. The State Government refused to refer the dispute to the Tribunal for adjudication. The appellant filed Miscellaneous Petition No 29/69 for a mandamus to the State Government to refer the matter to the Tribunal. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of the State Government dated 15th March, 1969. In the present appeal, it is contended by the appellant that the State Government had by refusing to refer the reference to the Tribunal gave an arbitrary and unilateral power to decide the dispute and did not pay any heed to its own decision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State has no power to refuse to refer the industrial dispute to the tribunal merely because the Government has refused to refer it. [880C] 2. The Government could have refused to refer a dispute to the Industrial Tribunal if it was satisfied that there was sufficient cause for referring the dispute. But it cannot be said that the Government had acted arbitrarily or mala fide. [881D E] 3. The Government was justified in holding that the dispute was patently frivolous and that it would be appropriate to make a reference. [882F] 4. The Government had power to decide whether a reference should be made or not. The Government can refuse to make a Reference only when it finds that there are circumstances which justify the making of the reference. If the Government finds that there is no reasonable ground for the dispute having arisen, it may decline to make a Referral Order. [883A B]
5318: The appellant, a non resident company in India, was assessed to income tax as a representative assessee of ten non resident companies. In the assessment year 1957 58, the Income Tax Officer held that the non resident companies had business connection with them and so far as the only company under Group B was concerned, the assessee was liable to be taxed as an agent of the said non resident companies under section 163 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. 2081: The appellants along with others were charged under sections 302/149, Indian Penal Code and section 307/149, I.P.C. for having committed the murder of one Sheosahay. 3944: The assessee was a registered provident fund company. It had been paying its employees the salary of its salesmen and other allowances including commission on sales in India. In the accounting year relevant to the assessment years 1963 64 and 1964 65, the assessee claimed that it should be allowed deduction under section 36(1)(iv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, as it was not a part of its gross total income. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner disallowed the claim but the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section36(1)(v). On reference, the High Court held that the expression "salary" as defined in Rule 2(h) of Part A of the Fourth Schedule to the Act includes commission paid by the assessee to its salesmen. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "salaries" as used in rule 2(h), means the amount paid or payable by the assessee as salary or wages for the services rendered by him to its employees during the previous year. [790C] (2) The definition of "salary", as given in the Explanation to section 36(i)(iv) is inclusive and not exhaustive. The expression "wages" has been defined in the said Explanation to mean all remuneration including commission whether expressed in whole rupees or in kind or partly in cash and partly in kind, and includes any sum paid to an employee to defray special expenses properly incurred by him in respect of his employment; and the word "gross" does not include commission. [795D E] (3) The expression 'salary' as used in the Explanation must be understood in the context of the definition of "wages". [796E] (4) The expression, "wages", as used in Rule 2 (h) of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Rules, 1962, cannot be construed to exclude commission paid by an employer to its salesman. [797F] (5) The expression used in the definition of 'wages ' in Rule 2 of the Second schedule to the Income tax Act, 1961, is wide enough to cover all payments made by the assessee in connection with the service rendered by it to its employees. [799G]
2337: The appellant was a member of the Bombay Medical Service Class and as such was an employee of the State Government. He was posted at the Civil Hospital, Ahmedabad and on February 18, 1950, he was in charge of the Medico Legal Section of that hospital. On March 14, 1952, the appellant made a representation to the Government praying that he should be reinstated in service. On May 6, 1950, the appellant was placed under suspension pending further orders from the date of his receipt of the memorandum. On March 16, 1952, he made a representation for reinstatement but the Government applied to the High Court for leave to appeal against the decision if the High Court and on the application being rejected, the Government applied for special leave to this Court. The appellant contended that (i) the order of dismissal was invalid because it was passed without giving him full opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed; (ii) the order was bad because it was not passed by the competent authority who had power to pass the order; (iii) the order could not be passed by the Governor or the Governor of a Province; and (iv) the order having been passed by the Chief Commissioner of Bombay, the order was invalid because the Chief Commissioner had no power to make the order. Held, that the order of the Chief Commissioner was valid. The Chief Commissioner had power to dismiss the appellant even though he was not a member of a civil service of the State. The Chief commissioner had power to suspend the appellant and to withhold his salary. The Chief Com missioner had power to revoke the order of suspension. The Chief Commisioner had power under Rule 151 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules to suspend the petitioner. The Chief Minister had power to remove the petitioner from service. The Chief Secretary had power to appoint a person to hold the post of the Chief Medical Officer. The Chief Medical Officer had power to terminate the services of the petitioner after giving him notice. The Chief Engineer had power to reduce the pay of the petitioner. In the present case, the Chief Commissioner has power to reduce his pay. The Chief Inspector had power to impose punishment upon the petitioner.
2405: The respondent brought a suit for pre emption of the land in dispute, which was sold under a sale deed dated February 6, 1942. The appellant contended that the respondent was entitled to pre emption as a shafi i jar (i.e. a house in ruins) and therefore he was entitled to the pre emption. The trial court held that there was custom of pre emption prevailing in the city of Benaras and therefore he had right to pre empt the property sold. The High Court allowed the appeal and granted a decree for pre emotion. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the custom of preemption prevailed in Mohalla Baradeo in the city and that the respondent had no right to preemect the land. HELD: The respondent was not entitled to preemotion because he was not a resident of Calcutta. The respondent was entitled only to pre emotion if he wanted to do so. [558 D]
3961: The respondent was appointed as Sub Inspector of Police in the Uttar Pradesh Police Service on January 21, 1957. He was discharged from service by an order dated January 21, 1959. On March 13, 1958, he instituted a suit for a declaration that the order dated January 20, 1956 terminating his services was illegal and void and that he continued as Sub Inspector. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order of dismissal passed against the respondent was not made by way of punishment because it was an order of termination simpliciter passed in accordance with the rules applicable to temporary government servants. [801 C] (2) The order terminating the respondent 's services had not been made by way or at least by way of penalty. It was only after the original order of discharge was quashed by the High Court that the respondent was reinstated in service. [802 D E] (3) The order was not made in the light of the allegations against the respondent concerning the woman, the conduct of the respondent constituted a motive merely for making the order and was not the foundation of the order. [803 B] (4) The order did not amount to a stigma nor did it affect the character or reputation of the respondent. [804 F] (5) The order is not made by mere reference to any act or omission of the person who gave the said order. It must be made by the authority competent to remove him from service. [881 G H] (6) The order has to be read along with the order so interpreted. If the interpretation suggested by the appellant were accepted, then the order would have to be treated as having been made by the competent authority under the rules governing the conditions of service of the respondent, and the order would be deemed to be an order of dismissal. But if the order is made by the superior authority, the order will have to be ignored. [882 A B]
40: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 147, 148 and 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 29th November, 1949, a mob of about fifty persons came on to the field armed with ballams, lathis and other weapons and that the first appellant Logendranath Jha, who was leading the mob, demanded a settlement of all outstanding disputes with the complainant and that the complainant would not allow the paddy to be removed unless the disputes were settled. The complainant alleged that the appellants had been demanding a settlement of the disputed land and that the appellants were trying to grab the paddy crop. The trial court acquitted the accused but the High Court set aside the order of acquittal. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the evidence in the case was not reliable and that the story of the prosecution was not acceptable. HELD : (1) It is well established that the evidence must be cogent and convincing and must not suffer from any infirmity. If the evidence is such as to make out an offence against the accused, the conviction can be sustained only if it is corroborated by some independent evidence. [801 B D] (2) The High Court has taken into consideration the fact that the witnesses belonged to the opposite faction and there was no reason why they should have falsely implicated the appellants. [802 C] (3) There was no reason to interfere with the judgment of the High Court. [803 A]
1848:
The appellant was granted a right to cut trees in certain demarcated areas of certain forests of the Zamindari on payment of a sum of Rs. 7,131/8/ . Under the terms of the said document the period during which the appellant was given this right to cut the trees had been to end on April 14, 1955. On September 3, 1946, the Zamindar of Simlapal in the Collectorate of Bankura entered into a contract with the appellant for the grant of the right to cut and fell trees in certain forest of the Zamindari. The appellant started cutting and felling trees in certain areas of certain forest of which he was the proprietor. The Zamindar thereupon applied to the Collector for permission to cut and remove the trees and for permission to do so under section 5(aa) of the West Bengal Private Forests Act, 1948. The Collector refused to grant such permission but the appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the terms of section 5(a) were not sufficient to provide for the vesting of the right in the land to cut and cut trees in a forest, that the words "or any other person" in cl. (i) of sub section (1) of section 5 did not include a person like the appellant who might not have any right to the trees in that area, that the word "or any person" in the context in which it occurs in cl.

(i) of section 2(2) of the Act meant only a person like a proprietor or an intermediary who may not have any rights to the trees and that the word 'or ' in cl. 4(a) of the notification issued by the Government of West Bengal did not include the appellant '; Held, that the expression "or any such person" in el. (i), as used in cl. 1 of the notification, must be read as referring to persons like the appellant whose rights are extinguished by the notification. The word "or" in cl.(ii) of sub. s. (1) means a person like an intermediary or a person referred to in cl. 2(i).
2932: The respondent was appointed as a member of the Indian Police Service on 25th January, 1937 and at the material time he was holding the substantive rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police in Bihar. In June 1962 he was posted at Ranchi. He was transferred to Patna and appointed as Special Officer, Political, General and Transport Department on July 23, 1964. On July 23, 1963 he was served with a charge sheet alleging that he had committed offences under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 120B I.P.C. The charges were enquired into by the Government and after considering the report of the Enquiry Officer, the Government decided to place him under suspension. The respondent filed his writ petition challenging the order of suspension contending that there was no prima facie case made out against him and that the order of his suspension was not proper. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order was bad because the Government did not take into consideration the nature of the allegations and circumstances of the case before placing the respondent under suspension. HELD: (i) Rule 12 of the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1954 is not applicable to the present case. It is only when an enquiry is contemplated or pending against a person who has been suspended that the Government can pass an order placing him under suspension pending the conclusion of the inquiry. [718 E] (ii) The Government could have placed the respondent under the suspension if the charges were serious enough to justify the action taken by it. But the fact that the Government took into account the nature of charges and the circumstances in which they were alleged to have been committed does not mean that the Government was not justified in placing the respondent in suspension. [719 C D] (iii) The Government cannot be said to have acted mala fide in passing the impugned order. [720 B] (iv) The Government has power to suspend a member of a service under rule 7 of the All Indian Services (Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1955. [721 A]
903: The assessee, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of certain articles. In the year 1947, the assessee received from the Government of India, a sum of Rs. 47,120 as dividends for the assessment years 1947 45 to 1948 49. The assessee claimed that it had paid the said amount to the Government of the United Kingdom under protest and that the said amount should be treated as income of the assessee. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the assessee had not paid any dividend to the assessee. The Tribunal referred the following question to the High Court: " Whether the assessee is entitled to any concession under the Merged State (Taxation Concession) Order, 1948, with regard t o the net dividend of Rs. 17 per ordinary share free of income tax for the year 1947 45 to the Indian Income tax Act, and whether it is income accrued or deemed to have accrued to the assessee in British India ?" The High Court answered the question in the negative holding that the Tribunal ought to have decided and reframed the question whether the assessee is entitle to any concession in respect of the net dividend. The assessee was entitled only to the benefit under the Mercedeses (Taxation Control Concessions) order, 1949, and not to the benefit conferred by the Mercedezes (Taxations Concessions) Orders, 1948. [249E] The assessee was not entitled to any allowance in respect of its income from the sale proceeds of the shares of the assessee in the former Baroda State. The assessee had no case that it was entitled to any such allowance. The assessee did not make any claim to the said allowance. It was not open to the assessee to contend that the said allowance was not available to it. [251F G] The assessee had not made any
6210: The appellant, a Hindu, adopted Balu 's widow. The respondent, the daughter of Krishtarao, filed a suit for possession of the properties with mesne profits and a decree for money against her. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it on appeal by the defendant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that the mother 's power to adopt a son was revived when there was nobody to continue the line. The High Court had not correctly appreciated the decision of the Privy Council in Gurunath vs Kamalabai, ; and the High Court should have held that the mother had absolute right to adopt a daughter to her husband. [880 B] (2) The High Courts were wrong in holding the adoption of the respondent as valid. [881 C D] (3) The High court erred in law in reversing the judgment of the first appellate court. The High court could not go behind the decision of this Court in Gurunathees vs Kamalaben, ; and in any case it was not correct in holding that a Hindu widow 's power of adoption was revived on the death of her natural son leaving a widow. [882 E F] (4) The High 'Court was wrong in interfering with the finding of the first Appellate Court. [883 A] (5) The High, Court was wrong also in holding that in view of the decision of a Full Bench of the Bombay High Court in Ram Chandra vs Murlidhar, the High Court could not interfere with the finding in the present case. [884 G]
5544: The appellant was a partnership firm in which the respondent was the auction purchaser. The respondent purchased the property for Rs.1,65,000 and obtained decree for an amount of Rs.1 lakh against the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the arrears due to it. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the Corporation had not shown any undue interest with the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Corporation itself having accepted the highest offer, the Corporation must dispose of the property by public auction. The Corporation cannot lightly assume that the action taken by the Government is unreasonable or without public interest because as we said above, there are large number of policy considerations which must necessarily weigh with the Government in taking action. [1084 D E] 2. The Corporation has no right to sell the property at its sweet will. It is entitled to sell the same. The Corporation is entitled to realise the sale proceeds from the sale proceeds. The Corporation can always realize the sale proceeds by private negotiations. [1085 F G] 3. The Corporation should have done so before selling the property. The Corporation could not say that the sale was not fair. The Corporation would have sold the property if it was fair. The sale proceeds should be deposited in the Court. The Corporation may take possession of the property after paying the necessary expenses. [1086 C D]
245: The State of Uttar Pradesh was a Part B State. By the Instrument of Accession, the Ruler agreed to the continuance of all his sovereignty in the United State and the Government of India was also a party thereto. Under the terms of the Instrument of accession, the Maharaja of the United State had no right or power to revoke any such grant. The Maharaja of the State of Uttar Bharat was a party to the instrument of accession. The Maharaja was not a party to it but the Government of the United States was a party. The Maharaja had surrendered his sovereignty to the Government of U.P. under the Constitution. The Government of the U.P., therefore, became the sovereign of the United state. The Maharaja made an order on June 18, 1948, revoking the Instrument of surrender and directing that the properties of the State shall be vested in the United States. On August 26, 1949, the Government of Uttar Pradesh revoked the Instrument of Assignment and reassigned the properties of Maharaja to the Government. The Government then took over the properties of State of Uttar. The Government again issued a notification on September 9, 1949, revoking and revoking the instrument of surrender. The Government thereafter passed an order on October 10, 1949, cancelling the earlier order dated June 18, 1949, and reassigning the properties of Raja of the United Provinces to the Government with effect from November 1, 1947. The petitioners challenged the validity of this order by a writ petition before the High Court. Held: (i) The Government of India Act, 1935, did not apply to the United State of U. P. as the instrument of surrendered was executed in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Independence Act, 1947. (ii)The Government of India could not have the power to revoke the instrument of relinquishment without its consent. (iii)The Government cannot exercise the power to cancel the instrument of transfer without its consent and the act of revocation is void. (iv)The Government has the power to rescind the instrument of merger and restore the property to the Government after the merger. (v)The Government can exercise the power of cancellation without its consent if the conditions laid down in the section are satisfied. (vi)The Government could not have exercised the power of resc
5358: The petitioners, who were members of the Administrative Tribunal, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the Chairman and Vice Chair man and Administrative Members of the Administrative Tribu nal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the Chairman was not qualified to be appointed as Chairman of the Administrative Tribunals. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The observations made by Bhagwati, CJI in his Judgment are not binding upon the Government. [880C] 2.1. The appointment of Chairman, Vice Chair men and Administrative Member of the Administrative tribunal should be made by the concerned government only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. [881D] 3.1. It is open to the Government to appoint a person from amongst the retired Judges of the Supreme Court or of a High Court who have held judicial office for at least two years. If it is found that the Chairman has been disqualified, he may recommend the name of such person to the Government. If the Government finds that the Chairman is disqualified, they may recommend the names of the persons so recommended. If the recommendation is accepted by the Government, the Government may appoint another person to act as Chairman of that Tribunal. [882E F] 3.2. The appointment to the post of Vice Chair pear and Administrative Member should be made either by the Chief Justice or by some other Judge of the High Court nominated by him. [883A B]
3956: The appellant, a Research scholar and a research scholar, were alleged to have committed the offences of cheating and forgery. The case ended in their acquittal on 16th July 1968. During the pendency of the case one of the accused persons filed an application before the Magistrate praying that he may be given custody of the two pillars to enable him to make a detailed study. The Magistrate allowed the prayer and directed the police to take over the two pillers from the accused persons. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Magistrate had no power under section 494 of the Criminal Procedure Code to start a fresh investigation under the Criminal Procedure code and that the Magistrate could not proceed with the case without the permission of the Magistrate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Magistrate has no authority in law to commence a fresh investigation after he has already taken cognizance of the offence. [928B] 2. The Magistrate cannot start a fresh inquiry or investigate into the same offence again. [929C D] 3. The Magistrate can direct the police to submit a charge sheet if the facts disclosed constitute an offence. [ 930E] 4. The Magistrate is not bound to order further investigation under section 173(8) Cr. P.C. [931D E] 5. The Magistrate must apply his mind to the materials placed before him and then pass appropriate orders. [932F]
6954: The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1978 under the Banning Act. The Peerless Company had a scheme of prize chits and money circulation schemes, and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Panto Chits and Money Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978 was enacted to ban the promotion or conduct of prize chitors or money circulation schemes and for matters related therewith or incidental thereof. By a letter dated July 23, 1979, the Reserve Bank of India pointed out to the Peerless that the schemes conducted by it were covered by the provisions of the Banning act, which had come into force w.e.f. It is not necessary to consider whether the Peer Society is a banking company or not. The Poddar Group of Companies are not companies within the meaning of section 2(6A)(a) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The PIIF Group of companies are not companies as defined in the Banning and Money Circulatory Scheme (Banning) Act, 1977. The Piecy Group of Companies do not fall within the definition of 'banking company '. The PIL Group of Companies constitute a separate class of banks and the PIF
125: The plaintiffs in the suit for ejectment from and compensation at the rate of Rs. 370 per month from November 1, 1947, for use and occupation of the second floor flat of Sunama House situate in Cumballa Hill, Bombay, claimed a decree for possession against the defendants on the ground that they were tenants of the plaintiffs for the use and occupation and for arrears of rent. The defendants resisted the suit on the grounds that the Small Causes Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the plaintiffs were not licensees of the first floor flat and that the second defendant was a limited company and not a tenant of the first defendant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were tenants of a limited company, that the defendants were not liable to pay any rent or compensation to the plaintiffs, that the plaintiffs had sublet the flat to a third party, and that the defendants had sublet the premises to a third person. On appeal the Appellate Bench of the Small Causes court held that the plaintiffs could not be said to be tenants of the first and second defendants, that the suit was barred by section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and that it was not a suit between a landlord and a tenant relating to recovery of rent or possession of any premises to which any of the provisions of the Act applied. Held, that the High Court was right in its view that the suit as against the defendants was not a case of eviction but a suit between landlord and tenant. The question whether a suit is a suit between two landlords or one of them is essentially a question of fact depending upon the facts of each case. The question of law raised in this case was not one of fact but was a mixed question of law and fact. It was not necessary to decide whether the suit was a suit between the landlord and a stranger. The question was one of fact and the finding of the High Court on the basis of the evidence was correct.
5745: The Rajasthan Public Service Commission (hereinafter referred to as 'Commission') was constituted under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution by which, in respect of the scheme of competitive examinations to be conducted by the Public Service Commission for recruitment to certain branches of the civil services under the State, certain minimum qualifying marks in the viva voce test were prescribed. In the year 1986, the Rajasthan Public Service Commissiion issued a notification calling for applications from eligible candidates for appointment to various posts including the post of Assistant Engineer in the Rajasthan Engineering Services Class I and Class II service. The appellant, who was a candidate for the said post applied for the same. He was called for interview but he failed to secure the minimum qualifying marks. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court contending that the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus directing the Commission to make selections on the basis of the result of the examination. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Commission could not have issued any direction to the Commission to select any candidate without giving an opportunity to the appellant to represent his case. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the Commission is entitled to issue directions to the Commission for making selections on its own or on the basis or at its discretion. [312D E] 1.2 The High Court was right in holding that the Government could not issue such directions to the commission. [313E F] 1.3 The High Court should not have interfered with the selection process. The High court should have given reasons for the decision. [314F] 1.4 The High Court ought to have given reasons why it came to the conclusion that the Commission was entitled to issue the directions to the State Government to appoint the appellant. [315G] 1.5 The High Court erred in quashing the selection process on the ground that the Commission did not give any reason for selecting the appellant. The High Courts judgment was contrary to law. [316A C] 1.6 The High Court could not have directed the Commission to prepare a list of selected candidates after taking into consideration the aggregate marks obtained by the candidates in the written examination and
3941: The appellant was a manufacturer of Vanaspati. It had set up a Vanaspathi plant on the land in question. The plant was to be installed for the manufacture of Vanadium and Vanaspaulin. The plant had been set up by the appellant in the year 1970. The appellant, however, started commercial production from January, 1970. In March, 1971, the State Government took a policy decision that new Vanasapati plant would be given partial concession in Sales Tax for a period of three years commencing from 1st July, 1970. The State Government accordingly issued a letter dated 20th January, 1970 stating that the Government had taken a policy decision to exempt the appellant from payment of sales tax for a period upto 31st August, 1970. On the basis of this letter, the appellant applied to the State Government for exemption of sales tax under section 5(2) of the Act. The State government rejected the application. Thereafter, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Government had no power to grant exemption under section 5 (2). Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State has no power to make a promise or take any other action which it may be necessary to enforce with reference to its powers under the law. [655C] 2. The State is not bound to grant exemption unless there are compelling reasons to do so. The State cannot act arbitrarily in granting exemption without taking into consideration all relevant factors. [656D] 3. The State can always exercise its power under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue directions, orders etc., to carry out the purpose of the statute. But such direction, orders etc. must be based on some rational principle. In the instant case, the State has not made any attempt to bring about any change in the position of the appellant. [657E F] 4. The State had no power or authority to alter the position of its employees. The State could not have altered its position. [658F] 5. The State was entitled to impose conditions subject to which the exemption was granted
201: The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan who migrated to India after the partition of 1947. They were allotted specific areas of land under the statement of conditions contained in Notification Nos. 489 1/S and 4892 IS, dated the 8th July, 1949, on quasi permanent basis in lieu of the lands left by them in Pakistan. In pursuance of this policy the petitioners were settled on land in village Dhakala which was a first grade village, Tehsil Thanesar, District Karnal, in the State of East Punjab. After partition of 1947, the petitioners were allotted specific area of land under this statement of conditions. The petitioners moved the East Punjab Government for cancellation of allotment order. The Deputy Custodian General dismissed the revision petition on the 2nd December, 1953, holding that the order of the Deputy Custodian was not illegal or without jurisdiction on the ground that no notice of cancellation had been issued to them. The petitioners then moved the EastPunjab High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying for a writ of certiorari quashing the orders dated the 14th October, 1953, and the 14th November, 1953, passed by the Deputy Custodian General and the Assistant Custodian General respectively. The petitioners contended that the order was without jurisdiction as it was made without jurisdiction and that the order could be challenged only in a civil suit. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. The order of the Custodian was not without jurisdiction because the petitioners had not obtained possession of the lands allotted to them before they became displaced persons. The petitioners were not in actual cultivating possession of the land allotted to them but were in possession of the same as tenants. The petitioners had not acquired any title to the land allotted. The petitioners did not acquire any title to it. The petitioners could not claim any right to retain possession of the property allotted to them.
59: The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of aluminium products. In 1951, the Central Bank of India Ltd., a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, filed a suit against the Bank for recovery of its dues from it. The Bank contended that the Bank had no authority to sell the property of the company and that the Bank was not entitled to recover the amount due from it. Held, that the Bank 's action was barred by article 31(1) of the Constitution as it was not authorised by law to take possession of the property of a company. The right to enforce the claim arose when the property was taken over by the Central Bank and the right to sue accrued only when the property vested in the Central Bank. The right of the Bank to recover the money was not an absolute right but was subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution itself. The Bank 's right to recover the property was not an unqualified right and could not be enforced in any court or tribunal. The Bank was not bound to pay the amount due to the Bank because the Bank was entitled to recover it under the provisions of the Constitution. The Bank had no power to sell the properties of the Company without the consent of the Central Bank; and the Bank was, therefore, not entitled to enforce the Bank ' s claim against the Bank.

In the meantime, the State Government issued a notification dated May 14, 1975 under section 3(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Excise Act, 1910 appointing the petitioner as Excise Inspector. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: (1) The petitioner can be considered for promotions to the post, of Excise Inspector only if he fulfills the conditions laid down in rule 5 of the Uttaranchal Subordinate Excise Service Rules, 1983. Subordinate Excise Service, Rules, 1983 provides that no candidate shall be eligible for promotion to any post in the cadre of the service unless he has passed the departmental examination prescribed under rule 23. 49: The respondent firm was carrying on business in cloth and cloth. The appellant firm entered into an agreement with the respondent firm on the 17th of October, 1941 for the supply of the goods to it. The respondent firm thereupon filed a suit against the appellant firm for damages for breach of a contract. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court holding that the performance of the contract had been frustrated by circumstances beyond their control and hence the appellant 's claim must fail. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The doctrine of frustration is not applicable where there has been a clear and direct contract between the parties. The doctrine of "constructive contract" is applied when there is a clear and immediate relation between the parties to the contract and the intention of the parties is expressed in the words used by the parties themselves. [850 C D] (2) The doctrine applies only if there is a close connection between the parties and the contract being broken. It does not apply where the parties have intended to create a new obligation or affect existing rights. [851 E F] (3) The doctrine is applicable where there is a mutual understanding between the parties as to what the law shall be done and whether the contract is to be performed in future. Where there is no such mutual understanding, the doctrine would not apply. But where there is an express term in the contract which indicates that the parties intended that the contract shall be performed in a particular manner, then the doctrine would apply. [852 A B] (4) The doctrine can be invoked where there is no mutual understanding between them. If the parties intend that the contract should be performed in the manner prescribed by the parties, they cannot take recourse to the doctrine of frustrating the contract. [853 C D]

1201: The respondent was granted a bilmakta of the village in 1901. In 1918, the Nizam granted a lease to the respondent for a period of 20 years. The respondent claimed that the village had been granted to his ancestor by the Nizam and the respondent was only entitled to the pan muka of the village and no more. The appellants contended that the village was not a permanent grant but a bilamkatta and that the respondent was entitled to possession of the village as well as to recover mesne profits at the rate of Rs. 931 12 0 0 per year. Held, that the respondent 's case was that the village did not include the bilmas or the land in question. The grant was not a bilomaktta but a bazar. The grant could be made only if the grant was permanent and the grant was for a fixed term. The grant must be regarded as a permanent grant and not a bazar or a bazarary. The grant is not a bhoomi ng grant. It is a bazar and it cannot be said to be a bazarari. The grant does not create any title in favour of the grantee. The grant may be temporary or shortly limited. 4035: The appellant was detained under the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to make an effective representation against his detention and that the order of detention was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the detaining authority must invariably consider the possibility of launching a prosecution before making an order of detention and that if not, the order of preventive detention must necessarily be held to be bad. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of preventive detention is precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation. It does not overlap with prosecution even if it relies on certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched. An order of preventive detenlion must always be made with or without prosecution and in anticipation or after discharge or even acquittal. The fact that the detaining authori ty has failed to apply its mind to the vital question whether it was necessary to detain the person concerned or not would not vitiate the order of the Detenu as long as the order of bail remains in force. [548E F] 2. The order of detention must reflect that the detaining autho rity has considered all relevant aspects and has applied his mind to the relevant material. If some irrelevant considerations are taken into account the detention order will be vitiated. [551A] 3. The order can be validly passed either under section 11(2) of the Act or under section 8(b) of the COFEPOSA Act. The grounds of detention must show that (a) the detenu was habitually and habitually committing or abetting the commission of offences; (b) he was involved in a criminal case; (c) he has been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment by a competent court; (d) he has, in the meantime, committed any offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. The order cannot be struck down merely because the detenu 's activities were not found to be prejudicial to the maintenance of public order but they were found to be such that a rational view could be taken about his future conduct. 4920: The respondent, a tenant of the land in question, was inducted as a tenant by the appellant in the year 1955. He filed an application for ejectment on the ground that he had become a deemed purchaser under section 5(1) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887 and that he had been in continuous possession of the land since the commencement of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Second Amendment) Act, 1956. The Assistant Collector rejected the application holding that the tenancy had been reserved by the landowner for his personal cultivation and that the land comprised in the tenancy had not been reserved by him for his personal use. On appeal, the Appellate Authority held that the tenancy could be terminated on any grounds mentioned in sec. 7, but it did not agree with the view taken by the Assistant Collector. In revision, the High Court held that the provisions of secs. 7, 7A and 8 were applicable to the case and that the tenancy must be determined on the basis of the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The proper way of looking at the scheme of secs., 7, 7 A and 8 is to hold that while sec. 7 provides for additional grounds on which tenancies may be terminated, sec. 8 provides for additional ground on which tenitalis are reserved by the landlord for his personal occupation. [880C] The purpose of sec. 7 is to provide for the termination of the tenancy if the land is reserved by the tenant for his personal consumption. It is not possible for us to accept a construction which would lead to such disastrous results. The object of sec.7 is to ensure that the tenants are not put in jeopardy or harassed by the landlord who has acquired the land from the tenant. [881D E] The proper way to looked at the scheme is to hold the tenant in possession of the property in question as a tenant on the date of the commencement of sec.5(1). [882F]
6588: The respondents were tried before the Additional Sessions Judge, Sonepat for offences under section 302, I.P.C., and sections 323,325 read with 149, I. P.C. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to imprisonment for life and ordered to pay a sum of Rs.500 each under section 148, I.p.C. and six months' rigorous imprisonment respectively. The High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence of fine to one year 's imprisonment. The State appealed against the acquittal of the respondents. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the statement made by 665 Paras Ram at the time when the investigating officer made the inquest report a somewhat different version was given, the High Court was right in convicting the respondents under section 304 Part I, I.PC. [666 D E] 1.2 The prosecution case is that the quarrel arose out of a very insignificant matter like the burning of dry sugarcane leaves on the common boundary of the fields of the two parties. The altercation would probably have been forgotten had Partap Singh deceased not died. The altercations occurred because of a minor incident which took place in the field of the two sides. The alter ct would naturally have been forgetting the fact that the fight arose out of an insignificent matter. It is clear from the evidence that there was no prior enmity between the parties. The occurrence has taken place in the fields of one party. There is no reason why the accused should be acquitted. [667 C D] 1.3 The High Court has committed serious error in holding that the respondents were guilty of offence under section 302/34 I.P,.C. and that they were entitled to be released on probation. The High court has committed grave error in convicting the appellants under section 304 part I I.P., and recording their conviction under section 304/34 I P.C., on the basis that in view of the statements made by 664 Paras Ram at a time when the Investigating Officer made the inquest panchanama a somewhat different story was given. [668 B C] 1
4620: The petitioner, a member of the Indian Revenue Service, was convicted by the Delhi Special Police Establishment for offences under section 304B and 498A I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. He filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed his appeal on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity of being heard in respect of the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the trial court as well as the High Court were wrong in holding that the appellant was guilty of the offence charged; (ii) the evidence adduced by the prosecution did not establish that the appellant had committed the offence; (iii) the presumption arising from the circumstantial evidence could not be drawn unless the circumstances established that the appellant alone was responsible for the death of the deceased and that the appellant must have been responsible for her death; (iv) the appellant was entitled to acquittal because he was not shown to have been prejudiced in any manner by reason of the fact that he was acquitted by the trial court; (v) the appellant having been found guilty of the offences with which he was charged, there was no justification for interfering with the order of acquittal. HELD: (1) There is nothing in the Evidence Act or in the Code of Criminal Procedure which would lead us to hold that the appellant could not be convicted of the offence with which he has been charged. [116 A B] (2) The appellant was not shown who had committed the crime. It was not necessary that he should have been examined in the case. The appellant was entitled, therefore, to be discharged. [117 C D] (3) The appellant had been rightly convicted by the trial Court and the High Court. [118 E] (4) The appellant could not, therefore, be convicted of an offence under section 304 B and 498A IPC. [119 F] (5) The appellant cannot be said to have been properly tried for an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act. [120 B C] (6) The appellant can be convicted only if he is proved to have committed an offence under Section 304 B and not otherwise. [121 G]
3175: The respondent was appointed as Professor and Head of the Department of the University of Jammu and Kashmir. He was allowed to function as Professor and his probation was extended for a year by the Vice Chancellor under section 13(4) of the Ordinance, which had already been replaced on November 10, 1969 by the Jammu and Kashmir Universities Act, 1969. He continued in service till he was reappointed by the ViceChancellor under section 12(2) of the Act. On October 11, 1970, the respondent 's services were terminated by the Vice chancellor under section 13 (1) of the Ordinances. The respondent challenged the termination before the High Court. The High Court held that the termination was not valid and quashed the order terminating the services of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The respondent 's appointment was made by the Vice ChancellOrity, Jammu and Kashmir University, Jammu, and not by the University Council. [780C] 2. The Vice Chancellor is the appointing authority of the employee of the University. The ViceChancellor has power to make appointments only on the recommendation of the Selection Committee constituted for the purpose in accordance with the provisions of Section 36 of the Ordinance. The Vice Chancello ry can be delegated by him to the Vice Chancellor. [773D E] 3. The Vice chancellor may make appointments of teachers referred to in section 36 of the Act, but the recommendations of the Selection Com mittee constituted for the purposes in accordance with section 36 of this Ordinance shall be deemed to be an appointment, transfer or temporary. [774E F] 4. The Vice Chairman of the University cannot be appointed by the Vice Chairman of any other body. [775G] 5. The Vice-Chancellor can appoint a person from amongst the persons recommended by the Selection Committee. [776A B]
6448: The petitioner purchased property bearing No. 112 113, Gautam Nagar, Delhi at an auction conducted by the Income tax Department in the year 1988. The sale certificate was issued to him on 14.4.1988. On 14.4,1988 a certificate of sale was issued by the T.R.O. to the petitioner. On 14th April, 1988 a certificate of purchase was issued by T.R.,O. to him. On 14st April, 1988 another certificate of sale in favour of the petitioner was issued by Sub Registrar, Delhi. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid two certificates. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the expression revenue officer ' in section 84 (4) of the would include a T.R..O. and, if not, whether without an appropriate amendment of section 89(2) or (4) or (5) of the , the mere framing of a rule by the Central Board of Direct Taxes under the Income Tax Act, 1961 will be sufficient to oblige the registration officer to file a copy of the certificate of sale sent to him by the TRIDA. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The expression revenue officer' in section 84(4) of Income Tax Act is used in a comprehensive sense to include all officers who are empowered to issue a certificate of transfer of immovable property. [183C] 1.2. The expression Revenue Officer ' in section 80B(1)(a) of the Income Tax Rules, 1962 is used in the same sense as in section 84 of the Income tax Act, 1961. [188E] 1.3. The expression "Revenue Officer" in section 84 means the Collector of Stamps and Registration of the State of Delhi. [189F] 1.4. The expression Collector of Stamps & Registration of the Union Territory of Delhi is used in section 84 in the same way as the expression Collector of Stamp and Registration of other States. [187G] 1.5. The expression TRIDA is used in sections 84(4), 84(5) and 84(6). Section 84(4)(i) provides for the registration of documents of title relating to immovable property.

6061: The petitioners were serving in the Assam Rifles as Subedar and Assistant Subedars. They had been allotted land, grant of title deeds in respect of the allotted land, facilities for movement by air to and from Mohanbari, freedom to develop the allotted areas, grant of advance by way of loans, provision of marketing facili ties for disposal of surplus produce, guaranteed supply of essential commodities and provision of the basic require ments of life for the purpose of encouraging the all round economic development of the area. The petitioners claimed that they were entitled to allotment of land, grant, of title deeds and other benefits under the scheme approved by the Government of India. The Central Government made an order on 20th February, 1987 directing the Central Gov ernment to nominate a competent authority of suitable status to examine the problem and to look into the scheme and after hearing the petitioners, to report to the Central Govern ment, if necessary, to enable it to make an appropriate order for redress of the grievances of the petitioners. The petitioners contended that the scheme was not implemented and the Central Government did not take any action against the petitioners.
