795: The appellant, a Hindu, was the owner of a temple and a temple. He made an application to the District Court under section 3 of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, for declaring that the temple was not a public one. The District Judge held that the temple had come into existence for the religious and charitable purposes and that there was no need to join the deity because of an averment by the respondents that the temple itself was not a family or private one. On appeal, the High Court held that the suit properties were not the personal properties of the appellant but the temple and that the deity was not a necessary party. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The suit property was not the personal property of the appellant, that the temple and the properties were his personal properties. The appellant was entitled to maintain the suit as he was entitled to it under the provisions of the Act. [683 C D] (2) The appellant 's case was that the temple in question was a public trust and the temple was a private one. It was not disputed that the temple belonged to the appellant. The appellant could not be said to have any right in the temple. [684 E] (3) The appellant was estopped from making such a claim. The appellant had no right to make such a claim, that the deity itself was not the owner of the temple. The appellant did not claim any right in himself. [685 F] (4) The appellant had not been able to prove that the temple is a public trust. [686 G] (5) The appellant could only succeed if he proved that the temple belongs to him. [687 A B] (6) The appellant has failed to establish that the temple belong to him. The appellant cannot therefore succeed on the basis of the finding of the District Judge that the temple does not belong to him and that the temple has not come into existence. [688 H; 689 A] (7) The appellant can not be allowed to raise a plea that the temple being a public trust, the temple is not a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act, and that the appellant is not entitled to maintain an action for damages against the respondent
2383: The appellants were the owners of a steel plant at Calcutta. They sold to various parties goods in West Bengal and also manufactured and sold to different parties. The sales tax authorities assessed the outside sales of all the appellants to sales tax under the Uttar Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1954. The Sales Tax Officers of Uttar Pradesh assessed the outside sale of all the appellant to sales tax on the ground that they were not liable to pay sales tax under section 9(1) (b) of the Act. The appellants filed appeals before the Revising Authority under section 9 of the Act but their appeals were rejected by the revising authority. In revision applications filed by the appellants before the High Court, the High Court held that the out of State sales would be taxable (1) if the goods were manufactured or produced in the Province of Uttar Pradesh at the time when the contracts for sale were made, and (2) if the purchase price was paid after the contract for sale was made in respect of the goods in question, and the sales tax was levied at the rate of 3 pies per rupee subject to a rebate under section 5 of the Act and certain other adjustments. The High Court dismissed the revisions application. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that the sales tax authorities could not impose sales tax on sales which are exigible to sales tax. [515 B] The sales tax officer had no jurisdiction to assess the sales tax on those transactions. He had no power to assess them as sales tax. The sales of the appellants were exigible to tax. The Sales tax Officer had no jurisdiction under section 11 to assess the outside sales. [516 C D]
183: The appellant was arrested in pursuance of an extradition warrant issued by the Regional Com missioner of the United State of Rajasthan who is the principal officer representing the Crown in the territory of that State. He was produced before the Magistrate on the 9th August, 1947 and was remanded to judicial custody till the 15th August, 1948. On his return he was served with a notice under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for trial of the offences committed by him. The appellant contended that the Tonk State had no authority to commit the offence and that the Tons were not liable to be tried by the Court of Session. Held: (i) The treaty entered into between the British Government and the Tonki State on the 28th January, 1869, which was continued in force by the Ton k State, was still subsisting and its execution became impossible as the Tonka State ceased to exist. (ii)The treaty was no longer subsisting and its operation became impossible because it did not cover the offences now charged against the appellant, no extradition of the appellant could be demanded or ordered.
2299: The respondents were the owners of certain lands in a village. They applied for permission to sell the trees on their land and the Divisional Forest Officer by order dated August 30, 1957 granted them proprietary rights in the land. The Compensation Officer held that the respondents had no interest in the trees standing on their land as the trees were not 'land ' as defined in section 2(5) of the Punjab Alienation of Land Act, 1953, and that the compensation was payable only to the owner of the land. On appeal, the Divisional Forest officer allowed the application but he directed the appellant to pay compensation at the rate of Rs. 62.56 per tree. The appellant filed an application under section 11 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 for permission to transfer the trees from their land to the respondents. The Divisional Forest Officer rejected the application holding that the trees were "land" within the meaning of section 2(3) of the Act and that the trees could be transferred only after obtaining the consent of the owner. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Divisional Forest. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the trees standing thereon were not 'lands ' within the meaning Of section 2(6) of the , and (ii) the compensation was not paid to the respondents because they were not 'owners ' of the land transferred to them. HELD : (i) The trees standing on the land transferred by the Compensation Officer are not 'land' within the meaning given to it in section 2 (7) of the . It is not necessary that the trees should be transferred to the owner or to the person who has transferred them. [115E] (ii) The trees are capable of being transferred apart from land and if a person transfers trees or gives a right to a person to cut trees and remove them it cannot be said that he has transferred land. The trees standing thereon are not 'lands' within the definition of section 2 (6) of Act. [116A C] (iii) The trees stand on the land allotted to the respondents and not on the land which was transferred to them by the Compensation officer. The
253: The respondents, who were dealers in iron and steel, manufactured iron ingots and other iron ingots. They claimed exemption from assessment in respect of the sales effected by them on the ground that such sales took place "in the course of export" within the meaning of article 111(1) (b) of the Constitution. Held, that the sales were completed before the goods were shipped and could not be considered to have taken place in the course of the export. The sale was complete before the goods had crossed the customs frontiers of India and the goods were exported outside the country. Held further, that the exemption granted under article 286(1)(b) of Constitution was limited to sales by export and purchases by import, that is to say, those sales which occasion the export or import as the case may be, and that the sales tax was leviable only when the goods were actually exported and not when they were actually exported. Held also, that the sale was complete after the goods were cleared for home consumption and the sales were complete before the imported goods were exported.
2436: The surety agreed to pay and satisfy the liabilities of the principal debtor in respect of principal and interest. The surety was discharged by the creditor on demand. The surety had no right to restrain execution against him until he had exhausted his remedies against the principal. The surety became a party to the suit. He filed an appeal challenging the legality and propriety of this direction. The decree passed by the trial court was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The surety was not liable to be proceeded against for any default committed by the principal debtor. The surety could not be prosecuted under sec. 140 of the Indian Contract Act. [1235 D E] (2) The surety is entitled to enforce its dues in accordance with law. The surety has no right to interfere with the liability of the principal. [1236 A B] (3) The surety cannot be compelled to discharge the debt or to execute the bond as there is nothing to show that he has done so. The surety can only be discharged if he has discharged the debt or the amount due from him. [1237 C] (4) The surety has a right to recover the amount from the principal. It is not necessary that the creditor should have satisfied himself about the debt. [1238 D] (5) The surety may be asked to postpone his remedy against the principal till the creditor has exhausted his remedies. But in his view the surety must give sufficient reasons. [1239 E] (6) The surety can be asked to wait till the creditor is able to recover the debt. If he does not do so, the creditor will be subrogated to the rights of the creditor under sec.140 of the Indian Code. [1240 F]
2678: The Municipal Council, Raipur, under the Motor Transport Workers Act, 1961, was constituted and it was a body corporate. It carried on business in transport of goods and passengers. The Municipal Council was registered as a 'motor transport undertaking ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. The Municipal Committee issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be prosecuted for contravening the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The appellant filed a complaint before the Magistrate against the Municipal Council and the Chief Municipal Officer, Municipal Council, under sections 3(1), 4(2)(d) and 5(3) of the , and also under sections 255 and 276 of the , alleging that the Municipal Council had been guilty of offences punishable under sections 3 and 7 of the Act, and that the Municipal Committee had failed to discharge its duties under the Act. On the question whether the Municipal Council was exempt from liability to pay compensation under section 38(1) of the . HELD : (i) Section 38(1), Cr. P.C., is not applicable to the Municipal Council. The word "includes" has been used in the section and it is difficult to limit this specific meaning on any reasonable basis. [917 D] (ii) The Municipal Council does not fall within the definition of the expression "motor transport Undertaking" in section 2(h) of the and it is impossible to limit this particular meaning on any reasonably basis. This is undoubtedly so but we are unable to appreciate how this would help the appellants. [918 E F] (iii) The Municipal Committee did not come within the exemption under section 38 of the Act because the Municipal Committee was not a 'mundariya ' or a 'must have been employed by the Municipal Committee to carry out the work of road construction. The Municipal committee was not a "mundari" nor was it a 'mandri'. The Municipal Committee was merely an agent of the Municipal Committee. [919 C D] (iv) The Municipal committee did not come under the exemption under s.38(1) and therefore, the Municipal Committee could not be said to be exempted from payment of compensation under section 417 of
4311: The petitioners were recruited to the Central Secretariat Service (hereinafter referred to as 'the CSSS') in the grade of Rs.2000-3500 and were promoted to Grade I of the CSSS on the basis of a selection by a Selection Committee constituted under Rule 12 of the CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965. The petitioners contended that the Central Secretariat services (Amendment) Act, 1979 did not apply to the post of Section Officer Grade and that the Central Administrative Tribunal had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Central Secretariat Service is a separate cadre and the Central Secretariat Stenographers Service Rules, 1975 are not applicable to the post. [1189 A] 2. The Central Administrative Tribunal has no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the Central Secretariat is entitled to fill up the vacancies reserved for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe candidates in the Central Secretariat. [1190 B] 3. The Central Government has power to make rules regarding the conditions of service of persons appointed to the Central secretariat service. The Central Secretariate Service (Amendment)Rules, 1979 have been framed under Article 309 of the Constitution. The Central secretarial service (Amendment), Rules, 1979 have also been framed under article 148(3). The Central Secretariat Services Rules, 1975 have been
3195: The appellants were manufacturers of matches, and the respondents were manufacturers of a large number of matches. They manufactured matches in the appellant 's factory at Madras. The respondents claimed that they had been subjected to excise duty at the same rate as had been applied to larger producers, who have developed and marketing musclemenlys, having regard to their economic capabilities in the matter of production and marketing a sort of traumatic egality. The respondents contended that the appellants were entitled to exemption from payment of excise duty on matches manufactured by them and that the impugned notification was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The classification made between the small manufacturers of match boxes and the small manufacturers in category 'C ' is not arbitrary but based on intelligible differentia which distinguishes them from other manufacturers. [411 D] (ii) The classification has to be founded on an intelligible differentiation which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group. [412 E] (iii) The classification must be founded on intelligible differential which distinguishes those that are grouping together from others; it should not be arbitrary but must be based on some qualities which are recognized and established in law. [413 F] (iv) The classification cannot be based on mere differences of degree and it must depend on an agreement between the parties. It can never be based on an intelligent differentia which has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute. [414 G H]
725: The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that she was the owner of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal, the District Judge held that the respondent had based her claim on a special custom and dismissed the appeal. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to succeed in preference to the collaterals. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The respondent as the heir of her father and brother was entitled to succeed to the properties under the general custom of the Punjab. The respondent was not entitled, therefore, to succeed. [780 B] (2) The respondent was a collateral of Sahib Singh of the eighth degree and was entitled to the properties as his heir. The respondent could not be said to have failed to discharge the onus. [790 C D] (3) The respondent had relied upon the custom of the family of her father which was prevalent in Mauza Sultanwind. The respondent had also relied upon the Customary Law of the Punjab in support of her case. [791 E F] (4) The respondent 's plea that the respondent was not a collateral of the father or brother of the appellant was rejected. [795 A] (5) The respondent could only succeed if she established a special custom entitling her sister to succeed in favour of the collaterals and the onus of doing this must, therefore, be on her. [796 B] (6) The respondent has proved that the appellant had failed to discharge her burden. [797 C] (7) The respondent is not entitled to the property unless she established a custom entitling the sister to succeed on the collaterals as collaterals. [799 D]
5671: The respondent No. 3 was charged with having committed an offence punishable under section 111 read with Section 135 of the Customs Act, for which he was acquitted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate. On appeal, the Sessions Judge confirmed the acquittal but on revision, the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and directed that the prosecution be dropped. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the acquittal of respondents 1 and 2 was not a bar to the prosecution of the same person in connection with the charge of having committed the offence under the Gold (Control) Act, 1968. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The ingredients required to be established in respect of the offence under section 111 of the Customs act are altogether different from the ones required to be proved in respect of an offence under the Customs Act. [901C] 2. The gold is imported within the Indian Customs waters contrary to a prohibition contained under the Customs act. It is therefore evident that the ingredients required to constitute in respect of offence under the Act are altogether different. [902D] 3. The goods in question were imported within the India Customs waters contrary t o a prohibition contained in the Customs Act and the Customs Act cannot be said to have created any such bar. The ingredients necessary to attract the offence under Section 111 of the Act are entirely different from those required to be alleged in respect of a particular offence under the Sea Customs Act. The ingredients of the offence are totally different from the two offences under the Customs Acts. [903E F] 4. The gold was imported within the country and the respondents had been tried by a competent court for the offence under Customs Act. There was no bar to the trial of the respondents for the offence of being in possession of gold under the Customs law. [904F] 5. The respondents were tried by a Magistrate and the Sessions Judge. The Magistrate found them guilty. The High Court reversed the order of the Sessions Judge and convicted them. The High court held that the prosecution under the Customs Law was barred on the basis of the undermentioned facts: i) that the respondents had, in fact, been tried by the Magistrate; ii) they were sought to be prosecuted on the same facts for an offence under Customs.
2637: The respondent, a contractor, filed a complaint against the appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, alleging that he was not competent to file the complaint under section 20 of the , and that the complaint was not made by him. The Magistrate acquitted the respondent on the ground that the complaint did not contain any particulars as required by section 20(1) of the Act. On appeal, the Sessions Judge held that the complaint had been duly signed by the respondent and that the Municipal Corporation was competent to institute legal proceedings in respect of the complaint. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the complaint petition was not made and signed by the person competent under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 to exercise powers of the Corporation in the matter of institution of legal proceedings. HELD: (i) Section 537 of the Act provides that the Commissioners may institute, defend or withdraw from legal proceedings under the Act. Under section 12 of the Act, the Commissioner can delegate his functions to the Chairman and the Chairman may in his turn delegate his functions under section 12 to the Vice Chairman or to any municipal officer. [839 E] (ii) The words "any other authority" in section 537 are wide enough to include the Municipal Corporation of Howrah. [840 F] (iii) The Municipal Corporation of the Delhi is a local authority within the meaning of section 2(vii) of the , but the Municipal Corporation has no power to initiate legal proceedings in regard to the matters specified in section 20(2). 707: The appellant, a Head Master of a National Training School, was nominated for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Madras from Alangulam Constituency in the District of Tirunelveli. 1706: The appellants, who were the claimants in a reference made to it under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, claimed compensation for their lands at the rate of Rs. 10,000 per acre. 4714: The respondent, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation created under the State Act of 1950, was in appeal by special leave to this Court. 5256: The assessee was a manufacturer of woolen textiles and hides and leather products. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not been able to show any evidence in support of its claim that it was bound by an agreement with the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was bound by the agreement and that the amount paid to the assessee was a capital expenditure. The Tribunal also rejected the claim of the assessee. In further appeal to this Court, the assessee contended that the agreement between the assessee and the assessee was binding on it because it was entered into after the agreement was entered into and the assessee had no option but to accept the terms thereof. HELD: (1) The agreement between the parties was binding on the assessee. [880C] (2) The agreement was entered in the course of carrying out the contract between the assessee as well as the assessee. It is clear from paragraph 7 of the agreement that the assessee agreed to pay to the assessee a sum of Rs. 50,000 which was the price fixed by the assessee. The agreement was to be executed within six months from the date of the agreement. The agreement provided that the assessee would permit the use of the trade mark and the trade mark used by the assessee for the purpose of indicating the name of the manufacturer. The agreement stipulated that the assessee "shall have the right to use the trade mark " and the trade marks " mentioned in the agreement. This was in essence an integral part of the bargain for the acquisition of the technical knowledge to have this particular distributorship. [890D E] (3) The agreement did not contain any condition that the assessee should appoint the distributors for the sale of the goods manufactured by it. The agreement merely stated that the distributors would receive a discount of 15% of the sale price fixed by them. There was nothing in the agreement to indicate that the assessee could appoint the distributor for the sale.

3768: The Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 was enacted by the State Legislature in order to provide for the acquisition of property and for matters connected therewith. Sub section 2 of section 14 conferred upon a Hindu female a right to claim maintenance from her husband. The Hindu Women 's Right to property Act, 1937, was amended by the Madras Act No. XXV of 1961 which provided that a widow would have no right to receive maintenance from her father. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, was passed to amend the law relating to intestate succession and devise new rights in property. The Act was challenged by the appellant who claimed that the property belonged to his mother and not to his wife. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the property had been acquired by a Hindu female by means of a pre existing right and that the property was not acquired by a female. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the property did not belong to the mother but to her husband and that the provisions of section 14(1), as they stood at the relevant time, were not attracted to the case. HELD: (i) The Act does not confer any new right on the widow. It merely provides for the conferment of a restricted estate on a Hindu female. [273C] (ii) The Act neither takes away the right of maintenance nor conferred the same; it is only a provision conferring a restricted estate. The Act does nothing more than create a restricted estate in the property. [274D E] (iii) The Act has taken away the right to maintenance of a Hindu female from the husband. The Act neither extinguishes nor extinguishes the right of a Hindu woman to maintenance. The Act also does nothing more. [275E] (iv) The Act creates a restricted estate and vests the property in the widow. The Act cannot be said to impose an absolute restriction on the right of the widow to
992: The appellant was a shopkeeper in the State of Punjab. He had been working as a salesman and had been doing business in the shop for more than six months. On account of his ill health he could not be expected to work for more than three months. He was charged with having contravened the terms of the Act and was convicted under section 16 of the , for an offence under section 16, and sentenced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the Act would not apply to the shop or establishment for the reason that it was designed in the interest of the owner of the shop or the establishment himself and that his health and welfare was a matter of interest not only to himself but to the general public. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 7(1) of the Act which was enacted in order to limit the hours of work of the shop and the hours of employment of the employees was violative of article 14 of the Constitution because the Act did not provide for any such restriction and therefore the provisions of section 7(2) were ultra vires. HELD : (i) The Act is intended to cover the entire field of the operation of the Act. It is not meant to cover the whole field of operation of the statute. The Act does not contain any provision for the closure of shops or establishments where there are no employees nor is it intended to cover any particular class of persons. [294 D] (ii)The Act has been passed by the Legislature in order to regulate the conditions of service of the employees of the shops and establishments. The Act is not intended to cover all types of cases. It is intended to give effect to the policy of the legislature. The Act cannot be said to have been enacted for the purpose of controlling the working of the shops or establishments in the interests of the general public, and it must be held to be so for the purposes of the Act itself. 3978: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, and the High Court in appeal, confirmed his conviction and sentence. It is not merely vague but broad enough to cover all possible situations. [138 H] 2. The expression 'special reasons' used in sub section 3 of section 354 does not mean mere speculation or guessing but must be read as comprehending the necessity for exercise of judicial discretion in favour of the accused. [139 D E] 3. The expression means something more than mere speculation. It signifies that something which is carefully worded and is fairly susceptible of exact reproduction. It cannot be defined without reference to the context and other provisions of the statute. The phraseology employed in sub section 4 of section 354 is not limited to specific instances but it includes all such circumstances as are inherently improbable, incompatible with the innocence of the accused, so as to make it impossible for the prosecution to prove a criminal charge. [140 B C] 4. The expression is not confined to the actual words spoken or written; it extends to the actual terms spoken or written. The use of the expression in sub section 5 of section 354 makes it clear that the expression is intended to indicate the nature of the offence committed by the accused and its gravity. The expression may also include any other circumstance which the court may consider to be relevant. [141 F G] 5. The expression has been used in sub sections (1) and (2) of section 300, and the expression has been interpreted in the light of the object of the provision. The expression must be given its ordinary meaning. [142 A B] 6. The expression in sub sections 4 and 5 of section 300 of the Code is not restricted to specific instances. 6408: The appellant, a tenant in respect of certain lands belonging to the owners of the land belonging to the respondent, purchased the same under an agreement of sale. 1251: The appellants were in unauthorised occupation of a house situated in the village of Fakira. They filed a writ petition challenging the order of the Deputy Custodian on the ground that the Deputy Custodian had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 18(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and that the order was illegal as it was passed without notice to the appellants. The High Court held that the Deputy Collector had no jurisdiction in the matter and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The right of a non proprietor to occupy a house vested in the Custodian under the provisions of the Act. The right of the non proprietor to remain in possession of the house is not an interest in property but is a right in property. [205 D] (ii) The right to retain possession of a house vested with the Custodian under section 18 of the Act and not in the ownership of the person who occupied the house. [206 E] (iii) The right vested in the custodian is not an absolute or indefeasible right. It is a statutory right. It does not depend upon the time when the right is exercised. It depends upon the circumstances of each case. [207 G H] (iv) The right is not an enduring one. It is capable of being extinguished by statute. It cannot be extinguished except by express enactment or necessary intendment. [208 A B] (v) The right conferred by section 18(2) of the Act is subject to the restrictions contained in section 19(3) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The right is subject to certain exceptions. The right can be exercised only by the Custodian. [209 C D] (vi) The right created by section 18 is not an estate within the meaning of section 2(g) of the . [209 D] (vii) The right given to the non proprietor of a house is not a right in rem. The right given by section 18 to the non proprietors of a house includes the right to remain
6183: The plaintiffs filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 15,40,000/ as their dues from the owners of the vessel. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the first Special Leave Petition was not maintainable since the plaintiffs had already been granted interim orders in the suit and they had not challenged those orders before the trial court; that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case; that the defendants had not adduced any evidence in support thereof; that the trial court had wrongly excluded the entire oral evidence recorded on commission; that the evidence of the defendants was not admissible in view of the earlier Division Bench judgment dated 23.3.1989 on the main point in controversy; that the first appellate court had erred in excluding the defendants ' oral evidence recorded in the suit; that the second appellate court had misread the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 and had erroneously held that the plaintiffs could not be permitted to take advantage of their own wrong. The first appellant had not raised any objection to the admissibility of the said witness. The first respondent had not objected to the admissibility or otherwise of the said document. The first and second appeals were barred by limitation. [777B] 1
2172: The appellants purchased the land in suit from the respondents. The vendees sold it to the appellants. The vendee was not a party to the sale but was impleaded as a co sharer. The vendors filed a suit for preemption and obtained an order of pre emption. The vendes were parties to the suit. 2148: The Assam Primary Education Act, 1947 was passed by the State Legislature and came into force on October 5, 1962. Under section 15 of the Act the State Government was to appoint a Board for Basic Education consisting of a Chairman and two members. Section 16 provided that "all teachers existing or to be appointed in any Elementary School recognised under the Act except in the case of the Autonomous Districts, shall be deemed to have been employed by the State Board". The respondent teachers were not appointed by the State Government but by the Deputy Inspector of Schools. They were inter alia authorised to operate the fund placed at their disposal by the State. The State Advisory Board was constituted under section 15 of this Act with the same headquarter as the Deputy Inspectors of Schools. The State Government issued instructions regarding removal of under matric and non trained teachers from the Board. The respondent teachers challenged the validity of these instructions before the High Court which quashed them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the State Government had no power to issue directions regarding removal of teachers from the board; (ii) the State Advisory Board could not be said to be an authority within the meaning of section 14(3)(iii); (iii) the State had no power under the Act to terminate the services of the teachers who were appointed by it; (iv) the State was not competent to pass orders terminating the services of teachers who were not appointed in the exercise of its powers as appointing authority; (v) the State government had no power even to suspend the teachers who had been appointed by it. HELD: (i) The State Government had power to issue such directions as it thought fit. The State had no right to interfere with the working of the Board. [509 F] (ii) The State had power to terminate the service of the teachers appointed by it in the exercise Of its power as appointing authority. The State has no power to terminate their services. [510 G H] (iii) The State was not entitled to take away the power of the State Government to terminate the appointment of teachers who had already been appointed by the Board. It is only the State Government which can do so. [511 B C] (iv) The State has power to terminate services of teachers

2529: The plaintiff was a karta of a joint Hindu family and the defendant was a karnam. The plaintiff had bid for Rs. 53,025/ and had paid the bid amount in four installments. Appeals against the order of assessment preferred to the Commissioner of Agricultural Income tax and the Board of Agricultural Income Tax, Bihar, were unsuccessful. The appellant filed an appeal to the Board of Revenue which was unsuccessful. In the meantime, the appellant had been appointed Receiver and had been in charge of Court Receiver. The Receiver was not a party to the proceedings before the Board of the Agricultural Income Tax Officer. The appellant contended that the income received by him from the Receiver was exempt from payment of agricultural income tax and by virtue of section 3, agricultural income tax was charged upon the income for the assessment year in question, and the appellant was liable to pay agricultural income tax. The offence must have been committed in India. [779H; 797A] 6. The offence would be complete if the agreement between the parties to carry out the object of the conspiracy is established. [781D E] 7. The offence does not come into play at all. The conspiracy can be inferred from the circumstances. [782E] 8. The offence will be complete when the agreement is found to be impossible or abnormal. 2027: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It is a subsidiary of the appellant company. It has its head office in Bombay and its head office at Bombay. In the year 1956, it proposed to increase the age of retirement from 55 years to 58 years for clerical and subordinate staff and 55 years for factory workmen and to fix the age of superannuation at 60 years both for clerical and sub staff. The company agreed to this proposal and the appellant company accordingly fixed the age of the retirement at 60 years. The company also proposed that the age of superannuating should be 58 years for all workmen. The company however proposed that the retirement age should be 58 or 60 years as the case may be. The company therefore decided to reduce the age of retirements to 55 years. The appellant company contended before the High Court that the age fixed by the company was not reasonable and that the company had no alternative but to fix the same at the same level as in the case of the other factories. The High Court held that the company was entitled to fix the retirement age at 60 years and not at 55 years. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The age of retirement of the company is fixed at 60 years for clerical staff and 55 year for factory workmen. The age of superannuation is fixed at 55 years for clerical employees and 55 years in the case other factories. [526 E] (2) The company had the power to fix the rate of retirement at 60 or 60 years depending upon the circumstances of each case. The company had fixed the age at 55 years and not 55 years. There might have been some justification for fixing the age of retiral at 55 years but there might have been justification for fixing it at 55 years instead of 55 years. [527 F G]

The facts found by the High Courts were sufficient to justify the order of stay. The appellant had not sent any reply to this letter.

6920: The appellant purchased the land in question under a sale deed dated January 24, 1989 for a sum of Rs. 1,58,000/ and paid the balance amount on November 21, 1990. The Collector awarded at Rs. 1.58 per sq. yard and on reference, the Civil Court enhanced the compensation to Rs. 10 per sq. yards with solatium at 15% and interest at 4 per cent. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the award and dismissed the cross objections as well as the cross objectors ' appeals. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended that the High Court erred in taking into consideration the market value of the land in the locality in which the land is situated and awarding the compensation at Rs. 10/ per sq. yd. It was further contended that the sale deeds executed by the respondents relating to the acquired land were not comparable to the lands in the neighbourhood of the land acquired. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court rightly took into consideration the fact that the sale deed in question was executed by the respondent in respect of the land covered by the sale deed dated December 11, 1990. [766C] 2. The High court has correctly taken note of the fact that in building regulation, the land in dispute was not comparable to land in the neighbourhood. The land in dispute could be compared with the land in a neighbouring village. [767D] 3. The High Courts committed grave error in taking into considera tion the market value in the locality where the land in issue is situated. The High courts committed grave error of law in ignoring the fact that there was no evidence to show that the land in possession of the respondents was similar to the land in which the sale deed was executed. [768E F] 4. The Highs Court was right in holding that the land sold by the respondents in favour of the appellant was comparable to the land covered in the sale deed. [769A] 5. The High Cour t erred in taking the value of the lands in a nearby village as the basis for fixing the market value. [770B]

844: The appellant was a public servant and was charged with offences under sections 488/406 and 407 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923. He pleaded that he had been wrongly convicted by the Magistrate of Howrah for an offence under section 406 and section 407 of that Act as extended to the Municipality of Howrah and that the order dated April 7, 1951, passed by the Health Officer of the Municipality was illegal. Held, that the order of the Health Officer was valid and it could not be set aside on the ground that it was made in contravention of the provisions of section 537 of the Calcutta Municipality Act. The order of the Magistrate was not invalid because the order was not made in exercise of his powers under section 537. The order was not a general order which did not affect the order dated July 4, 1951, but only related to the delegation of the Health officer to the Chairman. The order dated April 6, 1951, was not a special order within the meaning of section 538 of the Calcutta municipal Act.
2519: The petitioners were the Chief Ministers of the State of West Bengal and the Chief Minister of West Bengal. They were working in the State as Deputy Collectors, District Magistrates and Sub Divisional Magistrates. In the course of their duties as Deputy Collectors they had to be present at the time when the Governor promulgated an Order under section 3(1) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, for the purpose of preventing disruption of public order. The petitioners were not present at the place where the Order was issued but were present at the meeting of the Council of Ministers held on March 21, 1971. The petitioners ' case was that the speech was likely to have the effect of misrepresenting a piece of illegal legislation before the Court, that the speech could have any such effect as misrepresented a piece of unlawful legislation before the court, that the object of the Order was to prevent widespread agitation in connection with the Order, that the propaganda had misled certain sections of people about the object, purpose and nature of the Order and that the consequences thereof, particularly with regard to the position of supply of fluid milk in the area, and that the question of continued employment of the persons working in the sweetmeat shops in the area did not arise. The petitioners contended that the speech amounted to contempt of court and that it was therefore necessary to take action against the Chief Minister and the Chief Secretary for his willful disobedience of the orders passed by him. Held: (i) The speech was intended to be used as a weapon or device to scandalise the Court and to lower its authority in respect of the administration of justice. The object of the speech was to incite people to commit acts which are calculated to bring disrupt the administration of Justice. The object was to create public disorder and to maintain law and order. The object is to prevent disharmony amongst the members of the public and to deter them from discharging their duties and obligations by resorting to violence and other methods. The object and scope of the speech are to ensure that there should be no interference with the free exercise of the judicial power. The object in making the speech is to prevent evil tendency to bring disgrace to the good of the community
5497: The appellant, a franchise of the Government of India, was elected to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Andhra Pradesh. He filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(1) (b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that he had committed the corrupt practices specified in sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 123 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had not made out any case for declaring him as duly elected. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant had failed to prove that he was either a candidate or a candidate at the election; (ii) the appellant was not entitled to be declared elected because he had not been able to establish his allegation that he was disqualified under section 14A of the Act; (iii) the appellant could not be said to have been proved to have been guilty of any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(5); (iv) the appellant having failed to prove his allegation of corrupt practice, the High Court should not have declared him as duly nominated candidate. HELD: (i) The appellant had not established his allegation of undue influence at the election. [831 E] (ii) The appellant did not make out any case of corrupt practice alleged against him. [832 F] (iii) The appellant was not a party to the election petition. His election was void by reason of the provisions contained in section 100(1)(c) of the Act read with section 123(6). [833 G]
96: The appellant was charged with the murder of his wife and son. The prosecution case was that the appellant administered potassium cyanide poison to a woman who died in the house. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had given her poison to a lady who died in a road accident while she was going to her parents' house. The defence evidence was that the deceased had been ill treated by the appellant and his relations for about two and a half months prior to the death of the deceased, and that he had been living in the house in which the deceased resided with his family members. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 201 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to seven years rigorous imprisonment. On appeal the High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the circumstantial evidence in the case was incompatible with the innocence of the accused and that it had been contradicted in most material particulars by the prosecution evidence itself. Held: (i) that the circumstantial evidences in the case were complementary to each other and could not be used as evidence against the appellant; (ii) that the appellant 's conduct in administering potassium cycle to the deceased was quite unnatural and the circumstances established clearly showed that the appellant was guilty of the offence of murder.

5599: The lands in question were situated at village Bhairav, Taluka Kamrege, District Surat. The Land Acquisition Officer declared the intention to acquire the said land under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Appellant challenged the acquisition by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the notification was not vitiated on account of the absence of any material to show that the lands were not suitable for extension of the village site. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the lands in question did not fall within the purview of section 4 of Land Acquisition Act and that the notification issued under section 6 of the Land Acquisit ion Act was invalid. It is common ground that the extension of the said village site was required for the purpose of housing families who had been rendered homeless because of floods in Tapti river. After consideration and rejection of the objections, the notification for acquisition of the lands under section 6 was issued on December 8, 1970. The notification for acquisition was also challenged on some other grounds. The challenge to the validity of sections 4 and 6 must fail. [901B C] 2. The lands were situated at a distance of about one furlong from the village boundary. There was no evidence to show that they were so near to the village boundary and were likely to be affected by the construction of the new road. The lands could not have been acquired without the prior permission of the State Government. [902D E] 3. The notification dated December 8,1970 was not vitiated as the lands were situated within the limits of the village boundary, and were not necessary for the extension of village site before any acquisition can be resorted to. The lands are situated at a distant place from the village boundaries.

1208: The appellant was a dealer in cotton and cotton. In the year 1939, the Municipal Committee of Khandwa imposed a tax on the sale of cotton by means of steam or mechanical process within the limits of the Khandwa municipality which was imposed by Notification No. 2639 1298 VIII, dated the 21st November 1922. The appellant filed a suit for refund of the tax paid by her on the ground that the imposition of the tax was illegal and ultra vires. The Judicial Committee held that the tax was not validly imposed by the Municipal Committee but it was only a measure of taxation which could be said to have been lawfully imposed by the Provincial Legislature. Held, that the tax must be held to be validly imposed by a competent legislature. The tax is not an impost on goods but a tax on services and it is not possible to hold that the tax is not validly imposed. The tax can be said to be validly levied if the legislature has power under Entry 54 List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution to impose tax on professions, trades, callings and employments.
