914: The Mysore Public Works Engineering Department Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1960 were promulgated by the State Government in exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of the Mysore Public Works (Regulation of Promotion and conditions of service) Act, 1957. Under section 4 of the Act, the Public Service Commission was required to prepare a list of candidates for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineers and to make appointments to the said posts from amongst the candidates who had been selected on the basis of competitive examination held by the Public Service commission. The said list was prepared after considering the claims of all the candidates who were eligible for promotion to the posts. The said lists were published in the official Gazette. The said rules provided that the names of the candidates should be arranged in order of seniority in the cadre of Assistant Engineers. The said orders were challenged before the High Court by the promotees on the ground that they had not been appointed substantively to the post of Assistant Engineer as contemplated under the Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the said orders were illegal and invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the promotions of direct recruits to the posts were made in accordance with the provisions of the Rules and the promotions of the promotees to the posts could not affect their seniority. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1. The promotions of the direct recruits to higher posts are governed by the provisions contained in the Recruitment Rules. The Rules do not provide for any particular method of recruitment. It is only by way of abundant caution that the Rules have been framed in exercise of the power conferred by section 5 of the Mysore State Public Works Engineering Service Act, 1961. [944 C D] 1.2. The Rules have been made under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India. The Rules are not inconsistent with the provisions contained therein. The Rules can operate only prospectively. If the language used in the Rules makes it clear that the Rules cannot operate retrospectively, then the Rules must be read as it is. [946 E F] 1.3. The Rules of 1967 were framed under the proviso thereto. They were not inconsistent with any of the provisions of any of the Acts or the Rules. Therefore, the Rules of 1967 cannot operate retrospectively
333: The plaintiffs were partners of a firm known as Harnam Singh Jagat Singh. In the course of their business they used to make lump sum payments to the defendant against their purchases. When there was an adverse balance the plaintiffs paid the defendant interest and the defendant 's claim was decreed for Rs. 12,496 6 6 and this was upheld on appeal to the High Court. The defendant 's defence was that when India was partitioned on 15 8 1947, Lyallpur, where these transactions took place and where the money was situate, was assigned to Pakistan, and the Pakistan Government froze all evacuee assets and later compelled the defendant to hand them over to the Custodian of Evacuee Property in Pakistan. The plaintiffs ' case is that they carried on business with the defendant company for some three or four years before 1947 and purchased cloth from the company for certain three or four year before 1947 and sold cloth to the defendant. The defendant was not liable for any loss caused by the sale of cloth. The plaintiffs claimed that they had been put into possession of the cloth and that the defendant was entitled to recover the amount due under the contract. Held, that the suit was barred by limitation. The contract between the parties was one which was binding upon the parties and the question whether the goods were delivered to the defendant at the time of the contract did not arise. The contract was a contract for the supply of goods and not a contract for sale. The contract being one for the supply and not a sale, it could be enforced only if the contract was one for the delivery of goods. The contract in the present case was one for payment of money and not a transfer of property. The contract did not create any title in favour of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs were not entitled to recover any money from the defendant.
904: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of carding and drawing of carding. In the year 1948, the Government amended the U. P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 by substituting for the words " wages " in place of " bonus " in place thereof. The Act provided that where an employer has to pay a minimum wage under section 3 of the Act, he shall be entitled to deduct from the wages payable to him such minimum wage as may be fixed under the Act. The appellant company contended before this Court that the Government order did not require or justify the company in including the additional emoluments being paid by way of production bonus and incentive bonus, if so, to what extent. The contention was rejected by this Court. HELD : (i) The definition of " wages " is wide enough to include all payments which are made by the employer to his employees on account of wages, allowances, bonus, etc., but it does not exclude payment of bonus by way of incentive bonus. [493 D] (ii)The word " wages" in the definition of "wages" in section 2(g) of the U.P. Act means basic wages plus dearness allowance, and in the case of the appellant company there is no such term. It is only the basic wages which are included in the definition. The basic wages include dearness allowance, bonus, gratuity, etc. and the incentive bonus. Therefore, the appellant company cannot be said to have been paying any basic wage at all. [494 E F] (iii)The definition of " Wages " in section 2 (g) of U.P., Act, 1947, is wide enough and includes all benefits which are given to workmen by the Act. [495 B C] (iv)The definition in section 2 of the U P. Act is wide enough. The definition of 'wages' in section 2 is wide enough, and the definition of 'slubs ' in section 2, is wide. [496 A B] (v)The definition is wide enough even to include all benefits which would otherwise be available to the workmen. [497 G]
2946: The appellant was appointed as Head Mistress of a school run by the Madras Government. She applied for recognition and aid to the school under the Madras Elementary Education Act, 1920. The Manager refused to grant her recognition on the ground that she had not obtained the requisite permission from the Government. The District Educational Officer directed the Management to remove her from the post of Head Mistri. The Manager appealed to the Director of Public Instruction who set aside the order of the District Educational Officer. The High Court held that the order passed by the Manager removing her from the office of Head Mistry was illegal because the Manager was bound by rr. 13 & 14 framed under the Madras Act VIII of 1920, and the Rules framed thereunder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the school was receiving grant in aid from the Government; (ii) the school being an aided school, the manager could not be compelled to obey the orders of the Government; and (iii) the school having been established by a minority, the manager was bound by the rules and regulations framed under the Act. HELD: (1) The school was not a private school but was a private one. It was not a public school. [1046 F] (2) The school being a private one, the manager had no power to make any appointment or take any disciplinary action against the headmaster. The management declined to do so and refused to allow him to continue in service. The management refused to permit him to continue his service. The manager was bound to comply with the orders of Government. The management did not act in breach of the rules and regulation framed under the Tamil Nadu Elementary Education Act. [1047 C D] (3) The school is not a private one and the manager cannot be compelled to disobey the orders of a competent authority. The manager has no right to interfere with the management 's control over the school. [ 1048 E] (4) The school having been admitted to grant in aid under the Madras Primary Education Act, 1923, the manager became entitled to remain in possession of the school till its revival. The management failed to discharge its duties properly. The management was bound to obey the order of Government. [1049 A B
39: The appellant was arrested on the 27th of October, 1947 and was granted bail. On the 1st December, 1947, sanction under section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was issued by the Government to prosecute him for offences punishable under sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was produced before the Special Magis trate on the 28th of November, 1947, but was released on bail on the 31st January, 1949. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and, as no sanction of the Government was obtained before that date, the initiation of proceedings against him was illegal. Held, that when a warrant is issued by a Magistrate in respect of an accused person who is being prosecuted for committing an offence under section 161 or 165 of the I.P.C., it is only after the Magistrate takes cognizance of the said offence that he can proceed with the case. The word "may" used in section 319 of the Code does not mean "shall". The word "shall" used in the proviso to section 3 of the Act means "shall". In the present case, the Magistrate had taken cognizance of the case without the previous sanction of the Central Government. The order which may be applied for and made during the police investigation by virtue of section 3 of Act II of 1947, hereinafter referred to as the Act, was illegal.
2716: The appellant was tried and convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Declaration of Stock Order, 1964 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ in default further rigorous imprisonment for three months. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's R. I. R. and imposed a fine of Rs, 500/ in the case. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that (i) the rule laid down in section 114 of the Evidence Act is ultra vires the Defence of India Act; (ii) the rule is not ultra vires the Constitution; (iii) the rule made under section 3(1) of the Maharashtra Act is ultravires the Constitution; and (iv) the rule making authority has no power to forfeit the property seized from the house of the appellant. HELD: (i) The rule is intra vires the Defence Act. It is not ultravires. [766 C] (ii) The rule does not make any provision authorising the court to forfeit the subject matter of the contravention of cls. 3 and 4 of the Maharashtra Declarations of Stock Orders, 1964. [767 D E] (iii) The rule cannot be said to be ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114, Indian Evidence Act. [768 F] (iv) The rule can be said to have been enacted with a view to prevent the misuse of the rule. But the rule must be so construed as to give effect to the intention of the legislature. If the rule is so construed it would be unreasonable to hold that the rule is beyond the legislative competence of the State Legislature. [769 B]
5655: The petitioner was appointed as Additional District & Sessions Judge in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service on January 23, 1979. While he was on deputation to the Delhi High Court, he was sent on deputation as Registrar, Special Courts, New Delhi and he remained on deputation until March 26, 1980 when he was transferred to Delhi. On April 26, 1980, the Government of India appointed a Commission of Inquiry presided over by Shri Justice Ranganath Misra, Judge, Supreme Court of India under the provisions of section 3 of the for the purpose of making enquiries into a matter of public importance namely, the allegations in regard to the incidents of organised violence in Delhi following the assassination of Smt. On May 27, 1979, the petitioner came back to Delhi and joined as an Additional District & Session Judge. In June, 1979, he was posted as the Secretary of the Commission. When he was still working as the Member Secretary of the Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board, on April 26, 1979, his services were terminated by the Government of Delhi. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the termination order dated April 26,1980. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination order was not valid because it was passed without giving him any opportunity of being heard. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The appointment of the petitioner as Additional District and Sessions Judge is not in violation of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. [263C] 1.2 The appointment of a person as a member of the Commission is made after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The consultation contemplated by Article 320(3)(c) of the constitution is with the Chief Justices of all the States. The consultation envisaged by Article 320 (3)(c), therefore, is with the Governor of the State. [264E F] 1.3 The appointment of an Additional District Judge is made after obtaining the concurrence of the Chief Justice. The consultation is with the concurrence of two other Judges of the High Court. The consultation has no relation to the nature of the power exercised by the appointing authority or the appointing authority. It is only through the consultation that the appointing authority can make the appointment. [265F G
4019: The assessee appellant was a registered firm carrying on business at various places in the State of Kerala. In apportioning the profits of the two assessment years 1964 65 and 1965 66, the Income Tax Officer took the view that the losses in speculation business could not be apportioned between the partners but should be carried forward and set off against the profit in the said business made in the assessment year 1966 67. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the losses were not set off against future profits in the assessment for the assessment year 1960 61. The High Court answered the reference in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. In the appeal to this Court it was contended by the Revenue that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the losses of the two assessments for the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 should be set off against its speculation profit in the assessment of the firm for the assessment yea 62. The question whether the losses in the speculation business can be set off or set off against past profits in the said assessment year was considered by this Court in the case of Kantilal Nathuchand (supra) and it was held that the loss in the speculative business could not have been set off against any future profits in that assessment year. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly held that the profits and gains of the two assess ment years are not set off under section 2(1)(i) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [1275 C D] 2. The first proviso to section 2(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961 provides that where the assessee is a registered firm, the loss in speculation shall be set off only against the profits and gain if any, of the firm. The second proviso to section 4(3) of the Act provides that where any loss computed in respect of a speculation business carried on by the assessee is set off against his speculation profit, the loss so set off shall not be set off except against the profits of that speculation business. [1276 E F] 3. The second Proviso to section 4 (3) of Act 2 of 1961 provides that if any loss computed as aforesaid is set off in
5395: The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in shares and securities. In the assessment year 1966 67, the Income Tax Officer determined the tax payable by the assessee under section 147(b) of the Act on the basis of the return filed by it for the assessment year 1967-68. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the said order. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee had not shown any capital gain or loss as such and that the amount of Rs.2,51,222 representing 6% of the capital employed in the undertaking was not taxable. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the amount represented capital gains and not revenue profits. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal should have taken into account the provisions of Section 84 of the Act and should have deducted the same from the total income of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly taken note of the fact that profits earned during the year had already been taken into account in the process of computa tion and there was no warrant for its addition over again to the extent of a moiety. [591C] 2. The expression "in the case of assets acquired by purchase and entitled to depreciation ' used in rule 19(5) is to be added to the figure of actual cost to the assessee. The words "in the cases of assets acquired" are used in Rule 19(5). The word "income" is defined in the Explanation to the said rule as including any sum charged for anything done by the assessee during the previous year. [592E F] 3. The expression 'profits derived' in rule 19 (5) is not confined to the actual cost to be included in the total income but includes all income from whatever source derived which may be received or receivable by the assessee. [593A B] 4. The expression in the context of the provision of section 84 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 means the income from any asset or income from other sources. [594D] 5. The expression is used in a wider sense than the expression "income from other sources". It means income from property or income from some kind
569: The appellant company was carrying on business as manufacturer of iron and steel. In the course of its business it sold certain goods to the respondent who paid them in the State of Bihar. The sales were assessed to sales tax under the Act. The respondent contended that the sales were not taxable because the property in the goods passed to the purchasers in the State, and that the sales had been effected by the seller in the State and not in the State. Held, that the sales could be taxed only in the State where the goods were delivered in the State for consumption or use within that State and not where the goods are actually consumed or used in the State itself. The word " consumption" is not defined in the Act but it has been held by this Court in a number of cases that the word " consumption " would include consumption in the context of the Act. It is well settled that if a taxing statute authorises the imposition of a tax it must be presumed that the legislature intended the same thing to be done. If there is any ambiguity in the language of the statute, the rule which requires the court to give effect to the meaning of the words used in the statute should be applied.
38: The appellant was tried before the Sub Divisional Magistrate of Guntur in respect of offences under the Motor Spirit Rationing Order, 1941. In the first case, the charges against him and the employee were that they on the 27th June, 1945 at Guntur, supplied petrol to a cars without taking coupons in contravention of clause 22 read with clause 5 of the Order promulgated under section 81 (2) of the Defence of India Rules and that they, on the same day and at the same place, accepted coupons relating to two other cars without taking vouchers in contravention of the said clause. The plea of the appellant before the Magistrate was that he was the presiding officer of the sub-divisional magistrate Court, Chirala, that he was not guilty of an offence under rule 81 of the Defence Of India Rules and was liable for transgression of the rules committed by his employees. The plea was rejected by the Magistrate. On appeal, the High Court held that the conviction was justified but granted special leave to appeal to this Court. HELD : The view taken by the Privy Council is the correct view. The law as propounded by the Privy council is that mens rea must be proved to have been present when the act complained of is alleged to have been done or attempted to be done. [329 B] The question whether mens re an d not proved to have known of the unlawful acts of the second appellant does not depend upon the degree of mens reasness. It depends upon the facts of each case. If the evidence shows that the second appellant had knowledge of the unlawful act of the second petitioner, it would be difficult to hold that he was guilty of an offense under rule 81(2) of Order XLI of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [331 D E]
1758: The respondents were displaced persons who had been allotted evacuee agricultural land in Hyderabad State. They filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Regional Settlement Commissioner dated July 10, 1954, and also prayed for a direction to the Deputy Secretary to the Government of India to cancel the allotment made by the Central Government in favour of the respondents. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of cancellation was not vitiated on account of any error apparent on the face of it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Central Government had no power under section 33 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, to revise the order of Regional Settlement Commissioner. [439 E] (2) The Central Govern ment could interfere with the order of allotment only if it was shown that the order was erroneous or that it was based on some extraneous considerations. [440 F] (3) The Central Govt. could not direct the cancellation of the allotment without reference to the Central Government. [441 A] (4) The Central government could not interfere with the orders of the Regional Officer. [442 B] (5) The Central Governments had no power to issue directions to the Deputy Secretaries to the Government to cancel the allotments made by them. [446 C] (6) The Central Gov ernment had no power even to pass an order of cancellation of the allotments made in favour of a person who had been granted a lease of the land in question. [447 D]
6422: The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of respondent No. 1 from the suit premises on the ground of default in payment of rent for a period of more than six months. The trial court decreed the suit and confirmed the decree for eviction passed by the Trial Court. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the undertaking given by respondent No.1 was not unconditional and that the said undertaking was binding on the parties. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court rightly held that the undertaking furnished by respondent No, 1 was unconditional and the same could be enforced against respondent No. 2. [656C] 2. The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the undertaking should be unconditional and should not be subject to any conditions or restrictions. In the instant case, the undertaking given is unconditional and it binds respondent No.2. [657E] 3. The undertaking given by the respondent No. l cannot be said to be unconditional. It is an undertaking given by a person who has been in possession of the property as a tenant. The undertaking must be unconditional in nature. The undertaking can be enforced only against the tenant. [658F] 4. The undertaking which is unconditional does not bind the tenant. The tenant cannot be dispossessed without following due process of law. [659G] 5. The undertaking is unconditional. The undertaking cannot be enforced against the tenant unless he is able to establish that the undertaking is not uncondi tional. [660A] 660 A.B]
2624: The appellants workmen employed in the respondent company were working as depots of the Company. They were doing the work of collecting tobacco, though the company had given a notice to them that out of 21 depots mentioned therein would be closed down with effect from 30th September, 1963. The company gave a notice to the Union of the appellant workmen that out of these 21 depots, 11 depots were closed on 30th September 1963 and the remaining 12 depots were not closed on 30.9.1963. The company also gave a notice that the rest of the 12 depots would be closed on 30st September, 1963 and the rest of 12 depots will be closed on 31st October, 1963. On 16th August, 1963, the Company gave a notice under section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 to the Union for closure of the depots. The Union gave a notice on 16th August 1963 to the Union stating that it was agreeable to close down the depots at the end of March 1963. Thereafter, an industrial dispute was raised by the workmen which related to the closure of the Depot. The Tribunal held that the closure of depots amounted to closure of business and directed the Company to pay compensation to the workmen. The Company challenged the decision of the Tribunal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the closure was genuine and real and that the Tribunal had no power to adjudicate upon it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The closure of the depot is genuine and real. The closure of a depot does not amount to closure of the business of the company. [801C] (ii) The closure is genuine and true. The closure is not genuine or real. The question whether the closure is genuine or not is a mixed question of fact and law. [802B C] (iii) The closure has been proved to have taken place on account of the circumstances beyond the control of the management. The closure must be bona fide and real. [803D E] (iv) The closure cannot be said to be mala fide or without any material on record. It is only when the management is satisfied that the closure is bona fide and is real and real.
124: The appellant company was incorporated in 1937 with an authorised capital of Rs. 10,00,000 divided into one lac shares of Rs.10 each. In 1938 the Company resigned from the managing agency of the Mills and the shares were forfeited by a resolution of the Board of Directors of the Mills. The Company thereafter resigned and the shares became forfeited. The Company did not pay either of the calls made by the Company or the shares were not forfeited. The appellant company filed a suit for rectification of the register of the Company on the ground that the Company had committed breach of the agreement between the parties and that the shares were liable to be forfeited. The trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Company could not be said to have committed breach of any agreement entered into between the parties. On appeal by special leave it was contended: (i) that the Company was not entitled to claim relief under section 38 of the Indian Companies Act; (ii) that the shares which were forfeited were not available to the appellant company as the Company had failed to take steps to restore the shares to the register of members; (iii) that the appellant company was not entitled under section 38(1)(a) of the Act to claim any relief against forfeiture; (iv) that the allotment of shares was illegal and void; (v) that the company was not liable to refund the amount paid by the appellant company to the Company. HELD : (i) The appellant company cannot be said to be a shareholder in respect of 5,000 shares. The shares were not available for being sold by the Company at its own cost. The shares could not be sold without payment of the price. [356 B] (ii) The appellant was not entitled, therefore, to claim any benefit under section 38. [355 C D] (iii) The appellant is not entitled to any relief under section 39 of the Act. [354 E]
3112: The respondent was a citizen of India and was a citizen under article 5 of the Constitution. He applied for and obtained an Indian visa which was valid upto January 26, 1955. On January 27, 1955 he again applied for and obtain a permit under cl. 7 of the Foreigners Order, 1948. In the revision application filed by him in the High Court of Assam and Nagaland, the High Court relying on Fida Hussain 's case (1) held that as in the case of Fida Hussain(1), the respondent was a natural born British subject, that being so he was at the date of his entry in India in April 1955, a citizen of Pakistan, and therefore was not required to obtain a permit. Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent had migrated to Pakistan between March 1, and January 26, 1950, when he was a foreigner. Fida Hussain vs U.P.(2) The fact that the respondent did not leave India after January 26, 195 1, is immaterial because the question whether he had migrated or not has to be decided on the facts of each case. Fida Husain vs State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , relied on.
490: The respondent company was carrying on life insurance business and the appellant issued annual fire insurance policies and received a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as premiums thereof, the whole of it would be shown as income in the statement for the year 1939, and a sum of 40,000 will be shown as a liability under r. 2 of Sch. 11 of the Income Tax Act, 1922. In the profit and loss account for the year 1940, the respondent claimed that the amount of Rs. 40,000 should be deducted as a liability to pay for the unexpired period of the policies in the illustration given by the Tribunal. The Income tax Officer disallowed this claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the premium paid was not capital and that the profits were not taxable. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the respondent. Held: (i) The word " revenue" has been used in section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, in its widest sense, and is not confined only to such receipts as are brought into account by the assessee. The word " capital" means capital or income which is received or receivable, whether in cash or kind or partly in cash and partly in kind. It does not include capital gains arising from the transfer of assets or the acquisition of any rights or interest therein; and the word " capital " includes capital gains also. (ii)The word " capital receipt" in section 10 (2) (xv) of Act, 1922 means capital receipt, and not capital receipt. (iii)In the present case, the premiums received were capital receipts and not capital receipts. (iv)The word ' capital receipt ' in section 10 of the Indian Act means capital receipt.
3116: The appellant was tried for offenses under section 120B IPC. He was acquitted by the special judge, Ganganagar. The State of Rajasthan filed an appeal against the acquittal of Ram Swaroop and Bhagat Ram in respect of all the charges. The High Court dismissed the appeal against the conviction of Ram Swaroo P.W. 1 and Ram Swaroop P.W..2. The State appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the case against him had not been proved and the State appeal in that respect also was liable to be dismissed. HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove its case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. [306C] (ii) The evidence of the two witnesses clearly established that the appellant had accepted bribe from Puran Chand. The evidence of these two witnesses clearly showed that the appellant was a person who had come to the house of Puran Chand with a view to extort money from him. There is no reason why the appellant should have taken advantage of his position. [307D E] (iii) The evidence shows that the appellant took the stand that he had received the amount of Rs. 7000 from Puran Singh. This is very important and please do not be careless and slack in the matter. [308E]
3668: The appellant was the sole proprietor of a Hindu Undi sity and carried on business of various types such as money lending etc. The appellant obtained a certified from the High Court for appeal to this Court under sub clause (b) of clause (1) of Article 133 of the Constitution of India as it stood before the 30th Constitution Amendment Act, 1956 as it stood prior to the 30th amendment. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment proceedings and the orders passed by the Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not been able to show any ground which would justify interference with the order of the Income tax officer refusing to record partition and direct the Income tax authorities to take action for recovery of the taxes so assessed. In appeal to this court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the jurisdiction of the High Courts is very wide but the power of judicial review is limited to seeing that an inferior Court or Tribunal functions without jurisdiction, or there is no power to its authority; and that even if they have trappings of finality, it must be remembered that there is a distinction between competency of a suit and merit. [308 D] 2. The High courts are not constituted merely by designation as judges of appellate tribunals; they are constituted by officers of the Government. They can do all acts and deeds which affect the rights of individuals without affecting their own interests or who act in good faith in the course of the discharge of his duties or who decide cases as to whom the justice of the particular case should be ordered or done. [309 E F] 3. The High court has jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition when there is a failure of justice. But the High Court cannot interfere where the petitioner has acted in good faith or misrepresented facts which have come to the notice of the Income Tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. [310 C D] 4. The High has jurisdiction to examine whether the findings recorded by the Income Tax Officers are based upon some evidence or are perverse. [311 A B] 5. The High is not competent to enter into the merits of the matter and to set aside the
2272: The respondent was a tenant of the appellant 's premises. The respondent, a club, had obtained a licence from the Government of Maharashtra for running two race courses, one in Bombay and the other at Poona. The respondent was assessed to tax under the Bombay Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1947, as it was carrying on business in the said premises. The assessment was made on the basis of the Club 's accounts for the year 1953 54 that being the year concluded before the assessment. The respondent filed an appeal before the Small Cause Court, Bombay, under section 217 of the Act. The Small Cause Court allowed the appeal holding that the respondent was not entitled to claim any deduction from the gross annual rent and deducting therefrom the percentages allowable under section 15.4 of the Act, and that the respondent could not be allowed to deduct the amount of depreciation which would have been admissible under section 15, and that he should be given the benefit of the reduced rate of depreciation. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the respondent 's contention that it is a, machinery and its value therefore is not to be included in rating under section 154(2) was untenable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the proper method for determining the annual rent was the profits basis method but upheld the respondent ' s contention as regards the disallowance of the several items of expenditure. [1322 E] (2) The High court was wrong in holding that since the respondent ' firm was carrying on the business in the premises in question, the proper method of determination of the annual rent would be the profits basis. [1323 F G] (3) The High Courts decision was correct and the appeals must be dismissed. [1324 B C] (4) The High courts decision was correct. [1325 D] (5) The High 'Court was right in allowing the appeal. [1326 A] (6) The High. Court was right when it held that the proper test for determining the income of a club is the profit or loss of the club. [1327 B] (7) The High, Court was right on the facts found by the Tribunal in the present case. [1328 B]
364: The petitioners, who were the owners of certain lands in Touzi No. 28 of the Collectorate of Hazaribagh, filed a suit for declaration that the properties comprised in the disputed properties did not vest in the State under the provisions of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 and that they had become the owners of the said properties by virtue of the notification issued under section 3(1) of the Act. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 (1) of Act declaring that the estate of the petitioners was vested in the State on the 25th September, 1950. On the date of vesting the petitioners were the owners and the State Government issued notices to the petitioners under section 4(h) of the Bihar Act and after considering their objections, the State Government passed an order vesting the disputed properties in the State. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notices before the High Court which held that the properties stood vested in the state on the 25 th September, 1950, and accordingly quashed the orders of the State Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the vesting of the properties in the state took place before the Act came into force and therefore the notification issued by the State Government under section 3 of the Act was valid. HELD : The vesting of the property in the State is complete only when the Act comes into force and the notification issued thereunder becomes effective as soon as the Act comes in force. [990 E] The vesting of a property in the state does not depend upon the making of the Act or its commencement. It may be that the Act may have been passed but the Act has not yet come into force. The vesting of any property in the government is merely incidental to the creation of the statute. [991 F G] The vesting takes place immediately on the passing of the Act and the notification under section 4 of the Act must be published in the Official Gazette. The vesting takes effect only when the law comes into force. Therefore, the vesting takes place at the time when the Act is passed and the notification is published in the official gazette. [992 A B]
2670: The assessee purchased shares in a company which was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The shares were sold by the company to its shareholders and the sale proceeds were credited to the profit and loss appropriation account. The assessee received dividend on the shares in question from the company. The assessee claimed that the amount of Rs. 43,925/ should be treated as dividend and should be assessed under section 12 of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee acquired the shares on which the arrear dividends were received in the course of its share dealing business and that the sum of Rs.43,925/- was not income liable to income tax as it was merely a realisation of capital. The Tribunal confirmed the finding of the Income Tax authorities. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The assessee had no right to claim the amount of the dividend received by it as a result of the sale of the shares in the company. [880 E] (2) The assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 12 of Income tax Act. The assessee could not be said to have acquired the shares in a case where the assessee had no interest in the shares. [881 F G] (3) The assessee did not acquire any interest in the share of the assessee. It was only a realisation of the capital that was generated by the sale of shares. [881 D] (4) The assessee could be said to be carrying on business within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Act. The fact that the assessee was carrying on business does not make the assessee a person carrying on business. [882 C] (5) The assessee is not carrying on business at all. The assessee has no interest in shares. [891 D]
5086: The assessee, a company, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling plantations. It had obtained a loan from the Kerala State Electricity Board for the purpose of establishing a factory in the State of Kerala. The assessee claimed that it was liable to pay interest on the loan amount at the rate of 12% per annum from the date of repayment till the date of payment. The assessing authority disallowed the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment. In an appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the amount of interest allowed to be deducted in the assessment of the assessee fell under one of those clauses and was therefore rightly deducted in computing its agricultural income. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the amount received by the assessee was not agricultural income. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The remission cannot, in our opinion, be considered as amounting to the receipt of agricultural income. [647E] 2.1 The expression "agricultural income" has been used in section 3 of the Kerala Agricultural Income tax Act, 1950. The word "income" is defined in section 2(15) of the Act to mean "the total agricultural income of all the previous years". The word "gross" is defined to include agricultural income. Section 3 of the Act provides that agricultural income shall be charged for each financial year on the total agricultural income. In the judgment under appeal, the High Court took the view that it was immaterial that the assessees followed the mercantile system of accounting, because the case was not one of actual receipt or receipt. The High court did not take into account the fact that the assessee had paid interest on loans advanced by the Kerala State Government. The High 'Court was wrong in holding that it was not agricultural revenue. [648A B] 2.2 The remission in the present case could not amount to agricultural income. There was no evidence to show that the assessee followed the merchant system of accounting. The assessee had not produced any evidence to show what was the yield of the crop. The assessee was entitled to deduction of the amount of Rs.33,747.09 from
6032: The respondents were the owners of certain properties in Pakistan. They migrated to Pakistan during the disturbances of 1947 and continued to live there as an evacuee. In the year 1947, the Custodian General passed an order under section 8(1) of the Evacuee (Administration of Properties) Act, 1950 declaring that the sale was invalid since the property was evacuee property and belonged to one Shah Mahmood who had migrated to India during the disturbance of 1947 and remained there as an evacuees. Against this order, the respondents preferred a revision before the Custodian General which was dismissed on 5.2.1973. Thereafter, the respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the orders of the Custodian General and the Custodian General. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Custodian General had no jurisdiction to entertain any application made by persons laying claim to properties which have been notified as evacuee property under the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. Section 8 of the Evacuee Property Act, 1950 is not applicable to the present case because the Custodian General has no power to make a reference to the High Court under section 8 of the Act. [474C] 2. Section 8 provides for the procedure to be followed by the Custodian General while disposing of an application under section 8. It does not provide for any other mode of disposal of such applications. The Custodian General can dispose of the same in accordance with law. He cannot exercise his powers under section 8 in respect of matters covered by section 8. [475D E] 3. Section 8(3A) provides that the Custodian may, after making an enquiry into the matter, pass an order declaring the property to be evacuee property. The Custodian can also direct the Custodian to take possession of the property. [476E F] 4. Section 8 applies only where the property is evacuee property. [480F] 5. Section 8 does not apply to cases where the property has been declared to be evacuee properties. Section 8 is not applicable where the property was declared to be an evacuee property. Section 8 deals with the situation where the property had been declared to vest in the Custodian. [477G H]
1432: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 149 and section 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. They challenged their conviction by a single appeal, but the High Court acquitted them on the ground that there was no evidence to show that they had taken part in the murder. Held, that the eye witnesses who saw the occurrence did not say anything about the presence of the appellants at the time of the commission of the crime. The evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and the High Court was right in holding that the eye witness had seen the occurrence. The evidence was not sufficient to prove that the appellants had taken part at the time when the murder took place. The evidence must be accepted as true unless it is corroborated in material particulars. The evidence should be accepted only if it is corroborated by other independent evidence. The evidence given by the eye witnesses must be accepted without corroboration. The evidence which has been accepted by the High Court cannot be said to be unimpeachable.
3853: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court acquitted the accused on the ground that the evidence of the eye witness Hari Singh, P.W. 1 and Chandra Pal, P.Ws. 2 and 3 was not reliable. The High court held that the evidence was not reliable because the deceased had been shot at the place of occurrence and the injuries were caused by fire arm. The High 'Court also found that the prosecution case was doubtful as the deceased had received only one injury in the course of the incident. The High. Court further held that the defence version was not believable because the deceased was a young man of 25 years of age and he had no previous enmity with his family or any other person. The High, Court also found that there was no motive for the murder. The High' Court also found the evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 4 to be unreliable because they were related to the deceased and their presence at the time of the occurrence was highly improbable. The High _Court therefore convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no reason why the evidence of an injured witness should be discarded. [901 G] 2. The evidence of the injured witness cannot be rejected merely because he happens to be a relative of the deceased. If the injured witness has seen the occurrence, it is possible that he may have been present at the time when the occurrence took place. But if he does not see the occurrence, his testimony cannot be treated as effaced or tainted. [902 B C]
3072: The petitioners who were the hereditary Archakas and Mathadhipatis of some ancient Hindu Public temples in Tamil Nadu, filed petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious Institutions (Officers and Servants) Service Rules, 1964. Rule 12 provided that every 'ulthurai servant, whether hereditary or nonhereditary whose duty it was to perform pujas and recite mantras, vedas, prabandams, thevarams and other invocations shall, before succeeding, or appointing to an office holder, obtain a certificate of fitness for performing his duties, from the head of an institution imparting instructions in Agamas and ritualistic matters and recognised by the Commissioner, by general or special order or from the head Of an institution imparting instruction in Agamashram, by general and special order or such other person as may be designated by the Commissioner from time to time for the purpose. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of the Madras Hindu Religious Institutions Act, 1920, are applicable to the temptation of the math and reciting the spirituals of the religious faith of the matha sect. [819E] 1.2. The provisions relating to the appointment of a fit person to perform the functions of the office or performance the service after having due regard to the claims of the members of the family, power to make rules to regulate the mode of appointment and conditions of service of the persons appointed, do not violate the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 14 of the Constitution. [820B C] 1.3. The provisions regarding the appointment of fit persons to perform the function of the office holders and servants in the religious institutions of the temple are not violative of article 14 of
5205: The petitioners were employed in the State of Andhra Pradesh as Assistant Engineers. They filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of clause (3) of Article 371 D of the Constitution on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution and that they had been deprived of their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Administrative Tribunal constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission Act, 1958 had no jurisdiction to deal with the service matters specified in the order of the Administrative Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Administrative Tribunal is a creature of the statute and its decision cannot be impeached by way of an application for judicial review. [886 B] 2. The Administrative Tribunals are not courts of record but are meant for the people of India. It is not possible to accept the contention that the Administrative Tribunals have become necessary parties in the writ petitions. [887 C] 3. The Administrative tribunal has no power or authority to sit in judgment over the decisions of the administrative tribunals. [886 E] 4. The Administrative tribunals are not courts in the strict sense of being Courts of Record. [885 F] 5. The Administrative Tribun als are not courts merely because they have to decide questions of fact. [889 G] 6. The Administrative Tri bunal is not a court of record nor is it a court subordinate to the High Court. [891 H] 7. The Administrative authorities are not courts within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution and therefore they are not bound to follow the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure. [882 A B] 8. The Administrative Law Reforms Committee, New Delhi vs Union of India, ; , referred to.
5302: The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the sale deed executed by her mother in favour of the appellant was invalid and was not binding upon him. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the alienation was not something which a man of ordinary prudence would have effected had the properties been owned by him and thus held it not binding on the plaintiff. In second appeal, the question whether improvements made to the tune of Rs.4,000 could be ordered without payment of the value of improvements was decided against the appellants. In second appeals, the High court held that the alienations were not binding upon the appellants as they were not made bona fide. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the alienation of the property involved in the case was not binding on them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the sale of the property is not binding on it. [875C] 2. The High court was right in holding that there was no material to show that the appellants had made any improvements or that the improvements were made with the intention of defeating the claim of the respondent. [877D] 3. The High Courts decision does not operate as res judicata between the parties. [878E] 4. The High courts decision cannot be said to be final. It is open to the parties to raise objections at an appropriate stage. [879F] 5. The High Cour ts judgment does not operate in rem. [880A] 6. The High 'Court was wrong in holding that in case of eviction, the respondents would be entitled to Rs.4.164 as compensation for improvements. His further submission is that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of Section 2(d) of the Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958. [881B]
5814: The petitioners in the Writ Petition were appointed as Assistant Engineers (Civil) in the Central Public Works Department and were promoted to the post of Executive Engineer. In the year 1973, the Government issued a policy for reservation of posts for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the services under the Union of India. The said policy was adopted by the Government in supersession of the orders contained in an earlier Government Order dated 11.7.1968. The petitioners contended that the policy was not applicable to them because they belonged to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes and were entitled to be considered for promotion to the higher cadre on the basis of seniority subject to fitness. The respondents contended that the petitioners were not entitled to be promoted to the higher post on the basis that they belong to the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe. Allowing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy contained in the letter dated 23.12.1983 is not applicable to the petitioners who are working in the other departments of the Union of Indian. [628B] 1.2 The petitioners have been given the benefit of reservation of posts in the posts of Executive Engineers and Executive Engineers which are meant for Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes. They cannot claim any benefit on the basis thereof. [629C D] 1.3 The petitioners have not been able to show that the policy of reservation of the posts in the post of Superintending Engineer and Executive Engineer has been withdrawn or withdrawn in a manner so as to enable them to get promotion to the next higher post. [630E F] 1.4 The petitioners do not fall within the category of Scheduled Castes and Schedule Tribes. They are not entitled to get any benefit on account of the fact that they belong either to the Scheduled castes or the Scheduled Tribes. [631G H] 1.5 The petitioners have no right to claim promotion to the post in question. [632A] 1.6 The petitioners have also no right to seek promotion to the posts in question. They have only a right to be considered against the vacancies arising in future. [633F] 1.7 The petitioners have failed to show that there was any violation of Article 16(1) of the Constitution. 4741: The petitioners who were members of a State Legislature, had been organising lottery in the State of Maharashtra and organizing lottery tickets in other States. The Government of India issued a Press release of the Director of Publicity, Sachivalaya, Bombay dated September 24, 1969, to some of the petitioners individually. The Government had given permission for conducting State lotteries in the State without the express consent of the State Government. The Government was not competent to issue such a notification or order under Article 258(1) of the Constitution. The ban imposed by the Government of India was not a restriction on the right of the State to carry on trade or business in the State. The ban was imposed by the State Government with the object of regulating the sale of lottery tickets of other States. It was contended that the ban was invalid as it infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 301 and 304(b) of the constitution. Held: (i) The ban is not a restriction but only a restriction; it is a restriction which is reasonable and in the interest of the general public. The restrictions are reasonable if they are not calculated to promote the free movement of the state. [447C] (ii) The ban does not amount to an unreasonable restriction. The ban may be justified in the interests of the general community or the people of a particular State. But it cannot be said that the ban is merely an incidental or ancillary power to the carrying out of the policy of the State towards securing the principles specified in Clause (b) of article 39 of the Constitution, and that the ban must be reasonable in the interest and for the protection of the general welfare of the people. [448D E] (iii) The ban cannot be held to be unconstitutional because it offends against the provisions of article 301 of the Constitution and is therefore void.
6018:
The respondent joined service as a technical assistant with the Gujarat State Electricity Board (hereinafter referred to as 'the Board') on 1st March, 1974. While he was posted at Surat as Deputy Engineer he was transferred to Ukai subdivision under the order of the Superintending Engineer dated 29th March, 1974 and relieved him from his duties at Surat on 30th March,

1974. He made representation for cancellation of his transfer order on the ground that his mother aged years was ailing and it would cause great inconvenience to him if he was required to join at Ukai. His representation was rejected by the Chief Engineer on 27th May, 1974. He filed a civil suit in the Court of Civil Judge, Baroda challenging validity of the order of discharge. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the order of termination of the respondent was illegal and void but it set aside the order of dismissal on the finding that the order was issued without affording opportunity to the respondent before discharging him from services under Regulation No. 113. The respondent preferred an appeal against the decree of the trial court which was dismissed by the District Judge. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the lower appellate court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The respondent was entitled to be treated in service till he attained the age of superannuation or till the date of his retirement whichever is earlier. [362B] 1.2. The respondent had been working as a Technical Assistant with the Board since 1st March 1974. He was transferred to the Board on 1st April, 1974. The Board has no power to terminate his services after he attains the age of 55 years. The Board could not have terminated his services after attaining the age of 58 years. [363C D] 1.3. The respondent cannot claim any benefit of the provisions of the Transfer Policy. [364E] 1.4. The respondent having accepted the terms and conditions of his appointment as Technical Assistant, he cannot now turn around and question the legality of the order terminating his services. [365D] 1.5. The respondent has failed to establish that there was any violation of principles of natural justice. [366F]
4976: The petitioner was a Judge of the High Court. He retired on July 31, 1977 and his average monthly emoluments during the period October 1 , to July 31 , 1977 were Rs. 2,500 per annum. His pension was calculated at Rs. 11,820 per annum under clause (a) of para 2 of the First Schedule read with the Rajasthan Rules and to that figure was added the additional pension of Rs. 700 per annum under Clause (b) of Para 2 of the Second Schedule read with Rule 2 of the Rajasthan Rules. The petitioner 's case was that he had been appointed as a District and Sessions Judge in the year 1977 and his pay was fixed at Rs. 2200 per month. He was entitled to a special additional pension of RS. 700 per month under Clause (a) and that he should be given the benefit of the said additional pension. The petitioner contended that the additional pension should have been calculated on the basis of the last pay drawn by him and not on the basis that he would have drawn the same if he had been selected for selection grade. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to the benefit of additional pension under Clause (c) of para (2) of the First schedule read with the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The additional pension is to be calculated on the basic salary drawn by him as a District Judge. The amount of pension is to he arrived at on the basis the last pay which he would have received if he had not been appointed a District Judge or would have been eligible and not on that basis. [611E F] 2. The petitioner was entitled only to the benefit under Clause (d) of para 3 of the First Part of the Ist Schedule read with Rules. The additional amount of pension was to be calculated as on the date of his retirement. [612A] 3. The petitioner is entitled to the additional pension. [613B] 4. The petitioner has been deprived of the benefit of this additional pension because of the fact that he was not selected for selection Grade. The petitioner cannot claim the benefit of his additional pension from the date he became eligible for selection grade and the date he was appointed as District Judge. [614C
3344: The appellant, a new entrant, was granted stage carriage permits to the respondent. He filed an application before the Regional Transport Authority for grant of stage carriage permit on the ground that he had not obtained a 'short route ' in his name and that he had been awarded a 's short route ' by the Regional Transport Authorities. The Appellate Tribunal held that since the appellant had secured higher marks than the respondent, he could not be said to have been discriminated against. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant having secured higher marks, he could only be considered as a 'tentative category; (ii) the appellant being a new entrants, was entitled to preference; (iii) the respondent 's experience as lorry operator cannot be equated with the appellant 's experience in bus operation; and (iv) the respondent was entitled to preferential treatment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the appellant ' s experience as lor a passenger transport vehicle is not relevant for the grant of stage carriages permits. [701C] 2. The appellant 's contention that the respondent ' 's experience should be equated with a person who has business or technical experience in the road transport service as defined in clause (a) of Section 68 A of any class of transport vehicles for a period of ten years or more, is without substance. The respondent 's work as lorry driver cannot be equated to the appellant ' 's work in bus operation. The error that has crept into the order of the Appellate Tribunal consists in thinking that the rules or guidelines could be ignored in the name of Section 47(1). The view taken by the appellate tribunal that because the permit is for passenger transport, lorry service experience, even if it falls under Rule 155 A (3)(D), can be regarded as erroneous. [702E F] 3. The view taken in this context by the appellate authority that because the permits is for passenger motor transport, lor a particular class of transport vehicle for a period less than ten years, is not correct. The error which crept into this order of the appellate authority consists in thin remembering that the rules and guidelines
2809: The appellant was a dealer in timber and was selling timber to the respondent. The respondent sold timber to the appellant for the purpose of being used as raw material by the appellant. The appellant contended that after the judgment of the High Court and before the appeal was heard, the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959 was amended by the Maharashtra Act 15 of 1967 with retrospective operation, and by the amendment standing timber was included in the definition of timber, but the definition of "goods" was altered by providing that "goods" includes all materials, commodities and articles. The respondent contended that after amendment of the definition of goods, it was not necessary to include timber in the definition because the definition was prospective in operation and the expression "goods" had to be read as meaning "a thing". The High Court held that the definition of 'goods' was retrospective in operation and that the expression "in goods" in Entry 48 in List II of the Government of India Act, 1935, did not throw much light on the meaning of the expression "taxable goods" in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Held: (i) The expression "goods", in entry 54 in List 11 of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, means everything other than actionable claims and money; and includes all materials including machinery, tools, etc., produced or manufactured in the State. (ii) The expression 'goods' in Entry 48 of List II is wide enough to cover all materials, articles and articles which are intended to be used as raw materials for producing the goods. (iii)The expression "goods " in Entry 48 must be construed in its ordinary sense and in its popular sense, and not in its technical sense. (iv)The expression 'goods ' in Entry 48 cannot be interpreted in a narrow and pedantic sense so as to include all materials, substances and articles. (v)The expression has to be understood in its popular and commercial sense, and it would include all materials which are intended or required to be used in the manufacture or processing of goods. (vi)The expression goods means goods as defined in section 2(13) of the Sale of goods Act, 1930, and includes all goods for the time being in the possession or control of a dealer, and also includes all materials used
2835: The appellant company was incorporated in the United Kingdom and its business was carried on by a firm called M/s. M. K. Brothers, a partnership firm. In proceedings for assessment of income for the assessment year 1952 53 the Income tax Officer computed the income of the appellant company from its business at Rs. 3,39,899 and declined to take into account the loss suffered by the company in the share transactions. In appeal against the order to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the order of the Income tax officer was confirmed. The High Court held that the business activities of the appellant were not the "same business" within the meaning of section 24(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as then in force. Held, that the High Court erred in holding that the business activity of the appellant was about the nature of the two commodities and that the appellant had no control over the same. The fact that the appellant was carrying on the business of selling agency does not make it an independent business. The appellant was carrying out the business of buying and selling agency and selling agency. The appellant did not carry on any other business except buying and selling agencies. The appellant could not be said to have been carrying on the same business as the appellant. The appellant had no direct or indirect connection with the sale of the shares of the respondent company. The appellant 's case was that the two lines of business constituted one business and the other business. The High court rightly rejected the contention of the appellant that the two line of business constituted the same business.
4235: The respondent tenant had agreed to pay and discharge all taxes, outgoings imposed on the two plots of land. The appellant landlord had agreed to deliver possession of the two plots to the respondent. On the expiration of the term of 15 years or sooner termination of the lease the respondent agreed to deliver back the possession of the plots to the appellant free of all buildings, erections and structures and levelled and put in good order and condition to the satisfaction of the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent tenant on the ground that he was always ready and willing to pay all taxes and outgoings as well as the buildings and structures standing thereon. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate court held that it had no jurisdiction to give a decree for ejectment against a tenant under section 12(3) (b) of the Bombay Rent Act. In appeal by certificate the High Court held that the trial court had no jurisdiction in giving a decree for eviction against the tenant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction under section 12 (3) (a) of the Act to determine whether the respondent was actually ready and willing and was not entitled to relief from ejectment under section 12. HELD: The High Court had jurisdiction to decide the question whether the respondent is actually ready and is willing to pay the rent. [1099 E] The respondent 's right to recover possession of the premises from the tenant is only in respect of the building which has been constructed on the demised land. It does not affect the right of the landlord to evict the tenant if he is ready and willing. [1097 F] The respondent had agreed to accept the rent at the rate of Rs. 620/ per month from the appellant. He had also agreed to pay the taxes and outstandings. The respondent had paid the taxes and the outgoings were duly accepted by him. The respondent was ready and willing even to pay the tax and outgoures. The respondent could not be said to have committed default in payment of rent. [1101 G H]
4259: The appellant was convicted under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for ten years. He appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction is based on circumstantial evidence. The circumstances in which the crime was committed were not conclusively established by the prosecution. The chain of circumstances was complete and there was no possibility of any other hypothesis than that the appellant had committed the offence. [404C D] 2. There is no doubt that the prosecutrix was a minor at the time when she was examined by the doctor. She was subjected to sexual intercourse as well as rape. The evidence of the prosecutrix does not suffer from any infirmity or illegality. [405D E] 3. The fact that the victim was examined by a doctor after two days of her examination cannot be said to be a very strong circumstance against the accused. The medical evidence does not support the case of the prosecution. It is not possible to accept the contention that the absence of corroboration of the testimony of the prosecutrix would render the entire prosecution case suspect. [406E F] 4. The facts and circumstances often vary from case to case. The crime situation and the myriad psychic factors, social conditions and people 's life styles may fluctuate, and so, rules of prudence relevant in one fact situation may be inept in another. [407A B] 5. The fact of the matter is that the victim did not appear before the court despite service of summons. The trial court has rightly held that the appellant was guilty of the offence charged. [408B C]

5717: The petitioners were appointed as Stenographers Grade I in the Department of Revenue and Income Tax. They were given the pay scale of Rs.650 1040 with effect from 1st January, 1973. Their counterparts were attached to the Joint Secretaries and equivalent officers of the Department of Finance. In the year 1974, the Government issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, appointing the petitioners as Stenographers Gr.I. The petitioners claimed that they should be placed in the pay scale Rs.625 1040 with retrospective effect from 1.1.1973. The respondents contended that the petitioners discharged the same functions and responsibilities and were drawing their pay scale of pay of Rs. 650 1040. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court contending that their counterparts in the Department were attached to them and were at par in seniority/promotion with the counterparts of the Department. The petitioners also contended that the method of recruitment in respect of Grade I stenographers in the department is as follows: 1003 (i) Petitioners ' counterparts In the so called Secretariat & participating in the Department; (ii) Petitioners ' Counterparts in Department; (iii) Petitioners ' Junior Grade, the petitioners discharged their same functions and were at the same level and were drawing the same pay scale of the post of Junior Grade. The petitioners contended that the respondents had no authority to change the method of appointment of the petitioners. The petitioners further contended that the Government had not taken into consideration the fact that the petitioners were working in the Department for more than 12 years and were entitled to the pay scale applicable to the post of Senior Grade Stenographer. The petitioners relied on the decision of this Court in Union of India vs K.V. Jankiraman, [1991] Suppl. 2 S.C.R. 715, where this Court held that the principle of equal pay for equal work would apply only when there is complete similarity between two posts. The petitioners therefore prayed for quashing the order dated 5th May, 1982 passed by the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure, New Delhi and the order dated 27th March, 1983 passed by the Central Board of Direct Taxes, New Delhi
5524: The Public Service Commission issued a notification on July 17, 1973 determining inter se seniority of all the candidates appointed on the basis of 1970 examination in accordance with the provisions of Rule 19 of the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission (Limitation of Functions) Rules, 1951. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification by filing Writ Petition No. 1303 of 1979 under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification dated August 19, 1980 was not applicable to the case of the petitioners as they had been appointed prior to the notification dated July 17,1973 and therefore, the petitioners were entitled to be treated as having been appointed prior thereto. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The notification dated August 17, 1973 appointing candidates out of the list of 37 candidates prepared by the Commission under Rule 19 of U.P. Public Service Commission Examination Rules, 1951 is valid and does not suffer from any infirmity. [550C] 2.1. In view of the amendment of Rule 19 by the State Government after the selection process commenced, the Commission could have considered the cases of the candidates who had appeared in the examination but did not do so. But it cannot be said that the Commission has no power to make such an appointment. [552E F] 3.1. It is true that the Commission can make its own assessment on the basis Of the record of service and if it finds that the candidate is suitable for appointment to the post it can make its recommendation accordingly within the time specified in the advertisement. But the appointing authority cannot act arbitrarily and refuse to make the appointment strictly adhering to the terms of the advertisement. [553G H; 554A] 4.1. If there are any other persons who have secured more marks than the petitioners, the Commission may consider their cases also. [554B C]
1089: The appellants were under an agreement with the company for a period of 20 years commencing from 1st April, 1945. The company was assessed to income tax on the basis that the company had paid commission at the rate of 1% on all purchases of cotton and stores and 21/2 on all capital expenditure incurred from time to time. The company claimed that the commission should be added back to the total turnover of the company as a result of the chargeable accounting period ending 31st March, 1945. Held, that the Income tax Officer was right in taking action under section 34 and 15 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, and the Excess Profits tax Act, and that the Excess Profits Assessment Act applied to the case. The profits of the company could not be included in the assessable income of the company because the chargeable accounting periods were completed on 31st March 1945 and 31st March 1946. The assessment of income tax was made on the basis of the chargeable accounts which were completed on 30th March 1945 and April 1, 1945. In the present case, the assessment of income was made on 31st December, 1947, and the corresponding year was 31st March 1948. The assessment was made on 30th June, 1949, and the income was assessed on 31st July, 1950. The assessment order was passed on 31st August, 1951, and the assessment was made after the expiry of the chargeable account period. The assessment orders were therefore within the period of limitation prescribed by section 34(1) of the Income tax Act.
2093: The appellant was a workman and the respondent workmen were employed in the appellant. The appellant terminated their services on July 17, 1961, under section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The termination was challenged by the workmen on the ground that the retrenchment was unjustified and illegal. The Labour Court held that there was no violation of the provisions of section 25F and that the retrenchment amounted to an unfair labour practice. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the appellant had not followed the principles laid down in section 25F; (ii) the retrenchment was bad because the appellant did not follow the rule as to retrenchment; (iii) the retrenchment of clerks was not justified since clerks were not trained to handle only a particular kind of work; (iv) the retrenchment amounted only to an unfair trade practice; (v) the retrenchment amounts to an unfair Labour Practice; (vi) the retrenchment is violative of section 25 F of the Act; and (vii) the retrenchment amount was paid without any justification. HELD: (1) The appellant has failed to prove that the retrenchment of the clerks was mala fide or that retrenchment amounted to a fraud on the part of the management. [783 C] (2) The appellant was justified in retrenching its employees and that the number of employees required to carry on the work after the imposition of a ban could not exceed the number retained by the appellant. [784 D E] (3) The appellant had not been able to establish that the retrenchment amounts either to an unfair or unjust action. The appellant had also not been able even to show that the retrenchment amount had been paid without any basis whatsoever. [785 G H] (4) The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of its own wrongs. [786 A B] (5) Section 25F of Act provides that if the employer does not accept the order of dismissal or discharge passed by him, he shall pay compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months. The appellant was entitled to have the retrenchment of its workmen set aside. [787 C D]
5288: The respondent, a dealer in hides and skins and exports the same out of the territory of India, entered into an agreement with the appellant for the sale of hides and tins. 5543: The appellant joined the service of the Narang Bank of India as a clerk cum Typist and was confirmed in his service on October 1, 1974. 2744: The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Surgery in the Rajasthan Medical College, Jaipur.
