The proviso to subrule (4) was added to Rule 30(4) with retrospective effect during the pendency of the writ petitions in the High Court and the High Court was bound to consider the question whether the proviso was valid or not. [563 D E] The proviso to Sub rule (4), therefore, cannot be read as an independent provision. It is only if the proviso is read as a whole, it can be construed as a part of the main enactment. If the proviso is given retrospective operation it would amount to rewriting the statute which has
3779: The respondent, a resident of Punjab, was assessed to tax under the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948. He filed returns for the assessment years 1959 60 and 1960 61 in respect of his income from business. The assessing authority determined the total income of the respondent as Rs. 1,00,000 and the tax payable by him was Rs. 2,50,000. The respondent challenged the assessment on the ground that the provisions of section 5(2) of the Act were not applicable to him because he had been carrying on the profession of selling milk and milk products within the State of Punjab. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the contention holding that the respondent was not liable to pay tax on the income from the sale of milk and milk product outside the State of Haryana. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who upheld the order of the Assistant Commissioner. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the orders of the Assistant Com missioner. The High Court held that the provisions contained in section 5(1)(b) of the Punjab General Clauses Act, 1898, did not apply to the case and that the respondent could not be taxed on the income derived from the sale or purchase of milk and goods within the State. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in interpreting section 3 of the Act as the Act stood before the amendment of section 2 in the manner indicated above. [880C] (ii) The Punjab High Court has clearly erred in interpreting section 5(3) of the Central Sales Tax Act which is applicable only to sales made to registered dealers and not to sales made outside the State. [881D E] (iii) The Punjab decision does not lay down any proposition of law that the provisions relating to taxation are not applicable to sales made in the course of interState trade or commerce. It is true that the question whether the provisions of the Central Act are applicable to sales effected outside the State or outside the State, but it cannot be said that the Punjab decision is based on a very forced interpretation given to the provisions of Section 3 of the Punjab Act. [882F G]
4798: The plaintiffs filed a suit against the Union of India and the Union of Pakistan for a declaration that the notice exhibit A 8 dated August 10, 1956 served by the plaintiffs on the defendant 's father was insufficient and illegal. The defendants contested the claim inter alia on the ground that the notice was not sufficient and was not a valid notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court held that the notice could not be said to have been properly given but it came to the conclusion that the notice had been duly delivered to the defendant 'South Indian Bank Ltd., and that the suit was bad for want of a notice under section80 of the Code. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court holding that no further notice under section 78 of the Code was necessary as the notice exhibit 'A 8 was sufficiently complied with. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The notice must substantially fulfil its object and it is sufficient if it substantially fulfils its objection in informing the parties concerned generally of the nature of the suit intended to be filed and if it does so, it would be sufficient compliance with the requirement of section 80 of Code of Civil procedure. [230 D E] (2) The notice was not defective because it did not comply with the requirements of section 80. It was not necessary that the notice should state the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff or the defendant. [231 F H] (3) The notice can only be one of the modes prescribed by law for the service of the notice. The notice need not specify the mode of service. It may be vague or indefinite. It may contain a statement that the notice has been duly served. But the notice must also set out the grounds upon which the notice is sought to be served. [232 G H; 233 A B] (4) The notice is required to be served either by registered post or by affixing the same at the office of the Collector of the district where the notice is to be served and the person to whom it is addressed. If the notice is sent by registered post, it will be deemed to have been served at the time when the notice is actually received by the person to whose knowledge the notice is issued. [233
532: The respondent was dismissed from service by the Superintendent of Police, on December 20, 1948. He filed a revision application before the Inspector General of Police which was rejected by him on April 22, 1950. On May 7, 1949, he was dismissed from his service by the Inspector General. On June 7, 1949 he filed an appeal against the order dismissing him and the order of dismissal passed by the Inspector of Police on June 7,1949. The respondent contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to deal with the order of dismiss al in question as it had not become final until the Inspector General gave his assent to the order of the Inspector General and that as the last mentioned order had been passed after the Constitution had come into force, the High Court could issue a writ of certiorari under article 226 of the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 226 confers wide powers upon the High Courts to issue writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus or quo warranto etc., but these are not capable of being enforced in a court of law unless the same is required by any statute or held otherwise. In the instant case, the High court had no power to issue a writ under article 226 merely because the respondent had challenged the order of his dismissal. The High Court had jurisdiction to issue a Writ of Certiorari under article 226.
2083: The Mysore Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1957, were made by the Governor of Mysore under article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 4(2) provided that the Commission may invite Government to nominate an officer to represent the service or the Department for whom recruitment is being made to be present at the interview referred to in clause (3) to assist the Commission in its work of selection. The High Court held that the words "shall be as set forth in the rules of recruitment" used in rule 4(2), meant only those rules which were framed by the Governor and not those rules which had been framed by the State Government. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The word "shall" in rule 4 must mean "as set forth in rules 3 and 4". The word "may" in rule 3 means "as set out in rules 3 & 4". The expression "shall" does not mean "as may be given to a particular government servant." The word "will" in rule 2 means "to give to a particular Government servant "; it means "to make to him a particular method of recruitment". The word 'shall' in rule 4 means "to be appointed to a particular post or service or to a particular service or to any other service or to be specified class or classes of posts or to any one service or to all service or to do any act on behalf of the Government in the matter of recruitment to such service or posts". The word is used in rule 2 with reference to the appointment to a particular cadre or service or a particular service. It is not intended to confer power on the Governor to appoint a person to a particular vacancy or service. [158 E F]

3110: The appellant 's land was acquired by the Government for the purpose of construction of a house. 273: The respondent, a resident of India, was allowed cash credit limit of rupees three lakhs by the Central Bank of India Ltd. on the 23rd June, 1947, shortly before the partition of India, and thereafter acquired the status of a citizen. On the application of the respondent, the bank filed a complaint against him under sections 380 and 454, Indian Penal Code, read with section 412 of the Code before the District Magistrate of Gurgaon. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and committed the case to the Sessions Judge who tried it. The Sessions Judge held that the respondent had acquired Pakistan nationality by merely staying in India and therefore he could not be tried for that offence. He also held that the trial court had no jurisdiction to try the case. The High Court confirmed the order of the Sessions judge. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent was a native of India and therefore the East Punjab Government was not competent to grant sanction for his prosecution under section 188, Criminal Procedure Code, read along with section 4, Indian Penal code. [708 B] (ii) The respondent had been admitted to bail by the Magistrate at the time when he was produced before him and the Magistrate had taken into consideration all the facts and circumstances of the case including the fact that the respondent was a foreign national. The Magistrate had rightly decided that the respondent should be tried for the offence under section 412, Indian Penal Cods., and section 412. [709 D E] (iii) The respondent 's plea that he was a natives of India and was therefore entitled to protection under section 4, Evidence Act, was not proved. [710 F G] (iv) The respondent could not be said to have acquired Pakistan nationality because he was a foreign National. His passport was issued to him after the partition of the country. The respondent could therefore be charged only under section 4(1)(a), Indian Penal Code. [711 A B] (v) The respondent did not acquire any citizenship by merely staying abroad. He was therefore not liable to be tried for an offence under section 14 of the Foreigners Act. [713 D]
387: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 435 and 436 of the Indian Penal Code. The Assistant Sessions Judge disagreed with the jury on the ground that the evidence was insufficient to support a verdict, but he held that the reference was in the circumstances not competent. He also rejected the plea that the charge against the appellants was defective as he did not consider the evidence before him and had not considered it. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the charge was defective because the jury took one view of the evidence and the jury took another view of the same evidence. The trial court could not be said to have taken a different view of the case than that of the jury. The finding of the jury was binding upon the jury and the jury could not be convicted without taking a contrary view of the law. The finding was not conclusive and the jury ought to have given due weight to the opinions of the jury and should have acted on it. The finding must be supported by the reasons given by the jury.
6683: The appellant was prosecuted for offences punishable under the provisions of the Gold Control Act 1968. The appellant filed two revision applications before the High Court which were also allowed by the High Court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has gravely erred in allowing the second revision petitions filed by the respondent by ignoring the fact that the appellant has not challenged the legality of the impugned judgment of the High Court in allowing the two other revision applications filed by the Union of India. [718C] 2. The High court was wrong in permitting the prosecution to bolster up its case by filling up the lacuna and plugging the loopholes which if carried out would be detrimental and prejudicial to the appellant. [719D E] 3. The High 'Court was right in allowing the revision petitions filed against the order of the Magistrate allowing the two revision applications filed against the judgment of the Magistrate. The High courts are justified in allowing the revisional applications filed by a party who is aggrieved by an interlocutory order passed by the trial court. [722B] 6. The Highs Court should not have entertained the revision petitions at all. [723F] 7. The High Cour t could not have entertained such a petition without issuing notice to the respondents. [724G]
1878: The workmen of the appellant company were dismissed after a domestic enquiry commenced on February 4, 1957. [884 B]
6474: The appellant, a Part B State of Pakistan, was declared to be the Ruler of the East Bengal State. On 30th June 1947, the Governor General made an announcement that it had been decided that the Province of Bengal and Punjab shall be partitioned. In pursuance thereof, the Governor of West Bengal issued a notification on 30th June, 1947, fixing the date of partition as 1st July, 1947. The appellant challenged the said notification in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The notification dated 30th June was not a mere formality but a legislative process. It was a piece of legislation intended to be passed from the appointed day. [911B] (2) The notification did not amount to any amendment of the Constitution. The notification merely stated that the Governor General had decided that the two enclaves in Eastern India shall be partition ed. The notification does not purport to change the nature of the two enc losures. [912C] (3) The notification is not a mere legislative act. It is a legislative act. [913D] (4) The notification cannot be construed as a legislative act unless it is so expressed or necessarily implied. It must be read in the light of the entire scheme of the Act. If there is no such thing as a legislative instrument, then the language of the notification would be wholly unworkable. [914E F] (5) The notification has to be read along with the Act. [915G]

3630: The appellants purchased raw hides and skins from the State of Bihar in the course of interState trade and commerce. The State Government issued a notification under section 10(2) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, declaring that the tax on the sale price of raw hides or skins was to be levied at the rate of 1 1/2 per cent. The appellants challenged the validity of items 7(a) and 7(b) of the Second Schedule to the State 'Act on the ground that they were not liable to pay tax at the point of purchase of raw hide and skins. The High Court upheld the contention of the appellants but held that the tax was not leviable at the point where the raw hides were sold. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State legislature had no power to levy tax at the time when the goods were sold and that the State legisla ture was only prospective in operation. HELD: (1) The State legislature has no power to impose tax retrospectively. [760 C] (2) The State Legislature is competent to legislate with retrospective effect if there is any reason for doing so. It may also make a law retrospectively. But such a law cannot be made retrospective merely because the legislature has power to pass a particular order. [761 D] (3) The State 's power to levy taxes on sales or purchases of goods must be exercised within the four corners of the law. If the State legislature has power under the law to levy tax on the same transaction, then the State legislature can levy tax on transactions which are already taxed by the State. [762 B] (4) The State legis lation is not a taxing statute. It is a machinery devised by the legislature for the purpose of collecting revenue. It is an independent and separate entity. It is not a mere machinery or machinery created for the purpose. It is essentially subordinate to the legislative power conferred upon the delegate by the legislature. [763 E F] (5) The State has power to levy a tax on the purchase of raw materials. The State has the power to levy the tax on purchase of raw material. The State is entitled to collect the tax as it
6931: The State Government in exercise of power under section 68D of the approved a draft scheme framed under section 68C through G.O.M.S. No. 753, dated June 4, 1975, published in the Gazette on June 4,1975, relating to the route Anantapur to Dharmavaram via Mamillappalli. 555: The appellant was appointed as a Civil Judge in the Rajasthan State on April 23, 1950. He was transferred to Ganganagar and thereafter to Ganganager. On September 11, 1950, he received an order from the new Rajasthan Government that his pay had been reduced by two months after the notification dated December 9, 1949, and that he would continue to draw his existing salary until further orders. On October 25, 1950, the appellant received a letter from the Government of Rajasthan informing him that his pay was reduced by two month 's after the notification. On November 24, 1950, when the appellant received the letter, the Government of India, in exercise of its powers under article 352(1) of the Constitution, issued a notification to the effect that the appellant shall be deemed to have been appointed as Civil Judge with effect from January 1, 1951, and that his pay shall be fixed at Rs. 540 p.m. with effect from the date of his appointment. The appellant filed a writ petition for mandamus against the Government of Jaipur and the High Court held that the posting of the appellant as Civil Judge was wrong and that it must be treated as an ad hoc appointment till proper appointments were made to the Judicial Service of Rajasthan according to the Constitution of India. Held, that the post of Civil Judge is a permanent post and the appellant cannot claim any right to hold it continuously or to continue to hold it until it is duly confirmed. The post of Civil Judges is a permanent one and the appellant has no vested rights in it. The post is not a permanent one but is a temporary one and the appointment can be terminated at any time without notice. The post does not cease to exist merely because the Government makes a regular appointment thereto. The post may be created before the expiry of the period of probation but the appointment is not a mere temporary appointment. It is a temporary appointment which is terminable at the end of the prescribed term either by the Government giving reasons for termination. The post being permanent, there could be no question of making a fresh appointment.

4879: The appellants were teachers in the service of the State of Punjab. They claimed revised scales of pay on the ground that they had taken graduate degrees and, therefore, were entitled to the benefit of the grade mentioned against Category 'A' in the Circular letter dated July 29, 1967. The appellants contended before the High Court that the circular letter was not applicable to them because they had acquired higher qualifications in the course of their service. The High Court rejected the contention. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the circular letters were not applicable to the appellants since they had acquired the qualification in the course when they joined the service. In second appeal the High Court held that the finding of the Rent Controller that the appellant is the legally w edded wife of the Sohan Singh could not be sustained because the appellant was not the legally wated wife of Sohail Mian. In the present case, the High Court has dealt with the case as if this was a matrimonial proceeding in which the status of the appellant as wife and the other whether on the facts found the ground of sub letting had been established. 6924: The State of Gujarat imposed a duty on the manufacture, import, export, transport, storage, sale, purchase and use of liquor. The State Government was empowered to levy excise duty on alcohol. [767B C] Synco Industries Ltd. vs Union of India, ; , referred. 2.2. The State has the right to control the production, supply and distribution of goods and to sell the products manufactured therefrom to the consumer at cheap rates. Synco Industry Ltd. vs. State of Karnataka, ; , approved.

Clause (a) of Explanation 2 to section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, provided that "the profits and gains of any business or profession shall be computed after making such deductions as may be prescribed". The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1957 58, 1959 60, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The words "as the case may be" are intended to indicate that the income tax payable by the assessee must be the income of the assessee. 4400: The appellant was a registered dealer under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969. During the period between May 6, 1969 and March 31, 1970, the appellant purchased raw materials from a Registered Dealer in respect of which he had furnished a certificate in Form No. 19 as provided under section 13(1)(B) of the Act read with Rule 24(4) of the Gujarat Sales tax Rules, 1970. The appellant did not produce any evidence to establish that the raw goods purchased by him are used in the manufactures of taxable goods for sale by him. [881C D] 3. 4960: The respondent was a tenant of a piece of land. He had been granted a licence to construct a building on the land in question. The appellant filed a suit for mandatory injunction directing him to vacate the premises. The trial court decreed the suit and dismissed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had purchased the property from its original owner by a sale deed dated 27.8.1979 and that the respondent became a sub tenant of a part of the demised premises after the expiry of the period he terminated the licence and filed the suit on 15.2.1973 for a mandory injunction directing him not to evict the respondent from the premises. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The respondent 's right under the lease by the original owner cannot be interfered with by the appellant when he is in possession of the whole of the demised land including the suit shed as tenant under the original owner. [183B] 1.2. The respondent had purchased a portion of the land from the original owner by an agreement dated 27.08.1979. The respondent has become a licensee of the suit shed. The respondent could not be evicted from the premises on the lease or licence. [184C] 1.3. The respondent was only one of its partners, was the lessee of the property. The respondent did not vacate the premises after the commencement of the tenancy or the licence. The respondent acquired the property from the original owners by a sale deeds dated 27. 8.1979. Even if there was some delay, we think that in a case of this kind attempt should be made to avoid multiplicity of suits and the licensor should not be driven to file another round of litigation with all the attendant delay, trouble and expense. [185D E] 1.4. The respondent would be entitled to the relief only if he succeeds in proving that he had purchased the suit shed from its original owners. [186F] 1.5. The respondent is entitled to the protection of section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act. [187E] 1.6. The respondent cannot be denied relief merely because he had executed a sale deed in favour of the appellant. [188G] 1.7. The
1255: The appellant was the owner of a forest in Bihar. He had granted a right to cut and remove bamboos and certain other timber to be found in a specified area of the forest village. The forest was then in the possession of the appellant as a tenant under him. The appellant entered into an agreement with the State for the supply of timber to the forest department. The forest department, however, took over the possession of a portion of the forest land on October 30, 1946. The forest officer thereupon issued notices under section 14 and section 29 of the Bihar Private Forests Act, 1948, calling upon the appellant to show cause why he should not be evicted from the forest land. The appellant filed a suit against the forest department claiming that the notification issued under section 14 of the Act was invalid and that the notification was invalid. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the notification did not have the effect of terminating the tenancy of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the notification was bad because the name of the landlord had not been mentioned in the notification issued by the State under section 14; (ii) the notification did no more than extend the rights of the landlord to cut and removed bamboo trees; (iii) the notification having been held to be invalid, the notification could not be said to be invalid; and (iv) the notification being invalid, the appellant could not be evicted without complying with the provisions of section 15. HELD : (i) The notification does not take away the right of the landlord or the tenant to recover possession of the forest. It merely provides for the mode of taking possession of the forests. The notification is only a step towards the taking of possession and does not affect the right of any person to recover possession. [701 E] (ii) The notification did not terminate the tenancy of a tenant. The notification was valid and the notification must be deemed to be valid. [702 F G] (iii) The notification was not invalid because it did not take away or deprive the right of a tenant to recover his possession. 5139: The appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. It was carrying on business in textile industry and its main activities were to manufacture textile goods. In pursuance of the provisions of the Act, the appellant company was appointed as a provisional liquidator by the Central Government under section 15(1) of the Act. The appellant company filed an application before the High Court for taking over the management of its two textile mills under the Act. On the question whether the appellant company had been able to establish that it was engaged in the manufacture or production of textile goods within the meaning of the Act and that the appellant company could not be said to have been engaged in the manufacturing or production of the textile goods within that definition. HELD: (i) The appellant company did not fall within the definition of a "workman" under the Act and therefore the appellant company cannot be said to be engaged in the business of manufacture or production. [942 E] (ii) The appellant was not a person who was engaged in any of the activities mentioned in section 2(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant was merely a provisional liquidator appointed by the Central Govt. under section 18A of the Act to take over the management and control of the two textile mills. The appellant could not be held to be engaged either in the manufacture of textile goods or in the manufacture thereof. [943 F G] (iii) The appellant is not a person engaged in the production or manufacture of textile articles. The appellant is a company which has been established by the Central government under the Act for the purpose of taking over the control of the textile industry. The appellant cannot be said, therefore, to be engaged only in the manufacture and production of textile articles within the meaning 'of the Act. [944 A B] (iv) The appellant cannot claim that it was carrying on the business of manufacturing textile goods within its own premises. [945 D]
5268: The respondent was appointed as a Subedar in the Central Reserve Police Force on 1.7.1976 and was confirmed in that post on 20.9.1985. He applied to the Andhra Pradesh High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for a direction for his absorption in the Force. The High Court allowed the petition holding that there was nothing in these rules to disentitle a retired or released army officer from absorption, directed the appellants to consider the respondent 's permanent absorption in the force. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In regard to the category of officers benefit of absorption is not admissible and consequently the respondent is entitled to the benefit of the amended provision from 20th September, 1985. [386B] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent has been given a promotion and in the promotional post he had worked for about 16 years. Therefore, he would be entitled to absorption in the cadre with effect from the date the amended rule came into force and he is, therefore, to be confirmed in the post of Commandant and absorbed in the appropriate cadre from that date. [385C D] 2.2 In regard to persons who have been given temporary promotions, the respondent will be entitled to the benefits of the amended provisions from 20th Sept. 1985. [390E]
6438: The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) and 3(1) (iii) of the COFEPOSA Act, 1974. He challenged the detention order on the ground that there was a delay in considering his representation to the Central Government and the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the detention order was passed after a lapse of eight months and that too it was a solitary instance and because of the delay, the same has become stale and there is no other material to establish any nexus or live connection between the alleged date of smuggling and the date of detention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of revocation of an order of detention under section 3 of the Act is a discretionary power and not a matter of subjective satisfaction of the authority concerned. [766A] 2.1 It is well settled that where the statute provides for a limitation on the exercise of the power within which the power can be exercised, the authority must act in good faith and it must have reasonable grounds for believing that the power has been exercised but such belief should be based on some material. If there is some material against the detenu, he must be given the same particulars as are disclosed before the authority can make a report to the appropriate Government about the existence of such material. [767B C] 2.2 The power of the Central Government to revoke an order of preventive detention under section 8 of the Act does not extend to making a representation to the detaining authority. The power to revoke an externment order is conferred upon the Central Government only when the order is made in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of COFEPOSSA. The power under section 8 is exercisable only when the authority passing the order is satisfied that the grounds on which the order has been made are sufficient to justify the order of detention. [768C D] 3.1 The power of review is a discretionary one. It is well known that the rule of law is the foundation of every legal system and if there is some substance in the contention of the petitioner that the order of the detaining authority suffers from certain defects, the court will not interfere with the order.
4364: The appellant company was a public limited company. The company terminated the services of its workmen on the ground that they had been retrenched by the company without complying with the provisions of section 25F of the . The termination was challenged before the High Court which held that the termination was illegal and directed reinstatement with full back wages. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The expression 'retrenchment ' in section 2(OO) of the , means termination of service for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include (a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or (b) termination of the service of the workman on the ground of continued ill health; or (c) termination of service of the workmen on the grounds of continued ill-health. [887 F G] Hariprasad Shivshankar Shukla vs A. In order to provide for the situations which the Supreme Court held is not covered by the definition of 'retrenchment' in section 2 (OO). The Parliament did not make any provision for retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(0OO) and it merely provided for the payment of compensation to the workmen in case of transfer of undertakings and in case of closure of undertakings respectively. The legislature has made no such provision in section 25FF. It cannot be said that the intention was only to exclude a bonafide closure or discontinuance of business by the employer. [887 D E]
159: The appellants were convicted under sections 297 and 500, Indian Penal Code, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal the High Court set aside their convictions and sentences. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the offence of which the magistrate had taken cognizance did not fall within section 195, Criminal Procedure Code, and (ii) the Magistrate could take cognizance only on a complaint by a proper authority under the provisions of section 195, Cr. P.C., and that the Magistrate was not competent to take cognizance of the offences mentioned in section 190, Criminal Procedure, Code. HELD : (i) The offence of which cognizance can be taken of an offence under section 193, I.P.C., is not committed by the person who gives the information but he must be charged with the offence. [401 B D] (ii) The offence under section 192, I. P. C., is not made out from the facts alleged in the complaint. It is only the offence under section 190, Cr. PC, which is punishable with imprisonment for three months or more. [408 A B] (iii) The offence contemplated by section 192, Cr.PC, is not committed when the offence is punishable with death or imprisonment for life. It is committed when the offender has been deprived of his liberty by the wrongful restraint or detention of himself or another. [410 E F] (iv) The offence is not committed while the accused is a public servant. [411 G] (v) The offence committed by the accused is not committed during the course of the commission of the act constituting the offence. It is not committed in the course of commission of the acts specified in section 2(1)(c), Cr. P.,C., as it is done in the discharge of official duty. [412 H]
2605: The appellant was a workman employed in the appellant company. He filed an application under section 33C(2) of the , for claiming a sum of Rs. 8,910/72 P from the workmen on account of over time work and compensation for work done on weekly off days. The Labour Court allowed the claim and directed payment of the amount found due to the workmen. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions by two separate judgments. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 20(1) of the Act is not applicable to the facts of the case before us. The jurisdiction of the Labour Court under the general Act is excluded because of section 20(1). [401 B] (2) The Labour Court has no jurisdiction to entertain applications under section 33 C(2) as it is not a 'workman ' within the meaning of section 2(s) of the . [401 D] (3) The Labour Courts are not courts of limited jurisdiction. They have only supervisory powers. [401 E]
5889: The appellant was granted permission to start a college of education in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Government granted permission for starting a college of study and research on payment of certain conditions. The appellant challenged the cancellation of his permission by filing writ petition No. 812 of 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the parties did not comply with the conditions prescribed by the grant of permission and recognition to the colleges. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 's college was not a minority institution. The appellant had no right to establish or maintain a college of its choice. [899C] 2. The appellant has not been able to show any violation of the conditions of grant of permission. The appellant is not entitled to the relief claimed. [900D] 3. The appellant was given permission to start an educational institution. The conditions were required to be complied with within a period of six months. The appellant failed to do so. The High court rightly refused to interfere with the order of the Government. [901E F] 4. The appellant cannot claim as a matter of right that it should have been granted permission for running a college of studies. The appellant could not be denied the benefit of the grant of affiliation only because he did not comply within the time limit prescribed. [902B C] 5. The appellant did not make out a case that the conditions imposed by the Government were arbitrary or unreasonable. The appellant can certainly seek appropriate directions from the Court. [903A B]
3809: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court for murder of his wife and two children. He was sentenced to death under section 302 I.P.C. and to imprisonment for life under section 302, I.P.,C. The High Court confirmed the sentence of death but reduced the sentence of life imprisonment to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the death sentence should be substituted in place of death sentence awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction by the Sessions Judge is not vitiated merely because he did not give an opportunity to the accused to adduce any evidence in support of his case. [713B] 2. The question whether the death sentence has been inflicted more than two years ago or the agony of such a sentence has been an excruciating experience suffered by the convict for a long period, does not arise. [714D E] 3. The circumstances which have influenced the courts below in awarding the capital sentence are not to be considered as irrelevant. [715E F] 4. The fact that no opportunity was given to the accused at the time of the commission of the crime would not make him guilty of the offence. [716A B] 5. The sentence of life imprison ment imposed by the trial Court and confirmed by High Court cannot be said to be excessive. [717F G]
4605: The appellant was appointed as Principal of a college on probation for a period of two years. He was given an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 by the Manager of the College to the effect that he would be on probation for one year and that his services would be terminated without assigning any reason. On May 18, 1981, the Selection Committee constituted under section 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 (Act 1 of 1921) held interviews for selection of Principal. The Selection Committee selected the appellant for appointment to the post of Principal. On April 27, 1982, the appellant wrote to the Manager of a private college informing him that the Committee had decided to appoint the appellant as Principal. The Manager of the college issued an appointment order on April 27, 1983 appointing the appellant as the Principal. On May 28, 1984, the appellant filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the appointment of the appellant as principal. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment of Principal was not valid because the power to appoint was withdrawn by the State Government. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1. The appointment of the Principal is not valid unless it is made by the State or the Managing Committee of the institution. [168D] 2.1 The power to appoint is conferred upon the Managing Committee. The power to make appointments is conferred upon it by the statute. The power of appointment is conferred upon a body which has power to make rules regulating recruitment and conditions of service of employees. The power is conferred upon such body by the statute itself. The power conferred upon the authority to make rules is not conditioned by the power to make the rules. The power can be exercised only by the authority making rules. It is well settled that the power to rule made under Article 309 is legislative power. The power under Article 309 of the Constitution is legislative power and the power of the State Legislature to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in List I of Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. The power includes the power to frame rules regulating recruitment to public services and the powers to remove difficulties in implementation thereof. [169E F] 2.2 The power to frame Rules regulating recruitment and other conditions of
5006: The appellants were the owners of certain documents seized during the search. They were directed to deliver them to the appellants, but they did not do so. On their failure to comply with the summons issued by the Income Tax Officer under section 132A of the Income Tax Act, the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the search and seizure. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that there was nothing illegal in issuing a search warrant when there was no material before him on which he could entertain a reasonable belief that any documents which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any investigation or proceeding under Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (Act for short) are secreted in any place. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the search warrant issued by the Directorate of Enforcement was illegal as the same was not supported by any evidence whatsoever and was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Directorate of Revenue under section 132 A of the Income tax Act is not an arbitrary one. It is a discretionary power. [766C] 2. The Directorate of Enforcement has been empowered to issue a search warrant if the circumstances exist which would justify the issuance of a search warrant. The Directorate has been given the power to make search of any place where the officer may have reason to believe that any document which in his considered opinion will be necessary for or relevant for the purposes of any investigation or proceedings under the Act is secreted in that house. [767D E] 3. The Directorate had no power to issue a warrant of authorisation under section 132(1). The Directorate had not recorded its reasons in writing. The Directorate was not required to record reasons in writing on the search warrant. [768E F] 4. The Directorate cannot exercise such powers in a fair and just manner. [769F] 5. The Directorate can exercise such powers only in a fair, just and proper manner. [752G]
6378: The respondent workman was detailed to work in the first shift for picking up certain employees of the second shift and general shift. On May 1, 1970, he was detailed to take charge of the first shift from the first shift and also to drop the children at various scheduled points. On May 2, 1970, the management sought approval under section 33(2)(b) of the Act of the action taken and towards meeting the requirement of the provision paid to the workman before hand a sum of Rs.607.90 as wages for one month, before hand a pare nt and drop the child at the end of the shift. On June 3, 1970, when the management sought permission to drop children at the end, the workman filed an objection statement raising several contentions denying inter alia the allegations made against him and challenging the validity of domestic enquiry. The Labour Court held that the two items could not be considered together because the two items were not relevant in fixing fair wage. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two item could not be treated as part of the respondent 's wages and had to be taken into calculation of the gratuity pay able to him. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The two items could be considered together. [976 F] (a) The two charges could not be said to have been proved but they must be taken to have been established. [977 G] (b) The two articles cannot be considered together in order to determine whether the two items are connected with each other or whether the two charges are connected with the same incident. [978 B C] (c) The two matters can be properly considered together. If the two items can be considered together, then the two items would be covered by the two items. [979 E] (d) The two entries could be considered separately. [980 D] (e) The two amounts could be considered to be part of the wages and not of the two items which are linked with each other. [981 E]
5478: The appellant was appointed as a Principal of the College on January 27, 1986. She was suspended by an order dated January 27,1986 on the ground that she had committed serious financial irregularities and had been guilty of misconduct. The order of suspension was challenged in a writ petition filed before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of suspension having been passed by the Vice Chancellor of the University without any authority or jurisdiction, the same could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated March 7, 1987 is clearly illegal and void. [365D] 2.1 The order of the Vice Chancellor dated March 7 is also bad for the reason that the order was passed by the Registrar of the University. The Registrar has no power to review his own order unless he exercises his powers under section 68 of the U.P. State Universities Act. The Registrar cannot review his own decision. [366E F] 3.2 The order of dismissal of the appellant from service was passed by him after giving her a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed punishment. The order was passed in collusion with the Authorised Controller. The order does not show that the said order was passed at all. It is only an administrative order. [367F G]
2126: The appellant, a religious endowment, was the owner of certain properties in suit. The properties were held by him as marfatdars and to have been acquired either by purchase or 'krayadan ' or by way of gift subject to the charge of some offerings made to Lord Jagannath. The properties in suit were also held by him for the support of his maths. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa, hereinafter called the Commissioner, demanded contribution under section 49 of the Act and took steps to enforce certain other provisions of the Act against the plaintiff and the properties in suit, and the properties were accordingly included in Schedule Kha. The Commissioner decided against the plaintiff. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the properties in dispute did not constitute 'public religious endowments ' within the meaning of the Act; (ii) the properties were not public endowments but were private properties; (iii) the properties constituted a 'religious endowment ' within the scope of section 6(1)(a) of the Act, and (iv) the properties formed a 'private endowment ' within section 6(2) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. HELD: (i) The properties in dispute were not public trusts or religious endowments but were public endowments to which the Act applied. The properties had been held by the appellant as a temple and not as a temple. [440 D] (ii) The properties were not a 'math ' as defined in the Act. The properties could not be regarded as public endowments because they were not public properties. [441 C] (iii) The properties must be held by the public as a trust property. The properties must not be held by any person as a trustee or as trustees of the trust property. [442 E] (iv) The properties are not public endowments. They are not public properties and therefore the properties cannot be treated as public properties. The properties are public properties and not private properties. [441 B] (v) The properties do not come under section 6(3) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The properties do come under section 7 of the Act. [443 F]
3656: The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the school. He made a complaint to the Education Officer of the Corporation alleging therein that the appellant had been found guilty of misconduct by the Deputy Commissioner (Education) and the order of dismissal from service being a quasi judicial order, he filed writ petition challenging the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appointing authority of the appellant being the Commissioner under section 92 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, his dismissal from service was not vitiated as the disciplinary authority having regard to its findings on the charges, was of the opinion that any of the penalties specified in regulation 8(9) of the Regulations could be imposed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the Deputy Commissioner dismissing the appellant from service is not vitiated as it does not expressly state either the conclusions of the dismissing authority or the findings recorded by the enquiring officer or that the dismissing authority accepted the findings of the enquiring authority or that the dismissal authority accepted the finding of the enqu inquiring officer. [10] 2. The order passed by the Deputy commissioner (Educaury) dismissing the appellant is not an administrative order but an executive order. It is only when the order is passed after giving an opportunity to the person concerned to show cause against the proposed punishment, that the order can be challenged before the appropriate forum. [11] 3. The appellant has no right to challenge the order of the appellate authority or the revisional authority unless they are specifically stated in the order itself. [12] 4. The appellant was given reasonable opportunity to defend himself and to show cause why the order should not be confirmed. The appellant did not avail of the opportunity. Therefore, the order of removal from service cannot be assailed on the ground that the notice served upon him under article 311(2) of the Constitution was void as it did not expressly indicate either the conclusions arrived at by the dismissing authority nor the findings recorded in the enquiry report. [13] 5. The appellant had no right to question the order of termination of his services. The order was passed without complying with the requirements of Regulation 8(9). [14] 6. The appellant submitted a representation to the Deputy Commissioner who rejected the same. The Deputy Commissioner (Enqu
4018: The appellants filed a suit for declaration that the notification under section 4 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from proceeding with the acquisition of the lands in possession of the appellants. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notification issued under section 4 was illegal and void as the Government had not exercised its power within a reasonable time. HELD: The Government could have issued the notification under sections 4 and 6 only after the expiry of two years from the date of the notification. [880C] The Government could not be said to have acted arbitrarily or mala fide in issuing the notification under s.4. It is true that the Government can issue a notification under section 6 only after two years from date of the publication of the notification but the Government cannot go beyond the period of two years prescribed by the statute. But the Government can do so only after the lapse of two years. [881D E] The Government can exercise its power even after the expiry period of two year from the date on which the notification under sec.4 is published. [882F] The Government has no power to issue a notification after the expiry. [883A] The Government may issue a notification in respect of any land acquired after the commencement of the Act after the expiry thereof. But the notification under the section should be issued within a reasonable period. [884B] The Government cannot act arbitrarily or at will without exercising its power within the period of limitation. [885E]
547: The respondents were employed in the appellant as a conductor with the appellant. They were charged for misconduct under section 33 of the , and after enquiry, they were dismissed from service by an order dated December 20, 1952. The Industrial Tribunal held that the dismissal was not justified on the ground that the respondents had committed breach of section 33 of The Act and that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order made by the Industrial Tribunal granting the appellant permission to discharge the respondents. The Labour Appellate Tribunal also found that the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) had no jurisdiction under section 33 to interfere with an order passed by the Industrial Court granting the appellant 's permission to discharge its employees. It further held that the Industrial Tribunals had no jurisdiction or power to interfere with such orders. Held, that the Industrial Courts have jurisdiction to interfere in cases where there is a contravention of any of the provisions of the Act or the rules framed thereunder. The Industrial Tribunals are invested with the powers which the High Court has to exercise while hearing an appeal against an award of an industrial tribunal. The Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, 1957, do not confer upon the Industrial Tribunals the power to interfere in matters involving a question of law.
6237: The appellant landlord filed an application under section 14(1)(e) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 for eviction of the respondent tenant from the premises in dispute on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his own occupation. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the respondent was not a specified landlord and that the appellant had failed to prove that he was entitled to recover possession of the premises. The respondent tenant preferred an appeal before the District Judge who allowed the appeal holding that the appellant was not a person who could be a specified landlord. The High Court held that on the facts the appellant could not be a specified owner and that the respondent tenant was not entitled to recover the possession of the residential building or scheduled building as the case may be. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the respondent 's right to recover possession was not available to him because the premises were not owned by him but were in his occupation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent is not entitled to get possession of the tenanted premises. [96C] 2. The respondent cannot be a specified tenant. He can only claim protection against eviction provided by law. [97E] 3. The respondent has no right to recover the premises. [97F] 4. The respondent 's contention that the respondent is not a specified owner is not correct. The respondent was not entitled either to recover possession or to recover possession. [97G] 5. The respondent had not produced any certificate signed by the Head of his Service or his Commanding Officer to the effect that he was presently a member of the armed forces of the Union or he was such member and was now a retired ex serviceman. The respondent could not be said to have been a specified owner. [97H; 98A]
347: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life under section 302 I.P.C. and a fine of Rs. 100/. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court had no power to alter the decision of the learned Vacation Judge dismissing the revision petition filed by the accused. [1010 D] (2) The High Courts have been invested with powers of revision under article 226 of the Constitution. But in cases where there is no express provision like section 439(6), it would be open to an aggrieved party to move the High Court for enhancement of sentence. If the accused person has already unsuccessfully exhausted the right conferred by section 439(4) he cannot be heard to contend that the order passed by the High Court dismissing the revision application of the accused was not correct or that the accused should be permitted to challenge the correctness of the order of dismissal. [1011 E F] (3) The High court could not interfere with the conviction of the accused merely because the accused had failed to show cause against his conviction. [1012 G H]
1969: The assessee company was a firm carrying on the business of land development in Calcutta. By an agreement dated July 7, 1948, the partners of the firm agreed to sell all the business of the firm to the Amalgamated Development Limited, here in after called the vendee, which company was promoted by the partners of firm. The sale price of the business as a whole was Rs. 2,50,000 and the profit arising out of the sale was Rs. 1,83,622. The Income Tax Officer held that the entire share capital of the vendee company (excepting seven ordinary shares) was taken over by the vendor firm in lieu of the sale price of its business as a part of the sale consideration and therefore, the profits arising from the sale were taxable under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that though the sale was the sale of a business as a going concern, the value of the stock could be traced, and, therefore, the profit arising from the transaction was taxable under the Income Tax Act. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the profits arising out of sale of the business must be deemed to have been received in the course of the relevant year and not in the previous year. [613 D] (2) The fact that in the schedule the price of land is stated does not lead to the inference that there was no profit in the sale of the goods. If so, there was nothing in the name of Mugneerarm Bangur & Co., regarding the sale of any goods. The mere fact that in a particular case the sale is the sale of goods would not make the sale of such goods a sale in the course or the export of the goods within the meaning of section 5(3)(b). [613 E F] (3) The fact of the sale being the sale of an article made up of the market value of the goods cannot be said to be a matter of mere speculation. [614 G H]
4656: The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for murder and sentenced to death. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the death penalty provided in Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the circumstances which found favour with the Courts below would be "special reasons" for awarding the death sentence as required under Section 354(1) of the Cr. P.C. 1973. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the facts found by the Courts below could be "special reason" for imposing the death penalty within the meaning of Section 354(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 is no longer res integra. [354B] 2. In the instant case, the only question is whether the circumstances that the appellant was previously convicted for murder and committed these murders after he had served out the life sentence in the earlier case, not the fact that these three murders were quite heinous and inhuman, constitutes a "special reason". [355D E] 3. The question is whether there are any special reasons for imposing the extreme penalty of death on the appellant. [356E] 4. The question has been considered by this Court in several cases including the one in the case of State of Punjab vs Ram Singh, [1976] Suppl. SCR 633; [State of U.P. vs Ram Naresh Pandey], ; ; and in the case before us, the Court has held that the circumstances that have been relied upon by the courts below do not show that they are "special reasons", and that the imposition of death penalty is not justified. [357F G]
2373: The respondent was a licensee under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925. He was assessed to property tax by the Municipality in respect of certain properties belonging to the respondent. In the assessment proceedings for the year 1957, the appellant claimed that the value of the properties should be taken as the capital value of the lands and not the gross annual rent. The Judicial Magistrate fixed the valuation at Rs. 90,000/ . On appeal by the respondent, the Judicial Magistrate reduced the capital value to Rs. 90.000/ . The High Court held that the courts below had committed an error in relying upon the probable cost of constructing a new building of similar type in order to estimate the capital value as contemplated by Godhra Municipality and accordingly reduced the capital values to Rs.90,000/ ; Held, that the courts were right in holding that the courts could not rely on the estimated cost of construction of a new building for determining the capital value. The word "rate" used in section 58 of the Bombay Municipal Act, 1925, is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the common parlance in the sense of the term 'rate ' in section 3(1) of the Bombay Electricity Supply and Transport Undertaking (Acquisition) Act, 1948. The expression 'rate ' means the rate or rates leviable under the Act. The word 'rate ' is not defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. It may be levied on the actual cost of construction or the capital value or the annual rent of the land or building. The word `rate ' is generally used with reference to the cost of construction. The word`annual rent' is used in the same sense in which it is used in section 3 (1) of Bombay Electricity Supply & Transport Undertaking (Land Acquisition) Act, 1894. The word, 'rate ' does not mean the rate or rate chargeable on the actual area of land or buildings. The word is used in a popular sense and is not confined to the meaning of ordinary use of the land and buildings. The expression "rate" is used in its popular sense in the sense in which the word is understood in common law. The word has been used to denote the amount of the annual rent which the owner of the land might reasonably have to
4079: The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land in dispute on the basis that he was in possession of the said land. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that under section 146 of the Criminal Procedure Code of 1973, an attachment of the subject of dispute could be effected in three situations: (i) if the Magistrate at any time after making the order under Section 145(1) considered the case to be one of emergency; (ii) if he decided that none of the parties was then in such possession as was referred to in Section 145, or (iii) if he is unable to satisfy himself as to which of them was in such possession. HELD : (1) The proviso to sub section (4) of section 145 of the old Code empowered the Magistrate to attach the subject of the dispute if the Magistrate was of the opinion that none of them was then in possession or if the Magistrate were unable to decide as to which party was in such occupation. It was not necessary for him to wait till the Magistrate was satisfied about the existence of the dispute. [326 F] (2) The proviso does not authorise the Magistrate to pass an order without reference to the facts of the case. The Magistrate can only attach the subject matter of dispute when there is no dispute regarding the possession of the subject matter. [327 A B] (3) The proviso empowers the Magistrate to proceed with the case even though the dispute may have been settled by the decision of the Civil Court. If the Magistrate has to proceed with a case, he cannot do so unless he proceeds under section 145(1). [328 C D] (4) The proviso confers power upon the Magistrate to make an order attaching the subject of a dispute until the decision of a civil court. The Magistrate is not bound to attach the property until the decision is given by the Civil Court or the Magistrate of competent jurisdiction. He can only attach a subject of dispute pending adjudication by a Civil Court. [329 E F] (5) The proviso gives power to the Magistrate to take action under section 145 of Criminal Procedure Code against any person who is in possession of any property, whether before or
6363: The Karnataka Contract Car riages (Acquisition) Act, 1976 received the assent of the President on 11th March, 1976. The Karnataka Contract Carriage (Acquisition) Ordinance, 1976 was promulgated by the Governor on 3rd April, 1976 and came into force from 30th January, 1976. By section 2 of the Karnataka Act 21 of 1976, the Act was repealed and replaced by the Karnataka Contract Carri ting Act, 1975. Section 20 of the Karnataka State Act, 1976 provided that the Act shall be deemed to have come into force on 30th January 1976. The Act was amended in 1976 and the Karnataka Contract Carriage Act, 1975 was enacted with retrospective effect from 1st February, 1976. In the year 1976, the Karnataka Contract Lines (Acquisition) Bill, 1976 was introduced in the Lok Sabha for enacting the Karnataka Contract car riage (Acquisition) Amendment Act, 1976. It was reserved for the consideration of the President who approved it. The Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha on 6th October, 1976. On the same day, the Karnataka Act was also passed. The Karnataka Act was brought into force w.e.f. 30th January 1977. The Karnataka State Legislature passed the Karnataka Contract Clausses (Acquisition) (Amendment) Act, 1978. The Karnataka Legislature passed the Bangalore Development Authority (Amendment) Bill, 1978. In the Bill, the Karnataka State Legislature sought to amend the Karnataka Contract Passing Act, 1976 by inserting a new section 20A in the Karnataka Contract Tranche (Acquisition) and the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Taxation (Special Provisions) Act, 1979. The Karnataka High Court upheld the validity of the Karnataka Contract Transport (Acquisition) Amending Act, 1976 and the Bangalore Development Authori ty (Amendment) Ordinance, 1978. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Karnataka Contract Links (Acquisition) ordinance, 1976 is not an 'acquisi tion Act ' within the ambit of Entry 42 of the Concurrent List under Schedule VII of the Constitution. [627B] 1.2 The Karnataka Contract Pass ing Act, 1976 is a piece of legislation which has been enacted with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurren t
6452: The appellant was a Muslim minority institution. She applied for the post of lady Principal in the degree section of the college. The College was selected by the Selection Committee and the appellant was appointed as a lady Principal. The appellant challenged the decision of the University by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court on the ground that the college being a minority institution, any interference by the University under the Act is violative of Article 30(1) of the Constitution of India. The High Court rejected the contention of the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have been consistent with the view taken by this Court in the case of State of Uttar Pradesh vs Dr. Vijay Kumar Singhal; , and the view taken in the case has been reiterated in the case reported in [State of U.P. vs Dr. Krishna Chandra Tripathi] ; , and in the case decided by this Court. In the view which we are taking in this case it is not necessary to go into the argument based on Article 30(i) of the constitution of India. [766A C] 2. The High court was right in holding that the provisions of the Act are regulatory and are primarily for the purpose of maintaining uniformity, efficiency and stand ard 99 902 condition of education in the minority institutions. The High Cour t erred in interfering with the decision of this Court in Dr. Vijaykumar Singhal vs State of U. P. & Ors., [1990] 4 SCC 537. [767D E] 3. The High courts were wrong in holding that there was no violation of Article 30 of the Constitution. The High has failed to consider the effect of Article 30 (1) of Constitution of India on the selection of the appellant as a lecturer. The High should have considered the matter afresh after giving an opportunity to the appellant to be heard. [768E F] 4. The High was justified in quashing the appointment of the appellant on the ground of violation of Article 29(1) and Article 30(2). [769C D]
3616: The respondent, a minor, executed three deeds of gift transferring his lands speci fied in the order of the Land Board. The respondent filed a statement under section 85(a) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1960 and showed there that the statement related to the family consisting of himself, his wife and children. The ceiling area allowed under section 82(1) of the Act for a family consisting of two or more but not more than five members was 10 standard acres which should not be less than 12 and more than 15 ordinary acres in extent. On 28 March, 1974 the respondent executed three deeds, one of which was executed by him on 1 January, 1970 and another by the respondent on 2 January, 1970. The respondent claimed that he and his wife were the only members of the family and that the deed of gift was invalid as it did not confer any title on them. The Land Board recog ssed the gift to the eldest daughter who was a major on 1 January 1970 and required the respondent to surrender 8.78 acres which was the subject matter of the other two deeds of gift. Section 82 of the Act only fixes the ceiling area available to the family and therefore the respondent would be entitled to have not less than 12 acres on the notified date, namely, 1 January,1970. The respondent contended that the transfer of excess land was void because the respondent had no right to transfer the excess land. The Land Tribunal held that the respondent was not liable to surrender any excess land. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondent is not entitled to claim that the transfer was void because he had no right over the excess land transferred. [947E] (2) The respondent has not produced any evidence to show that he had any right over the land transferred. The respondent has also failed to produce any document showing that he had purchased the land from the original owner. [948F] (3) The respondent could not be said to have acquired any title to the excess land by adverse possession. [949A] (4) The respondent cannot be said to be in adverse possession of the excess land since he has not been able to prove that he had perfected his title by adverse possession or that he had become the owner
940: The appellant, a company incorporated in the United State of Rajasthan, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51 corresponding to the previous year 1949 50. The Income tax authorities sought to tax its profits and income for the assessment years 1950 51 corresponding, to the previous years 1949 50. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income tax had been validly levied on the appellant as it stood before the amendment of 1953, and that the exemption granted by the Finance Act, 1950, was not affected by the amendment. The High Court dismissed the petition under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contention that the Explanation to section 14(2)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it stood prior to the amendment of the said provision in 1953, was retrospective from April 1, 1950, is untenable. The Explanation to section 2(c) of that Act provided that the income-tax shall be deemed to have been validly levied if the income was received or accrued within the territories of India immediately before the date of the commencement of the Finance Act of 1950. The Explanation was intended to enlarge the scope of the operation of the section so as to make it applicable only to such income which has been received or accrued outside the territories of the State. [460 D E] (ii)The Explanation was not retrospective but was merely clarificatory. It was introduced with a view to remove the hardship caused to the assessee. The Explanation did not affect the effect of the amendment. [461 F H] (iii)The Explanation does not apply to the facts of the present case because the Explanation was not intended to enlarge any of the provisions of the Act. The Explanation is intended to enlarge existing laws and to give new rights to an assessee. The language of the Explanation is plain and unambiguous. The Explanation cannot be interpreted in a manner which would render the language of the main section nugatory. [441 G H; 442 A B] (iv)The Explanation is not intended to alter the meaning of the main provision. The Explanation must be read as a whole and not in isolation. The Explanation should be read as part of the main enactment. If there are two provisions in the statute,
4507: The appellant, a tenant in the land in question, filed a return under section 21 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961. The return was accepted and possession was taken over by the authorities concerned. The appellant 's land was included in the holding of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the proceedings commenced with the filing of a return by a person holding on the appointed day land in excess of the ceiling area prescribed by the Act and the possession of such surplus land was taken over and the surplus land was not acquired by the State Government under section 18 of the Act, and therefore, the proceedings were not saved by section 21 of Act 31 of 1961. HELD: The provisions of sections 3 to 7 of the Act are mandatory and they do not exclude the operation of section 21 of that Act. [234 E] The scheme of the Act is that the land held by a person as a member of a joint family or as a tenant is deemed to be held by him as a tenant if he has been cultivating the land personally for more than six years continuously from the date of his tenancy. The Act does not provide for any reduction of the ceiling on holding of land by a tenant who had been cultivating the lands personally for more then six years. The Act provides for the determination of the extent of surplus land which can be utilised for the purpose of determining the ceiling area. The Act also provides for the procedure to be followed by the authorities for determining the extent of the surplus land. [235 D F; 236 A B] The Act does no doubt provide for the determination and fixation of the ceiling areas in respect of certain classes of persons. But the Act does not contain any provision for the determination or fixation of the extent or value of the land which may be possessed by a person who is a member of an undivided Hindu family. The Act only prescribes the mode of distribution of the surplus area amongst those who are landless and who otherwise deserved to be granted land.
