7009: The Rajasthan Educational Service Rules, 1970 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Rules') were framed by the State Government in exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of the Rajasthan Educational Service Act, 1950. Rule 2(a) defines "cadre" to mean a group of posts, number of posts, cadre or grade and the strength of each service. Rule 4 provides that the Government may from time to time make rules for the regulation of recruitment, appointment, conditions of service, pay, allowances, discipline, control and appeal, dismissal, removal and reduction in rank of persons employed in any class or category of posts. Rule 25(5) provides that the Committee shall prepare a list of members of the service who are suitable for promotion to Group 'D '. Rule 25 provides that the list shall be prepared by the Committee on the basis of merit and seniority in the respective categories of posts. The appellants were appointed as Assistant Teachers in the Rajasthan Educational Services. They challenged the constitutional validity of this provision in the writ petitions filed in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the orders promoting members of Group 'F ' holding that the said rule was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the rule was unconstitutional being violative of Articles 16(1), 16(4) and 337 of the Constitution; that the rule is discriminatory inasmuch as it gives preference to the members of the same class of employees in the matter of promotion to Group D posts; that the classification made between the two groups is not based on intelligible differentia; that the object of the rule is to give equal opportunity to all the members of one group to compete with others in the matter relating to promotion to higher grades; that the impugned rule has been made in violation of Article 16(1) of the Constitution, and that the rule violates Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution and is therefore void. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rule is valid and does not offend Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution [1100C] 2. The rule cannot be struck down on the ground that it contravenes Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.[1101E] 3. The rule can
4904: The appellant tenant had obtained a decree for possession of the premises in question against the respondent tenant. The respondent tenant filed an application under section 15(1) of the , before the Rent Controller, seeking permission to withdraw from the eviction proceeding on the ground that he had not given a notice to quit to the appellant. The Rent Controller allowed the application and ordered eviction of the tenant. The appellant appealed to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended by the appellant that the proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 of the Act is applicable only where the tenant has not given a written notice to qui tate the title of the landlord or has not made any payment or deposit as required by section 15(l) of the Act; that the proviso cannot be invoked when the tenant does not make payment or deposit of rent within one month of the date of the order; that the tenant having been permitted to withdraw from eviction proceedings under section 15 of the Act, the proviso to section 14(2) would apply only if the tenant makes payment or deposit and not otherwise; and that the proviso must be read as providing that no tenant shall be entitled to the benefit under the proviso unless he has given a notice in writing to the landlord. HELD: The proviso to sub sections (2) and (3) of section 15 of Act of 1947 are not applicable to the instant case because, in the first ejectment proceeding which was filed by the respondents against the appellant, the latter had not obtained any benefit under that sub section. [394C] The proviso to section 15(2) of the A.P. Act of 1947 is not applicable to cases where the tenant fails to pay or deposit rent within one months of the date on which the order of eviction was passed. It is true that the proviso applies to cases where a tenant has not paid or deposited rent within one year of the date fixed for its recovery but the proviso is not applicable where the tenant pays or deposits rent within one calendar month of the order of the court. [395D E] The proviso is not intended to cover cases where the default in payment of rent continues beyond one month after the date of service of the order. 6360: The Railway Employees (Railways) Act, 1963 was enacted to provide for the regulation of the conditions of service of railway servants in the construction, maintenance and management of railway services. Section 46 of the Act provides that the provisions of the Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law or contract or instrument having force of the contract between the parties. Section 46(1)(c) provides that the Central Government may by order establish a Board of Trustees for the Welfare of Railway employees. Section 46 (2) provides that no person shall be entitled to the benefit of the Act if he is employed on a regular basis in connection with the work of the establishment. Section 46A provides that the Board of Trustees constituted under the Act shall be deemed to be a Railway Board established under the Act. Section 46B provides that the Railway Administration shall not appoint any person as a member of the Board unless the appointment has been approved by the Central Government. Section 46C provides that the General Manager of the Railway shall be the appointing authority for the Railway employees. The Railway Board had framed certain rules called the Railway Establishment Manual. These rules were amended from time to time. The Railway Employees' (Railway Services) Rules, 1961 were made applicable to the Railway employees working in the statutory canteens. Rule 3 of these rules provided that the Railway employees would be governed by the Railway Service Rules, 1950. Rule 4 provided that the terms and conditions of service including pay scales, allowances etc., of the Railway employees will be regulated by the Railway Establishment Code. Rule 5 provided that the conditions of services including pay scales and allowances, leave, joining time, joining time etc. of the Railway Employees shall be such as may be prescribed by the Railway Board. Rule 6 provided that the staff of the Railway Establishment shall be paid salary at the rates admissible to the corresponding categories of posts in the Railway Establishment. Rule 7 provided that the railway employees shall be entitled only to the benefits available to the corresponding category of posts in their respective establishments. Rule 8 provided that the provisions relating to the recruitment, promotion, transfer and disciplinary matters of the Railway servants shall apply mutatis mutandis to the Railway servants. Rule 9 provided that the rules relating to the conditions of the service of railway employees shall apply mutatis mu r
2086: The appellant was the tenant of a non residential premises No. 281, Old Tharagupet, Bangalore City. He had installed machinery in the premises and he was carrying on business there. The landlord tiled an application under section 8(3)(a) (ii) of the Act for the eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises for his own use and occupation. The Rent Controller held that under section 8 (3)(a)(ii) the landlord was not entitled to possession of the premises in dispute unless and until he was prepared to vacate the shops in which he was trading at the time. The Appellate Authority confirmed this order. In revision before the High Court it was contended that the landlord was entitled to the protection of the proviso to section 5(2) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, as he was not in occupation of the premises since the date of the tenancy and that the landlord could not be said to have a right to possession of a nonresidential building. HELD: The landlord was not a tenant of a residential building but a tenant of the non residential building. The landlord was a tenant of another residential building. He was not in possession of the building in question. [801 G] The landlord 's right to evict the tenant is not affected by the provisions of the Act. The landlord ' s right to recover possession of the residential building from a tenant is not taken away by the provisions contained in section 5(4). The landlord ' 's right of recovery of possession from a tenant who has been inducted into the residential building cannot be taken away by section 5(5) of the Mysore Rent Control Act. [802 B C]
3366: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellants on the ground that the dying declaration was not made to an independent person but was made by a person who had no reason to falsely implicate the accused. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The oral statement which Bahadur Singh made cannot in the eye of law constitute a dying declaration because he did not give full account of the incident or of the transaction which resulted in his death. [766 C D] (2) The first information report which is lodged after the attack was not admissible in evidence as it does not contain any recital about the occurrence. It is only when the prosecution has placed great reliance on the same, that the court may be in a position to assess the evidentiary value of such a dying declaration. [767 E F] (3) The second statement which has been treated by the High Court as a dying declaration and is admissible under section 32(1) of the Evidence Act, is admissible under s.32(1) thereof. The third statement which has also been treated by this Court as a statement made to an official witness, though not admissible in the trial court, is inadmissible in evidence. [768 B C]
3199: The plaintiff, a carrier, was carrying on the business of transporting goods from one place to another. He had been in possession of certain goods and had been using them for the purpose of transportation. The goods were seized by the Customs authorities under section 110 of the Customs Act, 1962. The plaintiff claimed that he had suffered loss of goods as a result of the seizure. The defendants contended that the plaintiff 's suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief because the goods were not liable to be confiscated under section 111(d) of the Customs act, 1962. It is true that the plaintiff had no knowledge of the landing of the goods but it could not be said that the goods were actually landed or ready to be handed over. The fact that the goods are not landed or prepared at the time when they are delivered does not make the plaintiff 'superior to the actual owner of the goods. The plaintiff 's case was that the goods had been illegally detained by the Customs Authorities. The question whether the plaintiff had acquired title to the goods or not was a matter which could be decided only by the trial court. The plaintiff was not a party to the proceedings before the Customs authorities. The plaintiff had no right to sue. The plaintiff did not acquire any title to the property. The plaintiff could not claim any damages against the defendant.
470: The appellants were the plaintiffs in a suit for declaration that they had no right to execute a gift deed of the properties of their father, and that the gift was void. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the gift deed was not a valid one as it did not relate to the properties of the family of the parties but related to the properties which were the subject matter of the earlier marriage and that the deed was not executed by the father or his relations. In appeal to this Court on the question whether the gift deed could be said to have been made with the consent of the parties. HELD: (1) The gift was not a mere pretence or a device to get over the operation of the Hindu Law. It was intended to defeat the rights of the parties to the marriage. [460 D] (2) The gift is not a mere pious obligation arising out of the property gifted. It is a contract between the parties and the donee has every right to deal with the property giver in such manner as he thinks fit. [441 F] (3) The gift cannot be said to be a mere pretext or a device for getting over the operation or for securing the gift of the properties. [442 B C] (4) The gift must be proved to be a reasonable part of the estate of the donor. [443 A C] (5) The gift being of a purely temporary nature, it was not a part of the property of the parties at all. [444 E] (6) The gift does not amount to a transfer of property within the meaning of section 17(i)(a). [444 G]
256: The appellant and respondent No. 2 were candidates for election to the Legislative Assembly of Madhya Pradesh from the State of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent No. 1 filed an election petition against the appellant and the other respondents under section 81 of the Representation of the People Act alleging that the appellant had been guilty of corrupt practices by the returned candidate, respondent No. 3, and that he was disqualified to be chosen as a member of the Legislative Assembly. The appellant contested the petition on the ground that he was not qualified to contest the election and that he had not been duly elected. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not qualified and that the nomination of respondent No. 1 was improperly accepted. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant could not be said to have been disqualified because he did not suffer from any disqualification under the Constitution. The appellant was not entitled to maintain an election petition in respect of the election of respondent No.. 1. The appellant could not claim to be a person disqualified under article 173(1) of the Constitution because he was not a party to the petition. The appellant had no locus standi to file an election petition. The election petition was not maintainable.
826: The respondent company was a textile mill and its factory was situate at Jalgaon. The appellant, the Textile Mills Company Limited, issued a notice under section 42(2) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 calling upon the appellant to pay certain amounts as bonus for the period from January 1, 1956 to December 31, 1955. The appellant claimed that the said amount should be deducted from the gross profits of the company for the purpose of determining the available surplus for rehabilitation. The Labour Court held that the said sum was not available for rehabilitation and that the appellant could not claim any credit for the said amount. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Industrial Court had erred in holding that the reserves were used as working capital and that the said reserves were not so utilised. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to prove that the reserves had been utilised as working capital. [801 B] (ii) The Industrial Court has to determine whether the said reserves have been used as working funds or not. If the said reserves are not used as working expenses, they would be entitled to deduct the said amount from the available surplus. [802 C D] (iii) In ascertaining the available surplus the Industrial Court is required to take into consideration the fact that the reserves have been utilised as such for a binding purpose. [803 E F]
888: The petitioner was the eldest son of a Ruler of Vadia State. He executed two documents in favour of the petitioner granting him in perpetuity and in heredity a village called Mota Pithadia in the State for enjoyment as ' Kapal Giras ' as ' Bhayat '. On July 2, 1951, the Government of Saurashtra issued a notification recognising the petitioner as the Ruler of VadIA in the State with effect from May 16, 1950. On August 5, 1952, the Government issued another notification declaring that as the petitioner had succeeded his father as Ruler, the village Pithadiya should be treated as Khalsa or Khas village of the State. On September 3, 1953, the Government passed an order recognizing the petitioner as a Ruler of the former Vadia State and on October 1, 1954, the Government cancelled the said order. On November 9, 1955, the petitioner filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order dated October 1, 1953, contending that the order dated February 12, 1951, was illegal and void as it was not made by the Ruler of the State of Vadia. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The petitioner was entitled to succeed his father as a Ruler. His right to the property of the Ruler was not extinguished by reason of the fact that the Ruler had died before the date of the order. [525 D] (2) The petitioner could not claim any benefit under the order dated March 31, 1956, because the order dated April 7, 1957, was not made in accordance with the provisions of section 4(3)(a) of the Act. [526 A] (3) The petitioner cannot claim any benefit on the basis of the order of the Government dated March 31. 1956. [527 B] (4) The petitioner is entitled to succeed on the basis that the order of March 31, 1957, is valid. [528 C] (5) The petitioner has no right to claim the benefit of the order which he claims. [529 E] (6) The petitioner can claim the benefit only if he succeeds in establishing that the order was made in accordance therewith. [530 F
2685: The appellant was the sole proprietor of a partnership firm. He carried on business in partnership at three places in Madhya Pradesh, in the name of the Jaora Slate Pencil Works and in the name and style of the Nagpur Slates. In the course of his business he had entered into an agreement with the respondent for the sale of certain goods to be supplied by him to the appellant. The agreement provided that the goods would be delivered within four months from the date of the agreement and that if the goods were not delivered within the stipulated period, the appellant would pay to the respondent a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ as earnest money. The respondent paid the amount but failed to deliver the goods within the stipulated time. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for a decree for rendition of account of the dealing in respect of the Jao Slates and for appointment of receiver. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the Civil Court at Mandsaur had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for appointment of a receiver. The High Court also held that having regard to the proceedings pending in the High Court at Delhi it was a case in which without adjudicating upon the jurisdiction of the Subordinate Judge at Mandsour, the application for extension of time was maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Civil Court at the place where the suit is instituted did not have jurisdiction to entertain an application for appointment or appointment of a Receiver. [787 F] (2) The Civil Courts at Mandsurna were competent to entertain an action in the Court of the Additional District Judge, Mandsaur. [788 G H] (3) The Civil courts at Mandsul could not have any jurisdiction to pass orders for appointment of the receiver. [789 A B] (4) The Civil court at Mandsula had no jurisdiction under section 28 of the Arbitration Act to appoint a receiver. [791 C D] (5) The Civil judge at Mandsully had no jurisdiction in the matter. [786 E]
53: The plaintiff brought a suit for possession of the ghatwalis in suit. The defendant pleaded that the ghatwas were joint family properties and were im plicated by custom; that succession to them was governed by the Mitakshara law and that the plaintiff being the eldest surviving copartner in the eldest line of the community, was entitled to succeed to them in preference to the plaintiff under the Mitakshra School of Hindu Law which admittedly governed the family of the parties. The trial court held that the plaintiff was not entitled to succeed on the ground that the property was joint family property and that the defendant was entitled to inherit it as his separate property. On appeal, the High Court held that the property being the exclusive property of the plaintiff, the defendant was not entitled,to succeed to the plaintiff. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The rule of espionage is applicable to such estates as are the exclusive property or properties of the gattan-holder. [860 G] (2) The rule is applicable only where there is a joint family. It applies when there is a family and the property is joint family property. [861 A B] (3) The rule has no application to the case before us. The property being the joint family property, the defendant could not be said to have been excluded from inheritance because he had not been able to prove that the property belonged to him. [862 C D] (4) The rule applies only where there was a family and there was no other family. [863 E] (5) The rule does not apply where there is no family but only a single member of a family. [886 F] (6) The rule cannot apply where there are two members of a joint family and one of them is the sole heir of the family. [891 G]
176: The appellants were prosecuted for offences under section 120 B and 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the two appellants demanded on August 8, 1949, at Rewa (within the United State of Vindhya Pradesh) to obtain illegal gratification from one Nagindas Mehta, a representative of the Panna Diamond Mining Syndicate, and that later on November 11, 1949, the first appellant demanded on August 12, 1949, a sum of Rs. 25,000 towards it. The second appellant was sentenced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000 under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court convicted both the appellants under sections 120B and 161 of I.P.C., but the High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences. In appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of article 20(1) of the Constitution are not applicable in the present case because there is no express provision in the Act which makes any such provision applicable to the case. [1203 D] (ii)The absence of a right of appeal may be a lacuna, but that inasmuch as it has not been expressly provided, it cannot be implied from the fact that a provision has been made for the exercise of powers by the appellate court. [1204 A] (iii)The presumption against innocence is always a rebuttable one and the burden of proof is upon the accused person to prove his innocence. But once the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the exceptions mentioned in section 300, the burden shifts to the accused to rebut the presumption. [1205 C D] (iv)The presumption of innocence can be raised only when the facts alleged are established beyond reasonable doubt. [1206 E] (v)It is not necessary to establish that the accused had some sort of a positive evil or that he had an unblemished record of service. It is enough if the evidence establishes that the accused knew what he was being tried for and had no reason to suspect himself. [1207 F] (vi)There is nothing in the language of article 20 (2) of the constitution which prohibits the making of a statement without any authority of law.
4581: The appellant, a dealer in respect of sales to dealers in Orissa and to dealers in the State of Orissa, was registered under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947 as amended by the Orissa Additional Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1979. The appellant challenged the levy of additional tax on the ground that it was a single point levy or a multi point levy. The High Court held that the levy of the additional tax was a single rate and not a multiple point levy. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The levy of additional sales tax is a single point tax which is levied by the State Government on the sale of goods. It is a single rate for the purpose of levying tax. [701 B] 2. The State Legislature has enacted the Orissa Additional sales tax Act, 1975. Section 3B of the Act provides that every dealer whose gross turnover during a fiscal year exceeds Rs. 50,000 shall be liable to pay tax under the Act on sales and purchases effected after the date so notified. The appellant 's contention that the levy was a single charge or a multiple point tax is without substance. [702 C D] 3. The State legislature has enacted the Act with retrospective effect from April 1, 1975. The Act is prospective in operation. The Act does not provide for any fresh levy of additional taxes. The Act only prescribes the extent of the liability to pay tax. The Act imposes the liability to tax under the Principal Act on every dealer whose total turnover during a financial year exceeds Rs 50,000 but does not include a dealer who is otherwise liable to pay sales tax. The liability to pay sales and purchase tax is a distinct and separate liability. [703 E F] 4. The State Government has been empowered to frame rules under section 5 of the Act. The State has framed rules called the Orissa Additional Tax Rules, 1975. Rule 3(1)(a) of the Rules provides that every registered dealer shall be liable t o pay tax under this Act on every sale of goods other than those declared under section 3 B of the Principal Act. The appellant was registered under section 3A of the Act as a dealer in the State. The appellant had paid tax at the rate of 4% on its turnover. The appellant could not be said to have
1614: The appellant was a cashier in the Municipal Board of Hardwar. He had been working as such since 1932 and had been working for the Board as such since 1933. On account of his negligence, he was suspended and the matter was handed over to the police for investigation. After investigation, the appellant was prosecuted under section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and after investigation prosecuted the Executive Officer as well as the appellant and his brother. The Special Judge held that the joint trial of the appellant and the brother of the appellant was not possible with respect to some of the moneys which were said to have been embezzled. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the joint trials were not possible with the appellant 's money and that the evidence as found by the High Court did not establish that there was any conversion of the money into his own use. HELD : (i) The joint trial is not possible with reference to section 5(2) of Act 1 of 1947. Section 5(2), however, provides that where the prosecution has been instituted for an offence other than one falling under section 5(1)(c) of the Act, the court shall presume that the accused person has received or agreed to accept or attempted to obtain that amount of money by way of gratification or that he accepted or attempted to accept or abetted the doing of that thing. [93E F] (ii) The presumption under section 5 of the Act is only a rebuttable presumption and not a legal presumption. It is open to the court to raise a presumption that the accused has received or is willingly willfully accepted the money knowing it to be the subject matter of the charge. But once the burden of proof is discharged by the accused, then the onus shifts on him to prove that he has not received or agreed or accepted or attempted or accepted or abetted or attempted to do so. [94F H; 95A B] (iii) The presumption is rebutted when the prosecution fails to discharge its initial burden. [95C D] (iv) The presumption may be raised at any stage of the proceedings. If the defence raises a probable defence which if proved would be sufficient
4503: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. He filed an appeal before the High Court which confirmed the conviction and sentence of death passed on him. In the first place, the Sessions Judge ignored the provision contained in section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 which provides in so far as is relevant that when the accused was asked on the question of sentence, he did not say anything. The Sessions Judge overlooked this provision and proceeded to confirm the death sentence. The High Court also overlooked the provisions contained in section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 which provides that when the person who has been tried by a court of competent jurisdiction for an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment of either description for a term of ten years or more but less than seven years, shall be held guilty of having committed such offences. The High court overlooked the provision contained under section 354(1) Cr. P.C. 1973 which provides, in so far it is relevant, that when the convict is required to state what he has to say on the question whether he has to give any explanation about his conduct or why he should not be punished, then only the court can record its own reasons for doing so. The High 'Court overlooked these provisions and proceeded to pass the impugned judgment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken the view that the F.I.R. cannot be recorded at the police station when the accused is called upon to answer questions put to him in cross examination. [880D] 2. It is not necessary that there must be some evidence to show that the appellant had given any particular statement to the police officer. [881E] 3. 5785: The petitioners in the batch of writ petitions were promoted as Assistant Engineers (Deputy Executive Engineers) on ad hoc basis. They challenged the order of regularisation by filing a Writ Petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that the regularisation made by the Chief Engineer of the promotees to the posts of Assistant Engineers was without authority and was in gross violation of the prescription of the Rules. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the direct recruits that the retrospective regularisation made by Government is not permissible under Rule 3(1) of the Special Rules and that the regularisation was made by exercising powers under Rule 23 of the General Rules. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The regularisation made by Chief Engineer of promotees to the post of Assistant Engineers is without authority and is in gross violation off the prescription of Rules. [382C] 2. The regularisation of the promotees in the cadre of Assistant Engineers has been made by exercising power under Rule 23(3)(a) of the General rules. The regularisation is not automatic but depends upon the availability of substantive vacancies in the cadre. [384E] 3. The regularisation can be made only if there are substantive vacancies in a particular cadre and the promotees have been appointed against the substantive vacancies. If the promotees are placed in the substantive vacancies, they would be entitled to seniority from the date of their initial appointment. [385F] 4. The regularisation cannot be made with reference to substantive vacancies in any cadre. It will depend on the nature of the vacancy and the number of persons recruited. [386G] 5. The regularisation could be made only after the creation of a cadre and unless the quota rule provides otherwise. [387A] 6. The regularisation was not intended to be an adhoc or stop gap arrangement. The regularisation must be for a specific period. The regularisation should be based on length of service and not purely fortuitous. [388B]
3880: The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He appealed to the High Court which set aside his conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the Sessions Judge was in error in acquitting the appellant of the offence under section 302 IPC because he had not given any reason why he could not have given the fatal blow. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that even if the intention of the accused was limited to infliction of a bodily injury sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature, the offence would be murder. [747C] 2. The appellant was not guilty of the offence of causing the death of the deceased. His case was that the injuries were inflicted on the vital part of the body of the deceased and that the injuries caused by him were sufficient in the ordinary way of nature to cause death. [746D E] 3. The appellant did not offer any explanation as to how the injury was caused. It is true that the appellant might have been armed with a knife but that does not mean that he intended to cause the death of his wife. If the intention of an accused was limited only to the infliction of the injury that was sufficient to cause her death, then clause thirdly of section 300 would be attracted. [748E F] 4. The appellant had no intention to cause the injury which he was likely to cause. There was no reason why the appellant should have inflicted the injury with a knife. [749A B]

The word "manufacture" in the explanation to item 30 would refer to the manufacture of a piece of cloth. 1769: The petitioners are dealers in iron and steel. They have been assessed to sales tax under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The petitioners challenged the validity of the assessment on the ground that the transactions in question were inter State sales and had not been effected in the course of inter State trade. Held, that the petitioners cannot succeed on the ground of article 286(1)(a) of the Constitution. Article 286(1) (a) provides that no law of a State shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, any tax on the sale or purchase of goods where such sale or purchase takes place outside the State. The petitioners are not dealers in iron or steel. They are merely carrying on business as manufacturers of iron and steel and they do not fall within the purview of article 286. The petitioners cannot be said to be dealers in iron & steel. The petitioners have not been able to show that the contracts in question were entered into with the petitioners for the purpose of carrying out the contract. The contracts were not works contracts but were contracts for the purpose and could not be enforced against the petitioners. The petitioners were not dealers in steel or steel and therefore, could not claim the protection of article 286 (1) (b).
6677: The respondents were sureties for the respondent company. They filed a suit against the appellant and the surety for recovery of their dues. The trial court passed an order of attachment in respect of the properties of the surety. The appellant challenged the said order by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions of section 31 of the Act did not contemplate passing of a money decree, and that the relief claimed in the petition could not be granted under sections 31 and 32 of the Act inasmuch as these sections did not contemplate the passing of a sum decree not only against the principal debtor but also against the sureties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition; (ii) the relief claimed was outside the scope of section 31 and therefore could not be given; (iii) the provisions in the Act relating to enforcement of the liability of a surety were ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution; (iv) the provisions of the Act relating the enforcement of the liabilities of a surety could not be invoked unless the Financial Corporation intimated to the district judge that it would not appeal against any order releasing any property from attachment or rejecting the claim to transfer the management of the industrial concern to the Financial Corporation under clause (c ) or transferring the management of industrial concern to Financial Corporation under cl.(e), the district judge may make such further orders as he thinks fit to protect the interests of the Financial Corporation and may apportion the costs of the proceedings in such manner as he thinks proper; (v) the provisions contained in the Act concerning the execution of decrees, which are capable of being executed in the ordinary way, cannot be regarded as retrospective in operation; (vi) the provisions regarding the execution of the security bond and the like were ultra vires article 14 of the constitution; (vii) the provisions relating to the execution of a mortgage were ultra vires the Constitution; and (viii) the provisions for the execution of an order for sale of the attached property were ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 32 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, are ultra vires Article
5869: The Rajasthan University, the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 4 of 1981, was a medical college affiliated to the Rajasthan University. In the year 1975, the Rajasthan University had conducted an entrance examination for admission to post graduate courses in various medical colleges in Rajasthan. The appellant applied for admission to the post graduate course in the said medical college. He passed his final MBBS Examination from the same institution for which selections were being made. The result of the entrance examination was declared on June 30, 1976 and he was ranked at serial No. 1 in the merit list. The appellant challenged the validity of the said provision by filing a Writ Petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the provision was unconstitutional and in consequence struck down as unconstitutional. The High court also struck down the provision as unconstitutional. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provision contained in note (d) (ii) of Ordinance 278 E is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. It is only a rule of reasonable classification and does not amount to discrimination. [310D] 1.2 The provision in Note (d)(i) of Ordinance No. 278 E has been held to be unconstitutional. The conclusion reached by the High Court is right. The conclusion so far as it relates to the appellant is supported by the fact that the appellant had obtained 50% marks in the qualifying examination. [311E F] 1.3 The provision in note (b) (ii), which is in the nature of an exception to the general rule of reservation, cannot be regarded as unreasonable or arbitrary. The provision in the note (d)(ii) is not discriminatory nor can it be said to be unreasonable. [312A B] 2.1 The object of providing reservation in the State Medical Colleges is to ensure that the students who are admitted to post graduate medical courses in any one of the five Medical Colleges in Rajasthan will have the benefit of such reservation. The object of giving weightage to the candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes is to see that the meritorious students belonging to the scheduled castes get the benefit of reservation. This is a policy decision taken by the Government. [313B C] 3.

6607: The respondents filed a suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction against the appellant, the respondent No. 1, and the appellant, and also for a decree of possession of the properties in dispute. The trial court granted leave to the respondents under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that the grant of leave was not an administrative act of the court and no notice to the respondents was required before such leave was granted. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code confers on the court the power to grant leave to institute a suit of the nature referred to in section 91 of the Code. It is not necessary that there should be a formal order granting leave to institute the suit. [947 E] (2) An order refusing leave to institute or defend a suit of a nature referred to under section 92 is not a judicial order. It is only an administrative act which is subject to the jurisdiction of the court. [948 F G] (3) A person interested in a public trust must have an interest in the trust and he must have obtained leave from the court before he instituted the suit. If the court grants leave it would be void as being in excess of the powers conferred upon it by section 92(f). [949 C D] (4) The grant of leave does not amount to a judicial act. It is merely ministerial act. It may be done either by the court itself or by the court subordinate to it. It is therefore not necessary that the court should have been approached by the parties to the suit with a view to obtaining the leave of the court before it decides whether to grant or refuse leave. [950 B C] (5) The grant or refusal of leave depends upon the discretion of the court, but the grant or refusal is not conclusive. [951 E] (6) The grant is not a mere ministerial act. The grant of permission to institute a case involves the exercise of discretion by the court. It is a matter of discretion to be exercised judicially. [952 C]
1567: The appellant was the tenant of a house in Delhi. He had been in occupation of the premises since prior to 1950, at a monthly rent of Rs. 50/ . The respondents made an application before the Rent Controller for the eviction of the appellant on the ground that he was a licensee and that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between him and the respondents. The Rent Controller dismissed the application but the Additional Rent Controller allowed the appeal holding that the relationship of landlord was established on the basis of certain rent receipts granted by the respondents to the appellant. The appellant filed a second appeal before the High Court which was also dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the premises had been let out to the first respondent as a servant and that there were no relationship of the landlord and tenant. HELD : (i) The appellant was not a licensee and therefore the application for eviction could not be entertained. [263 B] (ii) The order striking out his defence against eviction was passed after the filing of the suit. The appellant did not make any attempt to bring the suit within the period of limitation prescribed under section 15(7) of the Act. The appellant was merely a licensee and there was no question of his being a licensee. [264 C D] (iii) The appellant had not raised any plea that the premises were bona fide required by the respondents for their own residence. The appellant had only raised a plea that the respondents were tenants and that there is no relationship of landlords and tenant between them. [265 E] (iv) The appellant has failed to prove that he was in possession of the premises. The appellant has not produced any evidence to show that he was not in possession of any part of the premises in dispute. There is nothing to show that the appellant was in possession. [266 F] (v) The appellant cannot be said to have proved that he was only a licensee. The appellant could not be said to be in possession of a part of the property in dispute. [267 G]

He brought the three suits out of which these appeals have arisen for obtaining payments which he claimed was due to him. The respondent filed a written statement denying the claim and contending that the contract was not intended to be done gratuitously. The trial court decreed the suits. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had no right to file a cross objection under Or. 41, r. 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court could not give relief to the appellant by allowing or dismissing the appeal of the State by dismissing the plaintiff 's suit against the State. [847 C] (2) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the appellant could not file a cross object under Or.41, r.22 of the Code. [848 E] (3) The High courts were wrong in giving the appellant a decree against the State of Madhya Pradesh. [849 F] (4) The High court was wrong in holding the appellant 's suit as not maintainable. [850 G] (5) The High 'Court was wrong in granting a decree in favour of the respondent. [851 A] (6) The High Courl cannot give a decree in respect of a matter which is not expressly mentioned in the plaint. [852 B] (7) The High. Court was wrong in giving a decree in its favour. [853 D] (854 A) The High, Court should have given a decree in the case of the respondent in respect of the matters specified in the plaint, if it thought fit. [855 B] (9) The High: Court was wrong on the basis of the assumption that the appellant 'sufficiently contended before it that the respondent was entitled to the amount claimed. [856 C] (10) The High' Court was wrong also in giving a direction to the appellant to pay interest at 6% per annum from the date of the suit till payment. [857 D]
5055: The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on vacant land in urban agglomerations. Section 2(f) defines 'family' as a person having an interest either in the total holding or in the entire area of land held by him as owner or tenant or partly as owner and partly as tenant. Section 23 which deals with disposal or distribution of excess vacant land acquired under the Act provides that where any excess vacant land is allotted to a person in lieu of or in addition to any other land held by such person in any urban agglommeration, he shall be liable to pay to the State Government at the rate of one and a half times the price of such excess land as determined by the competent authority. 1186: The appellant, a partner of a firm carrying on business in hides and skins, was the owner of certain properties which were transferred to his brother Fazal Bhai by a deed of partnership. On receipt of information that Abdulla Dhala had migrated to Pakistan after transferring his properties to his brother, Fazal Bhikhu, the Assistant Custodian issued a notice under section 7(1) of the Ordinance directing him to show cause why the property should not be declared as evacuee property. The appellant filed objections against the notice. The Deputy Custodian General rejected the objections. Thereupon the appellant applied for revision to the High Court. The High Court held that the notice issued by the Custodian of Evacuee Property was invalid and quashed the order of the Deputy Custodian. Held: (i) The notice issued by a person who is not an evacuee could not be challenged in proceedings under article 226 of the Constitution. A person who has been declared an evacuee can only challenge the order of his authority or jurisdiction if he is aggrieved by it. In the present case, the notice issued to the appellant did not suffer from any infirmity. It was not necessary for the appellant to show that the notice was invalid because the notice was issued by a competent authority.

4881: The Respondent, who was a Government servant, occupied a Government accommodation allotted to him by the Central Government. On May 17, 1976, he filed an application under section 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 before the Rent Controller, Delhi, for eviction of the Respondent from the said Government accommodation. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the Respondent had not been in possession of any suitable alternative accommodation as was required by the Act. The Respondent then moved the High Court under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Rent Controller. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent is entitled to protection under section 14A(1) of the Delhi Renusagar Urban (Customs) Act, 1957. [817E] 2. The provisions of section 14A (1) of which are mandatory in character, do not confer any right upon the landlord to recover possession of the premises let out to him. It only confers a discretionary power on the Rent Controller to grant or refuse relief to the tenant if he has failed to vacate the premises within one month of the date of service of notice. 5483: The appellant was the tenant of a premises in Delhi. He had been paying rent to the respondent. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The appellant contended that the rent was deposited on account of the appellant 's husband and after the death of his wife, the appellant was not a party to the proceedings in execution. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rent being deposited on account, the appellant could not be said to have any bona fide need or requirement of the landlord. There was no evidence adduced and no averment made that the tenancy is for first time created. 1825: The appellant firm was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. In the year 1950, the partnership firm entered into a partnership deed with one of its partners. The partnership deed provided that the profits earned by the firm during the previous year should be distributed among the partners in proportion to their shares in the capital of the firm. The firm was dissolved on April 1, 1950. The Income tax Officer issued notice under section 34(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, calling upon the firm to show cause why the assessment should not be cancelled. The firm challenged the notice before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the firm had no right to collect the commission of the entire match production of the larger partnerships whether they were members of the partnership or not. He also held that the partnership deed was not genuine and brought into existence only as a simple arrangement, that the profits which are distributed under the deed to the individuals mentioned therein were not the true profits of those individuals. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the said partnership deed was valid and that the firm was entitled to collect the profits from the firm. On further appeal, the High Court held that the partners of the firm were entitled to collect from the firm the profits earned in the earlier years by way of commission for the first time and thereafter, by way of profit bonus for the subsequent years. Held: (i) The partnership deed did not create any new rights but merely provides for the distribution of the profits amongst the partners. (ii) The partnership agreement does not create any interest in the firm. It merely provides for distribution of the income of the firm in future. The firm has no right to receive the profits of the firm after the dissolution of the firm, and the firm has no power to make any profit out of the profits of a firm. (iii) The firm is a separate legal entity and the firm is not an association of persons. 2270: The respondent 's land was acquired by the State Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. 6716: The respondent instituted a suit for eviction of the appellant from a building on the ground of arrears of rent, etc. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed in appeal by the appellate court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that as a result of the declaration by this Court of the constitutional invalidity of clause (ii) of section 30 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the suit was not maintainable; that the decree passed by the civil court was not a nullity for the Act had not barred the jurisdiction of the civil court, but only prohibits execution of a decree for eviction otherwise than in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions; and that the decree of the civil courts was a nullity for all purposes. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The decree passed by a civil court is not a nullity, because the jurisdiction of a civil court has been expressly barred under the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Amendment Act, 1961. [623E] 2. The decree of the Civil Court is not a mere nullity, but is a decree which is capable of being executed and enforced in due course of law. It is a decree of a competent court. [624F] 3. The decree is not a decree of the court. It is merely an order made by the court. The decree does not become a nullity simply because the court finds that the denial of title of the landlord or the claim of the tenant is bona fide. [625G] 4. The decree in the present case is not a void decree. The decree was passed by the court in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction. The decree became a nullity when it was passed. [626A] 5. The decree cannot be said to be a nullity for two reasons: firstly, it is a nullity for one reason or the other and secondly, it is not executable. [627B] 628

653: The appellant was a private limited company carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar and other articles. The company filed a petition in the High Court for an order directing the liquidator to pay certain amounts due to the appellant. The company 's liability to pay the amount arose only when the company was taken into liquidation and the liquidator was neither named nor any notice given to him of the commencement of the proceedings before the Tribunal or before the respondent No. 1. The appellant was not a workman within the meaning Of section 2(7) of the , and therefore could not be said to be a " employee".

929: The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of certain properties mortgaged to him by the respondent, filed a suit for recovery of the mortgage money on the basis that he was entitled to Rs. 2,37,503 5 6 as interest from March 19, 1932 till September 30, 1937, and a sum of Rs. 51 3 0 as costs in his favour by the respondent. The preliminary decree passed by the trial court was confirmed by the High Court in appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent was not entitled to any amount under section 14 of the Encumbered Estates Act, and (ii) the respondent had no right to claim interest subsequent to the final decree. HELD : (i) The respondent was not bound by section 14 of Act 1 of 1877. Section 14 of the Act is not applicable to the present case because the preliminary decree was passed after the application of the respondent under section 4 of the U.P. Encumbered Estates (Amendment) Act, 1936, was rejected by the Special Judge. [901 E] (ii)The respondent was not liable to pay interest on the amount due on the mortgage. The preliminary decretal amount was payable by the respondent to the appellant. 5347: The appellant was the accused in a case under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. He applied for bail and his application was rejected by the Sessions Judge on June 3, 1986. On June 4, 1986 he filed an application before the High Court for recalling his order dated June 3,1986, the application was directed to be placed before the Court on June 6, 1986. The High Court recalled its earlier order dated June 4,1986 and fixed the matter for hearing on July 7, 1986. In pursuance of the order of Justice D.N. Mean while, the respondent No. 1 made another application on June 3. 1986 praying that the trial should be concluded expeditiously and if necessary the court should hold day to day trial to conclude the same at an early date. The High court dismissed the application but granted three days time to file detailed counter affidavit in reply to the allegations made in bail application. The appellant 's counsel contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application as the trial was delayed because the appellant was not available for orders and there were other disturbances which have persuaded us to interfere with the order of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has power to consider whether the trial is delayed due to reasons beyond the control of the prosecution or the defence. [766A] 1.2 If the trial is not commenced within three months from the date of the first bail application, the accused shall be entitled to bail. [767B] 1.3 If the trial has been adjourned without any sufficient cause, the accused may be released on bail. [776C] 1.4 If the trial proceeds ex parte, the accused will be entitled to the benefit of section 436 Cr. P.C. [775D] 1.5 If the trial does not proceed, the accused would be entitled to get the benefit of Section 436 Cr P.C.[776E] 2.1 The fact that the trial is being delayed due to the reason that the accused was not available at the time when the first bail applications were considered, cannot be a ground for denying bail to the accused. [777F]
4083: The first respondent, a former employee of the appellant company, was arrested on the allegation that he had committed offences under sections 403, 409 and 477A read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. He filed a complaint against the first respondent alleging that he had been guilty of having committed offences under section 403, 406 and 477 A read with section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. The Magistrate issued summons to him for production of certain documents in his possession. The complainant moved the High Court for quashing the proceedings contending that the provisions relating to search warrant could not be issued under section 91 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court held that the provisions regarding search warrant were hit by article 20(3) of the Constitution and quashed the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions relating lo seizure of books, documents etc., were violative of article 20(1) of the Cons titution; (ii) since the search warrant was issued without any authority or power, the same could not be executed; (iii) since the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had committed offences punishable under sections 402, 409 and 471 of the Indian penal code, the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Magistrate was illegal and void; and (iv) since the provisions relating t o search warrant were violated, the proceedings should be quashed. HELD: (1) The question whether there is any element of compulsion in issuing a summons to a person accused of an offence under section 94(old) to produce a document or thing in his possession or power was considered by this Court in Swarnalingam Chettiar vs Assistant Commissioner of Police, Karaikudi, ; and the decision of this Court in Sreenivasan vs State of Madras, ; , followed. (2) The provisions relating to searches warrant were also violative of article 19(1)(a) of the constitution. [875 B]

7056: The Goa Legislative Assembly was constituted on 1.1.1967 under the Goa, Daman and Diu (Disqualified Members) Act, 1964. The petitioner, a member of the Goa Legislative Assembly, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated 15.2.1991 passed by the Speaker disqualifying Ravi Naik, the Deputy Speaker functioning as the Speaker of the Goa Legislature. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Speaker had no such power of review. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have been conferred with powers of review under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. [831C] 2.The High Courts are invested with the power of reviewing their orders made by the Speaker or the Chairman after hearing the parties. [832D] 3.Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court may exercise its jurisdiction even though the proceedings before the Speaker or Chairman were not subject to scrutiny by the High Court. [833E] 4.Article 136 is an extraordinary power which has been conferred upon the Supreme Court to be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases only when there is a manifest error apparent on the face of the record. It does not confer any new right on the applicant. [834F] 5.In the instant case, the Speaker, acting as the authority under the Tenth Schedule, having not acted judicially, the impugned orders cannot be sustained. [835G] 6.It is true that the Speaker has no such power but he can certainly set aside the order of disqualification if it appears from the facts and circumstances of the case that the Speaker did not act in accordance with law. [836A] 7.The High Court was wrong in dismissing the writ petitions. [837B] 8.The High court erred in dismissing the petitions. [883C]
1992: The mortgage deed provided that the mortgagee would pay Rs. 68 10 9 3 pies, and the mortgage deed provided for payment of Rs. 1,000 by the mortgagor to the mortgagee annually on account of rent of the land. The mortgagee was a mortgagee in possession of the land and the mortgagor was entitled to redeem it at the rate of Rs. 68 0 per acre. The mortgagee obtained a decree for arrears of rent and at the rent sale held on June 18, 1934, the mortgagee purchased the land in the farzi name of Dwarkalal. The mortgagee failed to pay the rent due from him and the mortgagor filed a suit for redemption of the mortgaged property. The mortgagee contended that the purchases were made by the mortgagee in his own right and not as a result of any contract between the mortgagor and the mortgagee and that the mortgagee had no right to sell the mortgaged property without the consent of the mortgagor. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the second appeal in part. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The purchase at the rent sold was a sale with the consent of both the mortgagor and mortgagee. The mortgagee did not acquire any interest in the land. He only acquired a right to redeem the same. [166 B] (2) The mortgagee was not a party to the transaction. The mortgagee could not be said to have acquired any interest in land. The mortgagor was not a person interested in the land and he could not be treated as a person interested within section 90 of the Transfer of Property Act. [164 C] (3) The mortgagee had no interest in the property. The mortgagor had no interest therein. The mortgagee had nothing to do with the land. [165 E] (4) The mortgagee could only redeem the land if he was satisfied that the land was fit for cultivation or other purposes. [168 F] (5) The mortgagee did neither acquire any interest nor any interest in it. He merely got a right to recover the amount due under the mortgage. [169 G] (6) The mortgagee is not a person aggrieved by the mortgage. The mortgagee has no interest in land and the mortgagee cannot be said to be a person interested. [167 A B] (7)
6522: The appellant was granted nautor land in his favour under the Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1954. He felled the trees on the land without waiting for necessary approval of the Divisional Forest Officer and as such he took the law in his own hands. The Divisional Forest Officer sanctioned Nazarana to Gopinder Singh on payment of Rs.552.50 as Nazarana. The Forest Department filed an appeal against the said order before the Deputy Commissioner, Simla which was accepted and the order of the Revenue As sistant Chopal sanctioning nautor lands in favour of Gopinder singh was set aside. Gopinder Sing challenged the order of Revenue Assistant Chopal by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not eligible for grant of nautor. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The second part of clause (a) of Rule 7 makes it clear that an income of less than Rs.2,000 per annum should be from all sources including lands. It is thus obvious that a person who has got less than 10 bighas of land but has an income of more than Rs. 2,000 per year from all sources shall be eligible for the grant of nauti cation. [799C D] 2. The second limb of clause (b) of Rule 3 makes it clear beyond doubt that an income from all sources other than those specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub rule (1) of Rule 4 shall be eligible to the grant of Nazarana in the following order of preference: (i) Such persons who have less than ten bighas of land, whether as owners or tenants or lessees either individually or collectively, or have an income of Rs.2 lacs per annum from all sources; (ii) an income of 10 bighas of lands, whether as owner or tenant or as lessees either individually, or have any income of more that Rs.2 lac per annum from any source including lands. [800D E]
5159: The State Government issued a policy decision on 30th December, 1984 for the grant of licences to distilleries and warehouses in the State of Madhya Pradesh. In pursuance of that decision, the State Government issued an order dated 30th December 1984 granting licence to respondent Nos.5 to 11 only for a limited period of 5 years commencing from 1st April 1986 or it was to be granted for a minimum period of five years with a clause for automatic renewal from year to year after the expiration of the period of 5 year so that all other persons would be totally excluded from entering the field and a monopoly would be created in favour of respondent Nos. 5 to 11 for all time to come so far as D 2 licence for manufacturing liquor in the distillery was concerned. On 31st March, 1985, the State government issued a notification under section 17(1) of the Act extending the period of licence for a further period of 5 months from 1st February 1985 to 31st March 1986. The writ petitions were filed by the respondents challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the policy decision dated 30thDecember 1984 was not applicable to the case of respondent Nos 5 to 11 because the earlier policy decision dated 31st March 1985 had been revived by the State Government and the new policy decision dated 3rd March 1986 was not applicable. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy decision dated 4th January, 1986 is not applicable to respondent Nos 5, 6 to 11 who are the holders of the land and plant and machinery in the distillery. [326C] 1.2 The policy decision of the State Government dated 30th Decem ber, 1984 cannot be said to have any application to the case on hand because the earlier decision dated 31.3.1985 was revived by a subsequent policy decision dated 2nd February, 1985 which was sought to be changed by the State Govern ment. [327D E] 1.3 The policy decision taken by the State government on 30th Decemb er 1984 is not applicable in the present case because the earlier order dated 31st Marc h, 1985 was revived and the new order dated 2nd Febru ary 1985 was passed
3068: The appellant was a workman of the respondent. He filed an application under section 78 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, before the Labour Court for relief under section 7 8 (1) D. The Labour Court dismissed the application on the ground that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(4). The High Court held that it was also not necessary for the employee first to approached the employer or seek his remedy under section 7. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The Labour Court had no jurisdiction to decide whether the order of dismissal was illegal or not. [739 E] (ii) The Labour Courts have power to give relief under section 78(1) D and the Labour Court has no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the order is legal or illegal. [740 F] (iii) The Labour Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the Labour Court. [741 B C] (iv) The Labour court can interfere only if the finding is perverse or based on no evidence. [742 A B] (v) The Labour courts are empowered to examine whether the order passed by the employer is legal or not. If they find that the order is either illegal or improper, then they will have to pass appropriate orders according to law. [743 B C]
2861: The appellants in these appeals are the representatives of the mortgagees of the suit properties. They claim to represent the interest of the mortgagors. The respondents in both the appeals claim that they were insane at the time they sold the suit properties to the appellants. The trial court dismissed both the suits except as regards the mortgage, but the High Court on appeal held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit is within time and that the courts below erred in holding that the suit should be dismissed. HELD: (1) The suit is not barred by limitation; it is a suit for redemption which has been filed after the period of limitation prescribed under section 4 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913. [108 E] (2) The mortgagee had no right to redeem the mortgage. He could only redeem the mortgage if he satisfied himself that he was insane at that time. The mortgagor did not have any right to redeem his mortgage. The mortgagee had not made out a case that he was an insane at a particular time. The mortgagee was not entitled to redeem the mortgaged property. [109 B C] (3) The mortgagee was a person who was not a stranger to the mortgage. The mortgage was executed on December 21, 1895. The mortgage deed was registered on December 21. 1895. It was not necessary to prove that the mortgage was executed before the date on which the mortgage deed was executed. [110 D E] (4) The mortgage was not created by the mortgagor in favour of any third party. The mortgage itself was not created in favour of the mortgagee. The mortgage did not create any interest in favour of third parties. The mortgage therefore did not come into existence. [111 F] (5) The mortgage being voidable, the mortgagor could not redeem the mortgage without proving that he was a stranger. [114 A B] (6) The mortgage having been created in favour one of the mortg agors, the mortgage was not binding upon the other mortgagors, namely, the mortgagor and the mortgagee. [115 B C]
1423: The appellant, a guarantor of a loan advanced by the respondent Bank to the respondent Bank, was a surety for the repayment of Rs. 20,000/ advanced to him by the respondent bank. The respondent Bank had agreed to allow an overdraft account to the appellant for Rs. 20.000/ and this amount was reduced from Rs. 20 to Rs. 20 per month. The appellant 's case was that he never stood surety for the respondent Bank and that he stood surety for Rs. 25,000/ and that the respondent Bank had altered his contract with Sankaran in order to carry out the common intention of Sankaran. The trial court held that the letter of guarantee was not a new document but only a modification of the original agreement. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the letter dated 5.5.1948 was a modification of an earlier letter of guarantee which was subsequently altered to Rs.20,000/ in the letter itself and therefore the alteration was not a change of the original contract. HELD : (i) The letter of guarantee is a fresh document and the alteration has been made in order to effect the common intention between the parties. [860 E] (ii) It is true that the letter was written by the appellant as a result of the agreement between the parties but the alteration was made in order that the appellant would give a letter of guarantee for the repayment. The alteration was made without the consent of the appellant. The alteration could be done only if the appellant gave a notice to the respondent bank that the letter should be modified or cancelled. 26: The respondents were the tenants of a building in their possession. They paid rent to the appellants for the period from April 1, 1957 to March 31, 1958 and thereafter paid rent to them. On July 9, 1959, the appellants filed an application under section 11 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1947 for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had committed default in payment of rent for one month and had been liable to be evicted. The appellants contended that the respondents had not committed any default in payment or non payment of rent within the meaning of sub section (1) of section 11 of that Act and that the respondents could not evict the appellants without resorting to the ordinary law in the matter of determination of tenancies. Held, that the respondents were entitled to protection against eviction under the Bihar Act. The Act does not confer a right upon the landlord to evict a tenant unless he has paid the arrears of rent due from him before the order of his eviction is passed. The Act confers a right upon a landlord to recover possession of a building from a tenant if he makes default in payment thereof. The Act also provides for the procedure to be followed by the Controller while passing orders of eviction. The Act gives power to the Controller to determine whether a particular premises is required bona fide by the landlord for occupation as a residence for his own occupation or whether it is necessary for him to put the landlord in possession of the premises. The Act further empowers the Controller to pass such orders as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the amount of rent payable by the tenant. The Act therefore confers a right on the landlord to apply for eviction of a tenant on the ground of non payment of arrears of rent, and the Controller is empowered to decide whether the tenant should be evicted.

4113: The appellant, a widow and her two sons, were tenants of certain lands in village Bhanguri. They died in the year 1954 leaving behind their mother, the respondent, and his mother. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "surplus Area" is defined in section 2(5a) of the Act to mean "the area which is separately utilised or utilised for the resettlement of tenants". It means that the area which is actually used as a unit for the resetment of tenants would be taken into account for the purpose of allotment to other tenants. 544: The appellant, a religious denomination of Hindus, was appointed as the trustee of a temple in Madras. The temple was a public temple and the appellant was entitled to manage its affairs in matters of religion guaranteed under article 26(b) of the Constitution. The appellant filed a suit for framing a scheme for this temple and prayed that the temple be declared as a private temple and the trustees be directed to administer it according to law. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the temple was not a private temple but a denominational one and that the provisions of section 3 of the Act were not applicable to it. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the temple being a denominational temple, the provisions of the Act would apply only to such a temple and not to any other institution which is not a denominational institution. The Act does not provide for the appointment of a manager or a manager; it merely provides for the appointment and removal of a manager; the Act does not contemplate the appointment of any manager or a person who has been appointed to manage the temple. The Act did not provide for any other mode of administration of the temple and it could not be said that the temple itself was a denominational Institution. The Act had no application to the temple and the question whether the temple was a denominatory institution or not was irrelevant to the question of the nature of the temple.

The appellant 's case is that the contract was not a sale but only a purchase of materials for the execution of works. Held, that the State legislature having authority to enact a law imposing a tax on the sale or purchase of goods, the transaction being wholly incompetent, the State Legislature could not impose any tax thereon. The State Legislature having authority to legislate on the subject, the State Government cannot make a law levying a tax on such transactions. The State Legislature may also levy a tax thereon on the supply or distribution of materials used in a works contract but the State Legislature cannot make a provision for taxation on the supply and distribution of materials in respect of which the State Legislature has no power to make a law.
