1385: The appellants were accused in a case under section 120B read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. They filed a complaint against the two appellants and others for offences under sections 467, 471 read with section 34 of the Indian Panel Code. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint on the ground that the prosecution had not been able to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court set aside the order of dismissal. In appeal by special leave it was contended before this Court that the Magistrate 's order dismissing the complaint was illegal as the sanction of the Government was obtained from the Chief Presidency Magistrate and the proceedings were vitiated because the sanction was obtained without authority from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. HELD : (i) The Magistrate 's power to dismiss the complaint is not affected by the fact that the sanction was granted by the Chief Presidency magistrate. [314 D] (ii) The Magistrate could not be said to have taken cognizance of the offence without the sanction of that court. The question whether the sanction was necessary or not depends upon the facts of each case. If the sanction is necessary then the sanction must be given by the Chief Metropolitan magistrate. [302 B C] (iii) The Magistrate has no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the case unless he gives his reasons for doing so. It is only when he gives his reason that the sanction is valid that the Magistrate can take cognizance of that case. [304 E] (iv) The Magistrate cannot act merely as a post office or mouthpiece of the prosecution but has to consider the entire evidence including the documents produced by the prosecution and defence and the result of that consideration. [305 A] (v) The Magistrate can take into account the conduct of the parties while considering the question of sanction. [306 F]
3425: The respondent was promoted to the post of Assistant Education Officer in the Punjab Education Service (Class I) on October 1, 1949. In June 1961 he received a copy of letter No. 5137 ED I 60/9269 dated May 2, 1961 addressed by the Secretary to Government, Punjab, Education Department to the Director of Public Instruction, Punjab, Chandigarh, conveying sanction of the Governor of Punjab to the grant of pension and death cum retirement gratuity to him under rules 5.27 and 6.13 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Vol. II read with para 9(1) (a) of the New Pension Rules, 1951. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the aforesaid decision of the Government to apply a cut of 10% in his pension and gratuity. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order imposing the cut in the pension and gratuity were invalid as it was not passed by way of punishment but only because of the fact that the respondent had been dismissed from service for misconduct. On appeal to this Court, HELD : The order imposing the penalty of reduction of 10% of pension and gratuity is an administrative order and the case does not fall within the purview of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. [523 B] The order imposing penalty of reduction in pension and gratuity are not in accordance with law as superannuation pension is a bounty and must be given to the employee concerned. [524 C D] The order of the Government imposing the penalty is an administrative act and the case did not fall within its purview. [525 F] The order is an administrative action and the case cannot fall within the scope of Article 311 (2). [525 G]

2933: The respondent was a watches carrying on the business of winning and winning of watches. The Collector of Customs issued notice to the respondent under section 124(a) of the Act for extension of time for giving notice under section 124 (a) of that Act. The Collector 's order was confirmed by the Collector. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the Collector had no power to extend the period for giving notice. HELD : The proviso to section I 10(2), therefore, cannot be construed as conferring a right upon the respondent to claim return of the goods seized under section 110 of the Act. [808 E]
975: The appellant, a non resident assessee, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 75. He filed returns under section 22(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, and claimed that he had not been served with notices under section 34 of the Act. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 34 read with r. 18 requiring him to file return within eight years from the end of the year of assessment. The appellant contended that the proceedings were commenced within the period of limitation prescribed for serving notice of assessment under section 34(1)(a). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the notice under section 22 was not necessary because the notice was served only in the case of a resident resident and that the notice could be served only if a person liable to pay tax was residing outside the taxable territory. 1488: The appellant was a registered trade union of jute mills and was carrying on business in Calcutta. In the course of its business, the appellant purchased raw jute from the respondents and sold it to the respondents. The respondents were all jute mill companies which purchase raw jute and manufacture finished goods therefrom. The appellant 's case was that the respondents had entered into contracts with the respondents for sale or purchase of raw jute and for supply of raw jute to the appellant. The respondents contended that the contract was not binding on them as they did not enter into any contract with the appellant. Held: (i) The contract was not voidable under section 10(2)(b) of the . It was not void because the respondents had no notice of the agreement. (ii)The contract was not enforceable because the respondents were not parties to the contract. (iii)The contract being one of sale and not of supply of raw materials, the respondents could not be said to have entered into an agreement with the appellant for the sale or purchase. (iv)The contract having been terminated by the respondents, the respondents were entitled to claim damages. (v)The contract is not voidable merely because the respondents did not enter upon the contract with the respondents. (vi)The contract between the parties was not void but only voidable. (vii)The contract in question was not void. (viii)The contract did not create any special right in favour of the respondents.

6596: The appellant, a tenant of a shop in the city of Jammu & Kashmir, was evicted from the premises under section 13(1)(c) of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966. The respondent landlord filed an application for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his own occupation. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to protection of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the clause did not take into account the nature of the building but only the income of the tenant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. 4229: The respondent was searched by the Customs authorities and a sum of Rs. 65,500/ was found from his person. The Income Tax Officer took proceedings under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 for assessing the assessee 's income and determining his tax liability. He came to the finding that out of Rs. 60,500/ incurred by the assessee in carrying on the business of smuggling gold he was entitled to a deduction under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act of the entire sum of Rs 65,500/-. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that out of the sum of Rs 60,500/- incurred by the respondent in carrying on his business, he was not liable to income tax. The Income tax authorities held that the assessee was engaged in the business of import of currency notes across the border and that he was therefore liable to income-tax on income from that business. The Income 'Tax authorities found that the assessee had been dealing in the business as a money lender and was also doing the business of export of currency notes. In second appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal the assessee represented that if he was regarded as engaged in the activity of smuggling theft, he was entitled, under section 10 (1), to a deduction of loss incurred in the business on the confiscation of the currency notes. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee being an individual was not carrying on any business or undertaking in India and therefore the provisions of section 10(2)(ii) were not applicable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "business" has been defined in section 2(6) of the Act to mean any trade, commerce or manufacture or any adventure in the nature of trade, commerce, or manufacture. [880C] 2. The expression 'business' is defined in section 3(5) to include any trade, business, profession or vocation
932: The appellant, a Muslim, was a resident of the villages in which an additional police force was stationed. He was exempted from liability to bear any portion of the cost of the additional force. The State Government issued a notification under section 15 of the , exempting Harijan & Muslim inhabitants of these villages from liability to pay the cost of additional force. Under sub section (1) of section 15 of . the exemption is granted only on the ground that persons belonging to such communities were found to be peace loving and law abiding citizens, in the villages additional force has been posted. The High Court held that the exemption was not based on caste or religion but on other criteria set out in article 15(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the exemption of the Harijan & Hindu inhabitants of the villages was not based solely on the ground of caste or religion and that the exemption should have been confined to those who belonged to the community or religion in whose favour the exemption had been given. HELD: The exemption was not founded on the basis of caste or race but on other factors. The exemption was intended to apply to all persons belonging to the same community or religion irrespective of their caste or religion. [880C] The exemption was granted on the ground only of religion, race or caste and not on other criteria. It was not necessary that the exemption must be based on caste alone. [881D E]

931: The respondent firm was carrying on business in hides and skins. The appellant firm, a licensed dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the assessment order on the ground that the order was illegal and not supported by the authority of law. The High Court held that the rule limiting the operation of r. 16(5) of the Madras General Sale Tax Rules, 1939, hereinafter called the Turnover and Assessment Rules, was ultra vires as it contravened section 5(vi) of the Act and section 6 A of the Act. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the rule was ultra vires. The contention that the rule is ultra vires must be rejected. The rule does not apply to sales which are made by a licensed dealer after the goods have been sold or purchased. It applies only where the goods are sold or purchased at the time when they are manufactured or are intended to be used for the manufacture of such goods. The rule cannot apply where the goods have already been subjected to tax before the sale takes place. The rule can apply where the sale has taken place in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The rule is applicable where the sale is effected by a licensed manufacturer after he has obtained a licence from the Government. The rule will apply where the purchase is made by a person who is not a licensed dealer but by a licensed vendor. The rule applies where the purchaser is a manufacturer and not a licensed manufacturer. The rule may apply where the purchaser has obtained a license from the Government and the Government has no power to make a special provision for the benefit of a licensed manufacturer or a licensed vendor in respect of his transactions in hides or skins.
1225: The respondents entered into contracts for the construction of a aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. After the work was completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and ultimately by an agreement dated February 6, 1948, they were referred to arbitration of one Col. S. K. Sinha who signed the award on behalf of the Government. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The arbitrators returned a copy of the award duly signed by the Executive Engineer and signed it as a certified copy of the same. The arbitrators then sent a copy of this award to the parties and after receiving the copies of the award, filed in court a petition under section 17 of the , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the award was not binding on him and that the arbitrator had no authority to execute it. Held, that the award passed by the arbitrator was a nullity and could not be executed. The award was not a decree within the meaning of article 136 of the Constitution. It was not a "decree" within the meaning Of article 136. The award did not fall within the purview of item 2 of Schedule I of the Act. The award being a decree, it was not executable against the Government.
1982: The appellant, a sugar factory, was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. The State Legislature passed the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply & Purchase) Act, 1961, which provided for the constitution of a Central Board and the power to levy and collect cess. Section 23 of the Act empowered the State Government to make rules providing for the method of collection of cess. Rule 60 of the Madhya Pradesh Sugar Factories Control Rules, 1959 made under the said Act required the Cane Development Council to prepare a statement showing the quantity of cane grown in each factory and the area in respect of which it is proposed to levy the cess. The appellant, however, contended that the State Legislature had no legislative competence to enact the Act because the Act did not authorise the State Government either to frame rules or to issue notifications under section 5 of the Act. Held, that the State legislature could validly impose the cess under section 3(1)(a) of the Act and the State Legislature could not be said to have been authorised by the State Legislature to do so. The State legislature could not be held to have been competent to enact the law. The State Government could not be deemed to have been authorized by the State Government under section 5 to frame rules under section 5.
4832: The Appellant, a school established in the State of Orissa, was selected as a book vendor for the year 1982. The Selection Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of Director of Public Instruction (Schools) Orissa, decided to select more books and accordingly constituted a committee under the Chair person 's Committee. The selection of the books was challenged by the Appellants on the ground that the State Government had no power to fix the price of the books which were purchased from the grant made by the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition filed by the Appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellants that the State had no power or authority to fix the prices of the books purchased by the Appellants from the grant received by them from the Central Government and that the State could not change the price fixed by the State Government without the approval of the Central Government; that the State was entitled to reject any book out of the cyclone and flood relief grant made by Central Government and since the State Government did not act fairly and properly in fixing the price, the State Government was bound to accept the value of the books sold by the Appellants; that the Government had no right to reject any books out of the cycle of cyclone, flood relief grant, etc., and that the Government was not entitled to reject the books out of cyclones and flood relief grants made by the State. HELD: 1. The State Government has the power to fix a price which is reasonable having regard to the circumstances of each case. [330G] 2. The State cannot be compelled to supply the books to the students who are charged with the duty of preparing them for the examination. It is for the State Government to decide whether the books should be accepted for the purpose of the examination. If the State Government decides to adopt the course of selecting the books for the purpose, the State cannot be said to have acted arbitrarily. [331C D] 3. The State can not be compelled to accept the books for consideration. The State may not accept the books but if the State decides to accept the same for consideration, the State must accept the books. [332E] 4. The State has no power to alter the price fixed under the Act
2885: The petitioners who were traders in foodgrains, edible oils and other articles of food, challenged the validity of section 7 read with section 19, section 2 (i) and section 1 0 read with section 13 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 37 of 1954 and rules framed thereunder. The petitioners contended that section 7 was ultra vires the Constitution as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. Held:(1) Section 7 is not violative of article 14 because it provides no limitation on the power of the State to make any law imposing reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19(1)(g). The object of the Act is to prevent adulteration of food. It does not impose a restriction on the exercise or the right of the State under article 19(6) to carry on trade or business. The Act imposes restrictions on the right of a trader to sell or store or distribute articles of food which are adulterated or misbranded. The Act does not impose any restrictions on the State in the interest of public health. The Act is not intended to control the sale or distribution of the essential commodity but only regulates the sale or storage for sale of the same. The Act has been enacted to regulate the manufacture, sale, distribution etc. of the essential commodities. The Act therefore cannot be said to offend article 14. The Act also does not provide for the imposition of any restrictions on a person carrying on his trade or business in any essential commodity. The Act, however, does not prohibit the selling or distributing of any article of food which is adulterated or is otherwise unfit for human consumption. The Act thus seeks to regulate the sale or purchase of any article which is adulterant. The Act further prohibits the sale or stock of any article containing such article which is misbrandable or unfit for human food. The Act makes no distinction between an article of food and an article of clothing. The Act provides no limitation upon the power of a State to make laws regulating the sale or quantity or quality of the article. The Act can be passed by legislation with respect to a matter which is declared by this Act to be a matter within the exclusive competence of the State Legislature. The Act cannot be struck down on the ground that it violates article 14 of Constitution. The
4973: The appellant and the respondents were the heirs of one Gopal Ji who died in 1944. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that they had validly executed the will exhibit A 6 dated 21 12 1957, and for possession of the properties described therein. The trial court held that the adoption was valid and decreed the suit. In appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that as the widow of Gopal Ji had not become the heir of her husband under the will she could appoint her successor to the estate of her husband. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the widow of the deceased Gopal Ji was not entitled to succeed to the limited right of the widow of her husband and that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. HELD: (1 ) The widow of Gopal ji was not competent to adopt a son or daughter after the death of her husband, but she could only be appointed as a legatee under the will. [388 F] (2) The widow of the testator was not entitled, as the widow had no right to make any disposition in respect of the property of her husband after his death. She could not therefore, appoint her successor. [389 G] (3) The widow had no absolute right to appoint her successor and the right to appoint a legateee under the will was not an absolute right. [390 D] (4) The widow was not entitled as a legacies under the will to the extent of the property bequeathed to her. [391 E] (5) The widow could appoint her own successor. [392 C] (6) The widow did not acquire any interest in the property of the deceased. She could only appoint her successor if she so desired. [393 B] (7) The widow would have no right to appoint another person as a legacy. [394 C] (8) The widow cannot appoint a lega leyer without the consent of the other heirs. [395 D]
1518: The appellants purchased the properties in dispute from respondent No. 1 under a sale certificate issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Nagpur on November 13, 1946. They filed a suit for recovery of arrears due to them against respondent No. I and his brother, who had purchased the properties at the auction sale. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the sale was invalid as it was not made in accordance with law. On appeal, the Additional judge held that the sale could not be held validly for the recovery of arrears because the amount shown in the proclamation of sale as the arrear due from the appellants was not due; that as the final bid was not accepted by the Dy. Commissioner, it was invalid; that as respondent No. 2 had purchased the property in dispute under section 128(f) of the Act, he was competent to confirm the sale on November 13 1945. The High Court allowed the appeal of respondent No. l and set aside the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 145 provides for application to set aside sale on deposit of arrear of rent due from the appellant. The provisions of section 146 are mandatory and they must be strictly complied with before an order is passed under section 145. 351: The petitioners were tenants of certain villages in the former State of Hyderabad. 6740: The appellants were charged with the offence of rape on a girl aged about 16 years. The prosecution case was that on 19th March, 1983 at about 7.p.m. while the victim girl was going to her house for study, the appellant Gagan informed her that the other appellant Prafulla and others had tied her tutor Rabi Babu in a nearby mango grove and her father was present there. Thereafter both the appellants after having undressed her committed sexual assault on her. After investigation the I.O. sent the victim girl as well as the appellants for medical examination and after completion of the investigation the IO submitted charge sheet against the appellants under section 376(2)(g) read with section 34 of the I.P.C. The Trial Court convicted the appellants under sections 363 and 376(2) (g) of the I P.C. and sentenced each of them to rigorous imprisonment for three years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the Trial Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the evidence of the girl or the woman who complained of rape is not reliable. [880B] 1.2 The evidence of the prosecutrix does not inspire confidence. It is highly improbable that if she did not meet the accused persons even after knowing their names, then they would have taken her away from the place where she was residing. If she did not know the name of the accused persons, she would have certainly made an attempt to commit rape on her. [881D E] 1.3 There is no reason why the evidence of a girl or a woman should be rejected merely because it is not corroborated either by her mother or any other witness. [882F] 1.4 In the instant cases, the evidence on record clearly shows that the girl was more than 16 years of age at the time of occurrence. [883A B] 1.5 The evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 3 that the victim girl told them about both the accused persons committing rape on her cannot be accepted. [884E] 1.6 The evidence of a minor girl cannot be discarded only on the ground that she has been subjected to rape
1611: The respondent was convicted under section 323 and section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code. He was released on bail by the High Court but he did not appear before the District Magistrate, Patna, when the petition for his release was taken up for preliminary hearing. His application to the High Court for a direction that he be allowed to present his case to the High court was rejected by the District Magistrate. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the order of release passed by the District magistrate was an order for his unconditional release and therefore he could not be rearrested. The order of release by the District Judge was an order made in exercise of his discretion and it was not open to the High Courts to interfere with such an order. The order was not one of "exercise of discretion" within the meaning of article 226 of the Constitution. The order merely stated that the District Magistrate had considered the matter and found that the respondent 's detention was necessary. The order did not amount to an order of release because the District Magistrate was satisfied that there was no sufficient cause for the detention.
6366: The respondent filed a criminal petition for quashing the First Information Report in the Court of Special Judge for ACB, Hyderabad. The High Court quashed the First Infor mation Report on the ground that there had been lull in the investigation for fairly long spell causing inordinate delay and that the prosecution had not filed its report contem plated under section 173 Cr. P.C. till he filed the petition for quashing. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1. The High court was right in quashing the First Informatio n Report on the basis of the observations made by the High Court. [880D] 1.2. The High Courts power to quash an F.I.R. or a complaint is inherently discretionary in nature and it is not possible to lay down any rigid rules as to what should be done with reference to the facts of each case. It would depend upon the fact situation obtaining in each case whether such power should be exercised having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case and no straitjacket formula can be evolved. The exercise of such power cannot be for doing justice at all stages. [883E F] 1.3. The High courts power to quash proceedings pending before subordinate courts on the ground of laches is an exception and does not confer unbridled powers on the subordinate courts. They are meant to see that the parties do not resort to dilatory tactics and seek their remedy promptly. [884F G] 1.4. The High Cour t has rightly observed that where the investigation of a criminal proceeding staggers on with tardy pace due to the indolence or ineffectiveness of the investigating agency causing unreasonable and substantial delay resulting in grave prejudice or disadvi sion to the accused, the Court as the protector of the right and personal liberty of the citizen will step in and resort to the drastic remedy of quashing further proceedings in such investigation. [885G H; 896A B] 1.5. The HighCourt was justified in quashing the first information report on the ground, inter alia, that there had occurred inordinate delay in the inves tigation. [886

The Judicial Commissioner held that no sanction had been given by the Chief Minister to prosecute him and the Special Judge took cognizance of the case. 2791: The appellants were charged with having committed the offence of theft under section 379 I.P.C. The prosecution case was that the appellants and some other persons had stolen the buffalo from a village in Bulandshahr district in Uttar Pradesh. The police party went to the house of Gopi and Munshi, but they did not find him there. The police officer who was present at the scene of occurrence took the appellants along with them to the police station and took them to the place where the dead body was lying. The police also took away the buffle and the lathis. The appellants were acquitted by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of the police officer was not reliable because he had no reason to believe that the police party had come to search for the bufflow and that the police had taken the appellants along along with them. HELD: (1) There is nothing in the language of section 165(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which renders the statement of the accused inadmissible. [880 A] (2) The police party had been mixed up with the appellants and others. The police had taken away the bufle and the ocular evidence was sufficient to prove the commission of the offence. [881 B] (3) The police had not taken the appellants ' party into custody. The fact that the appellants were arrested after the incident would be enough to establish their guilt. [882 C] (4) The police officers had not taken away the appellants ' property or the articles from them. They had not even seen the appellants ' car. [883 D E]
1559: The appellants were dealers in sugar. They sold sugar to the Government of India under a licence issued by the Government of Madras on February 18, 1946. The Government of India Act, 1935 was passed and the Provincial Legislature had power to legislate for levy of tax on sale of goods as understood in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Under the Government of Indian Act, 1935 the Provincial Legislature was competent to enact legislation for levying tax on the value of goods used in the execution of building contracts and the judgment of the Court proceeded on the ground that power conferred by Entry 48 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution was restricted to enacting legislation imposing tax liability in respect of sale of goods. The question whether the power conferred by the entry could be exercised for taxing only those transactions in which by mutual consent between parties competent to contract property in goods was transferred absolutely from one person to another, was referred to a Full Bench of the High Court. The Full Bench held that the power conferred on the Provincial Legislature under Entry 48 of the List II was limited to enacting legislation prescribing tax liability in case of sale of any goods as understood In the Sale of good Act, 1930, and that the Provincial Legislature could not impose tax liability in cases where there was no transfer of property in goods involved in the execution or works contract. The appeal to this Court was filed by the State of Bihar against the decision of the Full Bench of that High Court. 3193: The appellant was the returned candidate from the Haryana Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent on several grounds, namely, (1) that the appellant had failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of section 81(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951; (2) that the spare copies were not filed along with the petition in the High Court and (3) that the returned candidate had not complied with the provisions of section 81 (3). The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant 's failure to file the spare copies within the period of limitation prescribed under section 81(1) of the Act did not vitiate the election. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the defect in filing the spare copies could not be cured by the non compliance with the requirements of section 81 of the Act inasmuch as the requisite number of spare copies had been filed beyond the period of time. HELD: (i) Section 81(3)(a) is a procedural provision which provides for the filing of an election petition after the expiry of the period of fortyfive days from the date of publication of the result of the election. [275D] (ii) The requirement of section 80(3) is not merely procedural but is also substantive. It is only when the requirement of section 82(4) is mandatory that the requirement of the section can be waived. [276E] (iii) The requirement regarding the filing of the spare copies is directory and not mandatory. [277B]
3421: The respondent company was a private limited company. The workmen were laid off in accordance with law with effect from 5th February, 1968. The lay off of the workmen whose names were mentioned in the notice was recalled by the management on the 22nd April, 1968. On the 17th April, 1968, the workmen were not given their wages or compensation for the period of lay off. An industrial dispute raised and referred to the Labour Court. The Labour Court held that the workmen were entitled to lay off compensation. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The lay off is an event which takes place during normal working hours on any day. The layoff is a pre requisite condition for the purpose of section 25F of the Act. [801 B] (2) The lay-off is a temporary suspension pending adjudication of the dispute. It is a permanent suspension pending adjudication. The workman is entitled to his full wages and dearness allowance for the period he has been kept out of employment. [802 C D] (3) The layoff does not amount to a closure within the meaning of section 2(kkk). The lay off may be a temporary suspension but it does not amount as a closure. [803 E F] (4) The lay Off is a temporary stoppage and the employer cannot be asked to pay the same unless the lay off is permanent. [804 A] (5) The layover is a temporary one and the employer can be asked to give the lay off without paying the lay off. [805 G]
2297: The appellant was appointed a Judge of the High Court of Assam. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of stay granted by the learned Chief Justice on November 3, 1966 and also prayed for an interim injunction restraining the respondent from acting as a Judge of that court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Chief Justice had no jurisdiction to pass any order as a Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Chief justice could not act as a Judge in the High Courts because he did not have the jurisdiction to entertain the petition and to pass the stay order. HELD: (i) The Chief Justice has power to appoint a Judge of his choice. [617 D] (ii) The Chief justice is a judge of the High court and the Chief Justice is a Judge of a High Court. It is therefore, clear that the Chief Jus tion can be said to be a Judge of High Court while he is working as a Commission of Enquiry. [618 B C] (iii) The Chief Justi cation is a judicial officer and the Chief J ustice must be a person who is not a Judge of any High Court. [619 E]

The power to take away the telephone connection from the subscriber is not an inherent power. It is an extraordinary power vested in the General Manager. 6645: The Government granted land to the Ziarat in lieu of his possessory right over about 400 kanals of land. The Ziarat was subsequently transferred by the Government in favour of the father of the defendants. The Zimdar, who had been allotted the land in dispute, filed a suit against the Zirat and the Government for recovery of possession of the land on the ground that the land was transferred by the Ziardar in favour of their father in his personal capacity. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the decree. In second appeal the High court held that the Ziawar was not entitled to claim the land as a matter of right under the grant made in favour of his father in his individual capacity. The High Court also held that the Government had no intention to dedicate the land to the ziarat. The Government took the view that the Zir was not entitled under the grant to the land in question as it was a property of the Ziarta of the Zamindar. 2618: The first respondent joined the State Service in 1937. He was absorbed as a Sales Tax Officer, Class III in the former State of Bombay after merger. In December 1962 he was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of attempt to obtain illegal gratification from certain cloth dealers. A departmental enquiry was held and on March 15, 1963, the Enquiry Officer submitted his report holding that the charges were proved against him. On March 15, 1964, the first respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of removal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the failure to send a copy of the recommendations of the Enquiry Officer containing his findings on the various charges was not a failure to comply with the requirements of article 311(2) of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The requirement of article 311 (2) is not mandatory but directory. [254 E] (a) The enquiry must be fair to the delinquent officer. It cannot be merely a formality. The enquiry must go through all the stages of the inquiry. The non-observance of the principles of natural justice would amount to denial of reasonable opportunity to defend himself. [255 F] (b) The non-supply of the report of the Enquiry officer vitiates the proceedings. [256 G H] (c) The non supply of the report may also result in violation of the principles 'of natural justice. But if the non-supply has prejudiced the delinquent officer or has caused serious prejudice to the charges, interference with the punishment cannot be justified. [257 C D] (d) The non communication of the findings of the Enquiry authority does not necessarily lead to the inference that the said authority has been prejudiced thereby. [258 B] (e) The non furnishing of the report amounts to denial of a reasonable opportunity to the employee to show cause against the action proposed to be taken against him. [259 C] (f) The non consideration of the report before taking action entails civil consequences. [260 D] (g) The non compliance with the rules of natural justice is a defect which the court can remove without the necessity of any further notice. [
2435: The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Gambling Act, 1887. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to make a representation against his detention and that there was no provision in the Act for the communication of the grounds of detention to him. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the delay in sending the report could not have been avoided by the Commissioner and that when they were sent by him, they were working at high pressure in maintaining law and order; (ii) the detaining authority was hard put to for time and the surrounding circumstances explain the very short delay; (iii) the delay was due to causes beyond the control of the State Government; (iv) the delay should be explained satisfactorily; and (v) the delay caused was unreasonable. HELD: (i) There is no provision in section 3(3) of the Act that such an approval must be communicated to the detenu. The reasons of rule 30A(8) are that the District Magistrate was hard put in for time and was writing clearly and unambiguously to indicate the decision. The reasons given by the District Magistrate were sufficient to justify the detention. [901 E] (ii) The detaining authority was not hard put to the for time and he was hard put. The reasons were sufficient to enable the detaining authority to form a subjective satisfaction. [902 F] (iii) The detaining authorities were not in any way prejudiced because the District Magistrate had written the grounds of the detention without giving any opportunity to the detenu to meet them. [903 C D]
1748: The petitioners, who were members of a joint Hindu family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law, filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Tripura against the Ruler of the former Indian State for maintenance allowance. The petitioners contended that they and respondent No. 2, their representatives were not entitled to any share in the income of the Ruling Family and that the provisions of section 87B(1) were ultra vires. The petition was dismissed by the District Judge. On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions contained in section 87B (1) were intra vires and that the condition precedent prescribed by it was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The provisions of section 86(4) are applicable only to the Rulers of an Indian State and not to the Ruler of an Indian state. Section 87B(2), which is a part of the Constitution, provides that the provisions relating to the maintenance allowance of the members of the Ruledi or the Ruler of a foreign State shall be applied to the maintenance of the persons belonging to the Ruling Community. [847 C] The provisions of sections 85 and 86 are not inconsistent with article 14 of the Constitution. They are intended to apply to the rulers of Indian States as well as to the Ruler of a foreign state. The provisions of the Act are not inconsistent therewith. [848 E]
3489: The respondent, a displaced person from West Pakistan, applied to the Estate Officer for fixation of standard rent which was dismissed by him. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order against him but the High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Estate Officer to take steps to recover the arrears of rent. The appellant took no steps to recover any amount under section 7 of the , but the Estate Officer made an order on September 28, 1960 under section 7(1) of the . The respondent 's appeal to the Additional District Judge from the Estate Officer 's order was disallowed. The respondent appealed to the Punjab High Court which held that the amount in question could not be recovered under section 7 because the time limit for taking steps under that section had expired. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since section 7 did not put a time limit for recovery of arrears of rent payable in respect of any public premises, the Estate Officer could not have taken steps to recover arrears of rent under section 7. HELD: (i) Section 7 does not bar the remedy of recovery of arrears due to the Government or the Estate Officer. [880 E] (ii) The word "payable" is quite comprehensive enough to include all payments which are made after the date of the order of eviction. It is not necessary to refer to the various proceedings arising out of these applications for fixation of standards rent which were ultimately dismissed by the High Court. [881 C D] (iii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the amount was recoverable under section 7 as arrears of rent from the respondent. The High Court should have been careful in its approach to the question whether the respondent was entitled to recover the amount in dispute from the appellant. [882 F G]

On appeal by the respondent, a single judge of the High Court set aside the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, the High Court held that the sale was not vitiated by fraud or undue influence but only because the respondent had made a bid at the auction and had paid the entire price. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The respondent has no right to be appointed as a trustee of the jewels. [817E] 2. The respondent being a minor could not have been appointed as a guardian of the jewelleries. [823G] 8. The respondent having failed to establish his right to the jealousy of the trust, he cannot now be heard to say that the trust was not binding upon him. [824H; 825A] 9. 5027: The appellant was granted a quarry lease for the period ending with 31st March, 1984. The lease deed provided that the lessee shall be entitled to extract stones from the leased area at the rate of Rs. 1,52,000 p.a. and the lessee shall pay royalty on the said quantity of stones at the rate specified in the lease deed. The appellant challenged the action of the Chief Minister in Writ Petition No. 2321/81 in the Punjab and Haryana High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed auction and therefore the decision of the Government was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in quashing the order of the Chief Secretary as it did not give any reasons for its conclusion. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts power to interfere with the grant or refusal of a lease is circumscribed by the terms of the lease itself and cannot be exercised arbitrarily. [547E] 2.1 The High Court has rightly held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the concession made by the State Government in its letter dated December 26, 1981. [548A] 3.1 The appellant had no right to claim the benefit of concession made by it in its letter of December 26,1981. The appellant could have only claimed the benefit of concessions made by it before the High Court but not before the High court. [549B] 4.1 The State Government had no right whatsoever to grant the concession in question. [550C] 5.2 The appellant had not even sought to challenge the action of Chief Minister in the writ petition filed by the State of Haryana. The High court was wrong in quashing the action of Government. [546D]
1145: The appellant Mill owners ' Association, Bombay, in respect of disputes relating to bonus for the years 1952 and 1953 filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the award made by the Industrial Court on March 13, 1956. The appellant contended that the award was not enforceable as an award by the Industrial court against the appellant. Held, that the award could be enforced only if it was made binding upon the appellant. The award was not binding on the appellant because it was made after the Government had issued a notification dated July 31, 1956, directing that the award made on March 13 1956 should be enforced against the appellant in exercise of the powers vested in the Government by section 114(2) of the Act. The notification did not make any reference to the Industrial Court for its opinion. The notification merely directed that the award be enforced against a representative Union in the same way as the award made in the present case. The notification was not intended to bind the appellant.
5346: The appellant landlord filed a petition under Section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that the respondent was in occupation of a part of a residential building. The Rent Controller allowed the petition holding that the respondent had not been able to prove bona fide requirement of additional accommodation for his personal use and that he was entitled to recover possession of the premises from the respondent. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Authority reversed the findings of the Rent Controller and held that the respondent could seek eviction only if he requires the ground floor for non residential purposes and not for residential purposes. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in interfering with the finding of fact rendered by the Appellate Authority as well as the Rent Controller. 1091: The respondent company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1954 55. The Income tax Officer, by an order dated January 25, 1954 rectified this error and imposed a penalty of Rs. 5,000 on the respondent company. The respondent company filed a revision petition before the Commissioner of Income tax but the same was dismissed. Thereafter the respondent company filed another petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Kerala challenging the validity of the order of rectification. The High Court held that the orders made were without jurisdiction and therefore quashed the orders. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no power to review its own order under section 35 of the Act and that the High court could not interfere with the orders passed by the Income tax Officer. HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that the necessary foundation for the exercise of the powers under section 35 had not been laid. [851 C] (ii) The High court was right in holding that there was no mistake apparent on the face of the record. The High court has rightly held that the necessary basis for the exercise or the inherent power of the High Court is not available to the Income tax Officers because the Income tax officer had no power under the Act to make the order which he did. [852 D E] (iii) The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the provisions of section 35 are applicable only where the mistake apparent on face of the order is patent on the face thereof. It is not open to the High Court to rewrite or modify the order merely because the High Court thought that the error was apparent on the fact of the record of the case. [853 F G]
6912: The respondent landlord filed a suit for possession of the suit premises on the ground that the tenant had not paid rent from 1.1.1980 to 31.3.1981 and thereafter made regular payment of Rs. 600 every month. The trial court held that the service of notice dated 7.8.1980 was not proved. The appellate court reversed the finding of the trial court and held that the evidence of the plaintiff showed that the copy of the notice was sent to all the defendants by registered post. The High Court in revision, set aside the order of the lower courts and confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the service was effected on the defendant company and that the presumption of service of notice under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act was drawn. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts decision is based on the view taken by this Court in Kulkarni vs M/s Kulkarnii & Ors., [1984] 3 SCR 623. [739E F] 2. The High court has rightly relied upon the judgment of this Court in D.V.S.Narayana Rao vs B.P. Suryanarayan & Anr., [1976] Supp. SCC 763. [740F G] 3. The High courts decision is based only on the view of this Court that the presumption raised under Section 114 of the Evidence Act is rebuttable. [741G] 4. The High Cour t committed an error in drawing presumption of service from the fact that the defendant company had received the amount as rent from the tenant. [742A] 5. The High 'Court was wrong in holding that there was no rebuttal on behalf of defendant as regards the notice served on the company and in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [743B] 6. The HighCourt was right in setting aside the findings of the trial Court and the first appellate court. [744C]
7118: The appellant, a Lecturer in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in the Medical College at Jabalpur applied for admission to the MBBS Course in the respondent University. He was selected by the Selection Committee on the basis of his performance in the examination. On the recommendation of the Selection Committee, he was granted admission. His application for transfer was rejected by the Government. The appellant challenged the rejection before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant is entitled to be considered for admission to MBBS Degree Course. [790C] 1.2 The appellant has not produced any document showing that he had passed G.C.E. Biology, Physics and Chemistry and 'O' level in six subjects i.e. It was also stated that he had studied the subjects in Anatomy, Physiology, Biochemistry, Preventive and Social Medicine including, Behavioural Science and Biostatistics, Medical Psychology and Developmental Studies and Medical Surgery. He did not produce any document showing the fact that he had obtained admission in the second year. Therefore, according to him, he possesses the eligibility criteria for admission to a medical course. [791D E] 1.3 The appellant cannot claim that he should have been admitted to the MBBS course in the first year itself. He must satisfy the conditions laid down in the prospectus. The appellant has failed to do so. [792F] 1.4 The appellant is not entitled to get any relief from the High Court as he does not possess the eligibility criteria prescribed under the prospectus. 6184: The appellants were tenants of certain intermediary landlords known as Girasdars. They filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that they had been in continuous possession of the lands since before the coming into force of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951 and that they were entitled to allotment of land under section 4(1) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the Girasdar was not a joint tenant but was a cultivating tenant. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The Girasdari tenancy is governed by the provisions of the Saurashtra Tenancy Act, 1951. Section 4(1)(a) provides that all lands of whatever description held by a Girasdar shall be allotted to him; and the total area of the holding of a Girasdidar shall be available for allotment. [839 E] (ii) The Girasadars are entitled to separate allotments in respect of the land held by them jointly and the separate allotments in their favour shall be made separately. [840 F] (iii) The Girasidars are also entitled to separate allotment in respect of land held by the Girasdar. [841 A] (iv) The Girasiadars are not entitled to separate plots in respect of their holdings. [842 B]
1946: The plaintiff, the first defendant and the second defendant are brothers. The first defendant was the mother of the plaintiff and the first defendant. The first plaintiff died during the pendency of the appeal before this Court and his legal representatives were the other defendants to the suit. The first respondent filed a suit for partition and separate possession of her half share in the properties described in the schedule to the plaint and for mesne profits. According to her, the property was the absolute property of her mother Puttananjamma and upon her death, she was entitled to the benefit of Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal preferred by the first defendant as well as the cross objection lodged by the plaintiff. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in awarding future mesne profit to the first defendant, who had not claimed any right in the suit property. The first appeal is directed against the decree of the High court. The first question is whether the High Court was right in awarding future interest on the amount of compensation awarded by the trial court. [767D E] 1.3. The first contention raised by the appellant is that the High court should have granted interest on the compensation amount. The first point urged by the appellant was that the High 'Court ought to have granted interest only on the amount which was found due to the first respondent. [768E F] 1.4.
