1277: The respondent K. Rangachari was a member of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Madras Division of Southern Railway, and was appointed as a Clerk in the scale of Rs. 260-400 on October 1, 1956. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Station Master in the scale Rs. 210-325 on December 31, 1957. On September 2, 1958, he applied for and obtained a certificate from the said High Court under article 132(1) of the Constitution as it involved a substantial question of law as to the scope of article 16(4). The respondent challenged the validity of the circular by a writ petition before the Madras High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Circular dated September 2, 1959 is not an order made under article 166 of the Constitution but only an executive instruction issued under article 162 of the Constitution. [617 B] (ii)The Circular dated September 3, 1959 cannot be construed as an administrative order or executive instructions. It must be read with the provisions of article 335 and the Rules framed thereunder. The Circular does not purport to make any provision for reservation in favour of members of the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribes. [618 C D] (iii)The Circular cannot be interpreted in a manner that would lead to absurdity. The Circular has been issued under article 166(2) of the constitution. The Circular cannot be construed in a manner which would lead to anomaly. [619 E F] (iv)The Circular is not an executive instruction nor can it be described as a statutory rule. It is merely an administrative order. [620 G H]
2660: The appellant firm was assessed to income tax for the year 1946 47, in respect of an amount of Rs. 3,99,587 received by it as profit on sale of shares. The firm paid Rs. 7,05,957 out of the total consideration of Rs. 6,00,000 and the balance of Rs. 1,07,548 was sold at a profit in the same year. The firm claimed that it had taken over the entire share capital issued by Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd., which was a subsidiary company of the appellant firm. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the transaction was one to facilitate acquisition of a capital asset being a capital investment and that the profit realised by sale of the shares was not liable to be assessed to income-tax. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The fact that the assessee had borrowed loans at interest to purchase the shares did not make the transaction a business activity. The fact that there was a loan of Rs. 70 lakhs advanced by the firm to the assessee firm was of no consequence. The fact, however, that the firm had purchased the shares at a profit did not make any difference because the firm had been able to sell the shares at the price fixed by the firm. [866 D E] (2) The fact, that the assessee firm had borrowed loans from the bank at interest to buy the shares was of no effect. The fact of borrowing loans at interest was of no significance. The fact was that the bank had borrowed money at interest to acquire the shares at profit in the bank. The fact could only have been relevant if the bank had made a regular payment to the assessee. [867 F G] (3) The fact of the assessee having borrowed loans at a higher rate than the rate fixed by the bank would not make the transactions a business activity or a commercial venture. [868 B C] (4) The fact was also relevant if the assessee had advanced loans at interest at a lower rate than the normal rate. [869 A]
1910: The appellant was a tenant of a land in the State of Assam. He had been granted a licence to run a market for a period of three years and he paid Rs. 600/ as licence fee for holding the market. In 1953, the local board issued a notice to the appellant to take out a licence and pay Rs. 600 as licence fee. The appellant filed a writ petition challenging the constitutionality of the impost on a number of grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the impost is unconstitutional because it infringes article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the impeached tax cannot reasonably be held to be a tax on land. The impost is not discriminatory but is imposed by the local board under section 62 of the Act. The impaction must be within the scope of the power conferred upon the local board. The impamed tax can lawfully be imposed by the board if it has been determined that a market exists.
1487: The respondent company was a dealer in sugar and the appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent company for the sale of sugarcane to the appellant company. The appellant company agreed to sell sugarcane to the respondent company at current market rates and to have the advances adjusted towards the price of sugarcane, agreeing to pay interest in the meantime. The respondent company paid the amount due under the agreement but the appellant company did not pay the amount. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant company for recovery of the amount. On the question whether the sum of Rs. 2,87,422/was deductible as a revenue expenditure, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the sum of money was deductible from the profits of the business. The word "incurred" is used in section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and it is used in the sense of trading in commodities. It is not necessary that the profit must be derived or earned by the assessee. [981 D E] (2)The expression "in the nature of trade" in section 10 (2) (xv) means something which is done with the object of earning profit. In the present case, the respondent company had no intention to carry on any business other than the business of supplying sugarcane to its customers. The respondent Company had no intention of carrying on any business in the manufacture of sugar. The respondent was not carrying on any trade or business. The respondent had no intention whatsoever to carry on the business of selling sugarcane to its own customers. The transaction between the parties was one of purchase of sugarcane and not of sale of sugarcane. [982 C D] (3)In the present case the respondent company was carrying on the business in the shape of a business of supplying cane to its customers and was not carrying out any business in respect of sugarcane supplied by the appellant company to its customers, and therefore, the amount of Rs. 1,87, 422/were deductible under section 10(3) (xi) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. [983 B C] (4)The High Court was wrong in holding that there was a capital receipt in the hands of the respondent company. The
5432: The respondent filed an application before the Competent Authority under section 19 of the Slum Act for permission to execute the order of eviction. The appellant resisted the execution application on the ground that the application was barred by limitation and it was not maintainable because in the meantime the came into operation. On the 19th April, 1978, the respondent filed a second application before the competent authority for execution of the decree. In June, 1979 the respondent filed an applica tion before the Competent Authorities under section 19 for permission to executing the order of ejectment. In July, 1979 the application was dismissed by the Competent Authority. Thereafter on or about 25th September, 1979 the appellant filed an application for execution of decree. The Rent Controller held that the execution application was time barred and it was further held that supplementary objections were not maintainable. The Appellate Authority confirmed the said order. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Appellate Authority. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Appellate Authority is final and binding on the parties. [818C] 2. The question whether the decree for eviction of the tenant under the Rent Act passed against the appellant was executable by the respondent or whether the same had become barred by limitation or by principles of res judicata does not arise. [819D] 3. The question that falls for consideration is whether the decree passed by the Rent Controller was executable or not. [820E] 4. The question as to whether the decree holder could file execution application after the expiry of the period of limitation, cannot be decided in these proceedings. [821F G] 5. The question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact and the court has to decide it in the first instance. [822G] 6. The question regarding applicability of the provisions of section 19 of Limitation Act, 1963 is a mixed issue of law and facts which can be decided only in the first place. [823A] 7. The question about the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to entertain the suit for eviction of a tenant under the Act is a mixed one. It is open to the landlord to move the competent authority under section 19(2) of the Act
710: The Uttar Pradesh Transport Service (Development) Act, 1955, was passed by the U. P. Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 246(1) of the Constitution and section 6 of the General Clauses Act saved the provisions of the Act from the operation of the Act. The U. P Act was enacted to provide for the regulation of certain matters relating to motor transport and for the control of the production, supply and distribution of motor transport and the maintenance of a register kept under the Act. Section 3 of the Act provided that the State Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act and it was provided that the rules so made shall be published in the Gazette. The U P Act was repealed by the U P Act. The appellants challenged the validity of the U.P. Act on the ground that the U.p. Act did not infringe the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the U P. Act did neither offend the provisions of article 31 of Constitution nor did it violate the fundamental rights conferred by article 14 of the Constitution; that the U, P. Act was a law which fell within the terms of article 13(2); that the U., P. Act had been validly enacted and that the provisions of section 6 of U. P.. Act were valid as they stood at the relevant time. The U, P Act was a piece of legislation with respect to the regulation of motor transport industry and the enforcement thereof. The U., P Act was not a law dealing with the right to carry on trade or business but was a law dealing directly with the right of the citizens to carry on their business. The U,. P. Act being a law dealing exclusively with the right and privileges of the citizens, it could not be said that the U . P. Act would prevail over the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Act, and therefore the U. p. Act was not invalid.
2966: The appellant was a manufacturer of cloth. It manufactured cloth by means of powerlooms. The cloth manufactured by it was not used in any building or a factory. The cloth produced by the appellant was not used for the purpose of storing or selling cloth. The cloth was manufactured on the basis of powerloom cloth and the cloth manufactured by the appellant were used for the manufacture of ice for sale. The cloth sold by the appellant to the respondent was not used as a leather cloth but was used for the purposes of storage. The cloth which was manufactured by the respondent was used for manufacturing ice for the purpose. The cloth supplied by the respondent to the appellant was used for storing ice for its own use. The cloth, therefore, was not used by the respondent for the purpose for which it was purchased. The respondent contended that the cloth manufactured and delivered by the appellant did not fall within the term "mill" as defined in the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, and that the appellant had no control over the cloth manufactured. Held: (i) The word "mills" has been used in the notification in question and the High Court rightly held that the cloth produced by it was "mill". [739 E] (ii)The word "mill", in the context in which it is used, must be given its ordinary meaning. In common parlance it would mean a building or a flattening mill where the cloth is manufactured. The cloth is not a mere paper of the type known as "millood" but is a piece of cloth. The word "ma chin" is not defined in the Act. The word 'mill ' in the notification must be construed according to its grammatical sense. The word is used in a wider sense than the word 'means of workings'. The word 'black ' is used in the popular and accepted sense of the word. The word used in the Notification must be understood in its popular sense. The meaning of the word "milk" is not restricted to the word "fabrics" but extends to all other forms of workings. [740 F H; 741 A B] (iii)The word 'polythel' in the
2721: The appellant, a company incorporated under the . was appointed as managing director of a company called the Rampur Company. On March 19, 1953, the company reappointed Govan Brothers, Managing Agent for ten years with effect from August 15, 1960, and applied to the Central Government that the extension be approved. The company applied to the Company Law Board on April 18, 1953, for an order directing the company to continue its managing agency till March 31, 1970. The company refused to grant extension until March 31,1970. The company moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the decision of the Board and for an order quashing the decision of Board. The High Court held that the company had no power to appoint or reappoint a person as managing agent of a company which was not a company in existence at the time when the company was reappointed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The company 's acts and conduct were not illegal but were actuated by malice. [801 B] (2) The company was not a mere director but was merely a managing agent of the company. The company was a company which had been formed by the managing agents of the company and the managing agents were appointed by the company. There is nothing in section 326 of the , which prohibits the appointment of a managing agent. [802 C D] (3) The company had no right to appoint or remove a managing agent if he was a director of the company, and the company could not have been made a party to the proceedings before the Board. [803 E F] (4) The company did not make any provision for the appointment of the managing agent. The company had not been able to establish that the managing agent was a director. [804 A] (5) The company has no right to be appointed or reappointed as a managing agent unless it is satisfied that it is necessary to do so in public interest. [805 G] (6) The company cannot be said to be a mere director of the managing agents. It is not possible to hold that the managing agents are not liable to be removed from the managing agency. [806 H]
6204: The respondents were recruited to the Indian Forest Service and the Indian Police Service in the year 1960. They were appointed to the Indian Police Services on probation for two years, which period was extended by the Government of India from time to time. In the year 1961, the respondents joined the Indian Forest service as direct recruits. On completion of their probation they were confirmed in the Indian Forest Services. The respondents challenged the validity of the rules before the High Court contending that the rules were ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India and had directed the Government of Indi a to assign fresh years of allotment to the ECOs and SSCOs who were some of the respondents before the Tribunal. The High Court allowed the writ petition and set aside the impugned rules. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The rule of seniority is not an inherent part of the service conditions of the members of the service but it is essentially a matter relating to seniority. It is well settled that seniority cannot be determined by reference to the date of confirmation or length of service. [841C] 2.1 The Rules of 1968 are framed under All India Services Act, 1954 and the Rules of 1954 are made under the Act. The Rules of 1969 are framed under the Act and the Rules are made under Section 3(2)(d) of the Act. Therefore, the Rules of 1968 have been framed under the provisions of All India Services (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954. [842E F] 2.2 The Rules of 1966 do not provide for any retrospective effect to the rules. The Rules do not provide that the seniority should be fixed with reference to the dates of appointment. The Rules are only procedural in nature. The Rules have been framed after the selection process has started. The Rules cannot be said to be retrospective in character. [843F G] 3.1 The rules of 1968 are not applicable to the Indian Administrative Service. [844A] 4.1 The respondents were appointed to Indian Forest Service in the years 1960 and 1962 respectively. They were promoted to the IPS in the year 1963 and 1964 respectively. Their seniority was fixed at the stage of their first or second chance in the year 1970
2971: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1943 under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. In its accounting years, it had a managing agency of Elphinstone Mills Ltd., and its managing agency was to be terminated on the ground that it was unable to pay its debts. The Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs. 11,88,000/ on the ground, that it relates to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company in Elphin mould Mill Ltd. In appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal held that the loss incurred by the company was not attributable to any commercial profits but was attributable to the business of the company. On further appeal, the High Court held that the amount of Rs 11,88.000/ which was claimed as compensation for loss of capital should have been allowed as a deduction in computing the income of the company under section 23A(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. Held: (i) The amount of Rs 1,00,000/ received by the assessee as compensation for the acquisition of the managing agency cannot be said to be a trading receipt; (ii) the amount of compensation is not deductible from the profits and gains of the company and is not liable to be taxed in the hands of the assessee. (iii)The amount of compensation must be regarded as a trading receipt and must be taken into account in computing the total income of the assessee; and (iv)the amount of compensation can only be ascertained after making such adjustment as may be necessary to arrive at the true market value of the assets of the company on the date of the sale of the shares.
2140: The respondent, a registered dealer in cotton and cotton seeds manufactured by the appellant, purchased cotton from unregistered dealers and paid purchase tax under section 10(a) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1953. The cotton was ginned and pressed by the respondent during the assessment period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1956. During the course of assessment proceedings the respondent applied for refund of the purchase tax paid on the unginned cotton under section 10 (a) of Bombay Sales Tax, Act, 1953, but the Sales Tax Officer refused to allow any refund on the ground that the conditions of r. 12(1) read with r. 6 (ii) of the Rules had not been fulfilled. The respondent filed a revision before the Gujarat Sales Tax Tribunal which held that the condition of r.12(i) read with rule 6(ii) of Bombay sales Tax Rules, 1954, was satisfied because the goods were sold to the respondent in the course of inter State trade or commerce and that the respondent was entitled to the refund. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the condition for refund was not satisfied because the respondent did not have the use of the goods for the purpose for which they were purchased; that the condition was not fulfilled because the respondent had no use of the raw material for producing the cotton seeds; and that the High Court erred in answering the second question in favour of the respondent. HELD : (i) The condition of rr. 12(i) and (ii) read with Rule 6(ii), read with rr. 6(iii) and 6(iv) of Bombay sale Tax Rules, is not satisfied because r. 12 (i) read along with r.6(ii) deals with the use of raw materials for the manufacture of the goods. [310 D] (ii)The condition of r, 12(i), read with rule 8(2)(b) of Bombay Sale Tax Rules, 1959, is not fulfilled because r.12 (i) deals with raw materials for manufacture of the specified goods. [304 E] (iii)The condition for refund is not satisfied since the goods are used for the purpose of producing the cotton seed. [305 A] (iv
1892: The respondent was a licensee under the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951. The appellant Corporation fixed the scale of fees on the basis of annual valuation of cinema houses made by a method which does not appear on the record. The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the resolution. His contentions were : (1) that the levy was not a fee but a tax; and (2) that the imposition was not a tax but a fee. Held, that the contention must be negatived. The word "fee" in section 548(2) of the Act is used in a comprehensive sense to include all payments which are specifically exempted from payment of any tax. The word 'tax' has been defined in the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, as meaning a tax levied or charged under the provisions of the Act. The word tax means a tax on goods imported into India. It includes a tax on sale or purchase of goods. The word fee is a kind of tax which is generally described as a charge for a special service rendered to individuals by some governmental agency. The word `fee ' is not defined in the Act. In the absence of any definition of the word `fee', it would be possible to take the view that the word `cessation is a tax. But the question is whether the levy is a tax or a fee. The word is used in the widest sense. The word has been used in the context of a tax. The expression 'fees for technical services ' is not used in the Act, but in the context in which it appears in the Act itself. The word fees is used in its popular sense as including fees for technical services. The word licence is used in common parlance with a licence for a limited period. The word license is used in relation to a tax. A fee is a compulsory exaction of money by public authority for public purposes enforceable by law and is not payment for services rendered. A fee may be levied for services rendered and the fee levied is a revenue receipt. The word lease is used in contradistinction to a licence. The word royalty is used in connection with the payment of a royalty. The word rent is used in respect of a tax payable by the owner of a building
4851: The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling paper. The respondent company paid a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 to the appellant for the supply of paper. The appellant claimed that it had paid the said amount as incentive bonus. The appellant contended that the said amount was not an "wages" within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Employees State Insurance Act, 1948. The High Court held that the said payment was not wages but was wages. In appeal by special leave, HELD: The definition of 'wages ' in section 2(i)(d) of that Act is wide enough to include all payments made to an employee during the period of employment. [718 E] The definition of "wages " in section 2 (1) (c) of the Act is wide and takes within its sweep all payments made in respect of any period of employment or in respect of wages to be paid to an employee who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched. It does not exclude payment of incentive bonus which are paid at intervals not exceeding two months. [719 D E] The word "wages", in section 2, means all remuneration paid or payable to an employee whether the terms of his contract of employment express or implied, or otherwise. The word "gross wages" is defined in section 2A(2) of the , to mean "any remuneration (other than dearness allowance) paid to an employed person if he is employed on full time work on a time-scale basis". [720 F G] The definition is wide enough and covers all payments made before or after the commencement of the Act. [721 A] The definition does not include any additional remuneration, if any, paid at intervals. But the definition is wide and includes all payments made under the terms of the contract of employment. The definition is broader and takes within it all payments made by way of bonus. 2331: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 467/471, 420/465/471 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted them for offences under section 380, I.P.C., and sentenced them to various terms of imprisonment and fine. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence to a period of one year. The trial Court rightly acquitted the appellants. [533 D E] 3. The prosecution had failed in proving its case beyond any reasonable doubt. [534 F] 4. The trial of the appellants was illegal and void. Section 3(1) of the Act empowered the State Government to notify areas of the State as "Kans infested areas" and on such notification officers of the State were enabled to enter on the lands within the notified area and conduct deep ploughing tractorisation operation with a view to eradicate the kans. The Act was amended by the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 which came into force from April 1, 1959. The Act made provision for the recovery of arrears of land revenue and for the recovery and collection of the said sum as an arrear of land revenue. The Act also made provisions for the recovery, inter alia, of the cost of eradicating and other ancillary operations therein. The Act, however, did not provide for the recovery in case of default of payment of the amount due. 2165: The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the plaint schedule land and mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents were in illegal possession of the suit land and that they had no right to continue in possession thereof. On appeal, the Additional District Judge held that the suit was maintainable in a civil court and dismissed the second appeal. In the second appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the revenue court on the question of title to the property was vitiated by an error of law by the courts below inasmuch as the said decision would be a bar to the maintainability of the suit in a civil Court; and that the suit being barred by limitation, the respondents could not reagitate the same subject matter in a civil suit. HELD: (1) The decision of the Revenue Court on the question whether the suit was barred by limitation is final and conclusive. [623 E] (2) The decision given by the revenue court under section 89(2) of the Act is binding on the parties thereto and cannot be reopened or reviewed by any other authority. [624 F] (3) The decision in the present case is not one which can be reopened under section 90(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [625 G] (4) The decision is not final and conclusive and cannot be reconsidered. [626 A] (5) Section 90(4), which provides for the exclusion of jurisdiction of civil courts, does not apply to the present case. [627 B] (6) The decision under section 89 (2) of section 90(1) is not final but only a preliminary finding. [628 C]
435: The workmen of the appellant company were employed by the respondent company as clerks and depots cashiers. In the pay ranges below Rs. 50 and up to the pay range of Rs. 250 and by a flat rate of Rs. 5 in the higher pay range, the clerical staff of the company was awarded dearness allowance at the same rates as the clerical staff. The award made by the Tribunal was challenged before the High Court on the ground that the Tribunal had not followed the principle laid down by this Court in the case of Workmen 's Union vs Their Workman, , and that the Tribunal committed an error in applying the principle laid in the case. Held, that the Tribunal was right in applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the said case and that the award made by it was correct. It is true that the Tribunal has adopted the principle laid by this Court but that does not mean that the Tribunal should have applied the principle laid therein in its fullest sense. The principle laid down in the case was that the Tribunal ought to have adopted the principle which it did in the case before it. The Tribunal could not go behind the principle laid out in the case and ignore the principle laid there. The Tribunal was wrong in adopting the principle laid before it in the case as it did in its earlier award. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to add to the basic wages and dearness allowance fixed under the award.
6500: The appellant was the second son of Raja Padam Singh, who had executed a lease deed in respect of the lands to a Patta granted by his father on 14th Maghar 1999. He claimed ownership over the lands to which he claimed title. The respondent State Government issued a notification under section 29(1) of the Indian Forests Act, 1927 declaring the lands as reserved forest for the purpose of the Act. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the said notification was invalid and that the respondent State was not entitled to acquire the lands. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the grant made by the erstwhile ruler was in respect of revenue yielding lands only admeasuring about 263.4 bighas and not in respect of forest lands. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the grant was in respect only of the forest lands and not in regard to the forest lands. HELD: (i) The grant was in favour of the respondent State Government. The grant was not in respect to the forest land. It was merely an assignment of the forests. The grant is not in respect thereof. [819E] (ii) The grant is in respect of a forest land. The grant does not create any right in the forest land or any interest therein. The grant itself creates a right in the land. The right is not created by the grant. [820F] (iii) The grant in favour of a person is not in relation to the forest area. The grant in question is in respect to a forest land and not in relation of the forest land in question. [821G] (iv) The grant has nothing to do with the forest lands in question. The grant has no connection with the forest land and cannot be regarded as a grant in respect of any forest land. [822A] (v) The grant does neither create any interest in the forest lands nor extinguishes the rights in the forest areas. [823B] (vi) The grant itself is in respect only to the forest areas in the State of Punjab. The grant also does not create a right in favour of any person. [824C]

The question regarding the comparative advantage or disadvantages or disadvantaged position of the landlord or tenant can be decided by the Court on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. The question relating to the comparative hardship or disadvantages cannot be decided by taking into account the facts and circumstance of each case and the question of comparability or disadvantages can be decided on the basis thereof. 3930: The appellant was the owner of certain lands in Hyderabad City. He executed a Power of Attorney in favour of defendant No. 34, who was a police Patel. 2302: The petitioners challenged the validity of the Taxation Laws (Extension to Union Territories) Regulation No. 3 of 1963, on the ground that the provisions of the Regulation were ultra vires the powers of Parliament as they infringed their fundamental rights under article 14 and 19(1)(f). Held, that the power conferred by section 4(2) of the Taxation laws (Extension to the Union Territories) Act, 1963, was not a legislative power but an incidental or ancillary power which could be exercised only in respect of matters specified in the Schedule. The power conferred by the proviso to section 4(1) of the Act was not a power to legislate with regard to matters enumerated in the Schedule, but it was a power to enact regulations for the peace, progress and good government of the Union territory. The power to make regulations was not a part of the legislative power of Parliament. The power of making regulations was a power incidental or ancillary to the exercise of the power conferred upon the Parliament. The expression "subject to" in article 240(3) is used in a comprehensive sense to include within its scope all possible circumstances existing at the time when the Constitution came into force, such as the framing of the Constitution itself, the formation of the new Union Territory, the creation of new States, the alteration of the boundaries of the new State, the division of the territories of the existing States into new Union Territories, the alteration in the boundaries of new States and the alteration of territories.
3266: The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in tea gardens and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In the course of its business, it entered into certain transactions in jute and the goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery orders addressed to the mills changed hands. The goods were in stock and were in the custody of the mills. The goods had been sold by the appellant to the mills at a price higher than the market price. The sale proceeds were credited to the appellant 's account with the bankers. The appellant claimed that the loss suffered by it should be set off against speculation profits under section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions involving transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods were of a speculative and consequently the losses could be set off only against speculation profit. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transaction involving transfer of the goods involved no speculation but was a speculative transaction within the meaning of explanation to section 24(i). The High Court dismissed the reference. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question is covered by the decision of this Court in Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta. , and State of Andhra Pradesh vs Kolla Sreeramamurthy, ; , which has been followed by this Court in Duni Chand Rataria vs Commissioner of Incometax, Calcutta, ; and State of A.P. vs M/s. Dungarpur Sugar Mills Ltd., ; , respectively. [193 F] (2) The question whether the sales in question were speculative or speculative was one of fact and could be determined only after giving evidence. The finding of the Tribunal that the transactions were speculative was not open to challenge before us. [194 C] (3) The Tribunal was right in holding that the transactions involved no speculative and therefore the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set off under section 24 (1) of Income tax Act, 1922 against the profits made by the assessee 's business. [195 B C]

The post being temporary, the incumbent must have been recruited through the Union Public Service Commission. The post cannot be filled up by promotion or deputation. [608E F] 3. 4772: The first respondent secured more votes than the appellant. He was declared elected to the Assembly seat. The High Court held that the Commission having been invested with the powers of superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, it could not issue a notification under article 327 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Article 324 does not confer any plenary powers on the Election Commission. It only confers the power of superintendence, directions and control over the conduct of elections to Parliament or the State Legislatures. They do not have the power to issue directions under article 324. They do so because they are empowered by the Constitution to issue directions and orders in respect of any matter relating to or concerning the elections to Parliament. 5384: The appellant was appointed as Chairman of the Board of School Education, Haryana on 10 12 1985. 150: The petitioner was detained under section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code on a charge of having committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for life. He challenged his detention in this Court by a petition under article 32 of the Constitution contending that (i) the order of remand made by the trial Magistrate was not valid and (ii) the order was passed at a time when there was no order of remand, and therefore, it could not be said to have been made at a time earlier than the date of the return; Held, that the order of the trial Magistrate directing the production of the accused in custody was illegal as the order of release had already expired before the return of the case to the Court and the order of retrial had become final. The order of remand was not a fresh order but only an extension of the period of detention which was beyond the date of return of the accused to custody. The order was not revisable after the expiry of the period prescribed by section 344(1)(a) of the Criminal P. C., 1898.

2643: The respondent firm was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Seth Brothers and the firm was registered under the Income tax Act, 1961. The Income tax Officer issued a notice to the firm calling upon it to produce certain documents. The firm filed an application before the Income Tax Officer for inspection of the books of account and other documents seized by the Income tax Officer. The Income Tax Officer rejected the application holding that there was no reason to believe that instructions were issued by the Directorate of Inspection for a general raid and seizure of all accounts books and papers which may be found at the premises of the firm; that marks of identification were not placed on certain documents at the time they were seized; that marks were not placed at the time the documents were seized; and that marks of identity were not placed. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the search was vitiated as the notices were invalid inasmuch as the search was made without any authority or sanction of law. He also held that the documents seized were not relevant for the purpose of proceeding under the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The provisions of section 132(4) of the Income tax act, 1922 are mandatory and the Income tax officer has power to refuse inspection of the documents seized. [601 B] (2) The provisions contained in section 132(5) of the Act are mandatory and if the Income tax officers have reasons to believe that the search is vitiated, the proceedings can be taken against the assessee. [603 C D] (3) The Income tax Officers have been empowered to make enquiries with regard to the nature and extent of the possession of the assessee. They cannot take into consideration the statements recorded during the course of investigation. [604 E] (4) The provisions relating to search and seizure are mandatory and must be strictly complied with. [605 F] (5) The provisions regarding search and seizure contained in section 131 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, are mandatory and they must be strictly followed. [606 G]

Interest will be payable only on the balance amount which remains to be payable to the appellants i.e. the amount due minus what has been paid from the respective dates. [989D] 4. 927: The appellant was a Sub Inspector of Police in the State of Pepsu. He was dismissed from service by an order dated August 16, 1950. The order stated that he would be put to heavy loss and that his pension would also be affected and that this decision of the Government tantamounts to his removal from service. The respondent State contended that the order of compulsory retirement did not amount to removal from service within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution and as the requirement of that article had not been complied with it held that the termination of service effected by that order was void in law. Held, that the order was not invalid because it was passed without complying with the requirements of article 311(1) of the Constitution. The order was not one of punishment but only of dismissal or removal from service and the order was therefore valid. The order could not be said to have been made under article 311 of Constitution. The rule does not apply to the case of compulsory retirement. The order is not a mere administrative order. It is not a punishment. The order has to be passed after following the procedure prescribed for imposing the penalty. The order cannot be said to be an order by way of punishment. The rules of natural justice are not embodied rules. The rules must be followed strictly. In the present case, the order of dismissal was passed on August 16, 1951. The order of compulsory retiring the appellant was passed on March 30, 1951. On the date when the order was passed, the appellant was already in service. The order therefore became illegal.
3306: The appellant was convicted under section 379 read with section 34 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He preferred an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence to the High Court but the High Court dismissed his appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the provisions of section 6 were not applicable in the present case because the offence was not punishable with imprisonment for life and that the appellant had not done anything since the date of the offence to deserve the mercy of the Court and it did not, therefore, see any reason to interfere with the sentence of imprisonment imposed on him. HELD : (i) Section 6 does not apply to a case where the accused is found guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment only or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years. [675 B] (ii) The provisions of section 3 are mandatory and they must be strictly complied with if the Court is satisfied that the provisions have been complied with. It is not necessary that the Court should call for a report from the police officer about the nature of the offence and the character of the offender. [676 C D] (iii) The provisions contained in section 6 are directory and not mandatory. [677 E F]
5056: The plaintiffs filed a suit for infringement of the patents granted to them by the defendant. They claimed that they had acquired patent in their favour and that they were entitled to be registered as a patent holder under the Patent Act. The defendant contended that the patents were not in the possession of the plaintiffs, that the patent was not a patent but only a patent. The trial court held that the patnists were not entitled to protection against infringement of patents granted by the defendant and that the pattees were entitled to protection from infringement of patent. On appeal, the High Court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to relief on the basis of the patent being a patent holder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the patts were not in possession of the patrons and that the plaintiffs could not claim protection against the patents. HELD: (1) The patents are not rights which can be enforced against the patters. [901 G] (2) The patent is a right to be registered under the Patents Act. It is a patent. It is an expression of art. It is not a mere name or a symbol. It is nothing more than a name or a design. It is merely a name or symbol. It does not cease to be a patent. [902 B C] (3) The patnist has no right to be a registered patent holder. The patents have no right to get themselves registered as a patnist. [903 D E] (4) The pattees are not entitled to protect against infringement of the patent. [991 F] (5) The patamists do not enjoy any special privileges like patents. They are not entitled even to protection against the patent. The patnists are not entitled, if they are not registered as patents, to protection against infringements of patents. [992 H] (6) The patency is a right conferred by the patents Act. [993 A] (7) The patron's patents are entitled to protection only against infringement of patent. 3921: The appellant was a Sub Inspector of Police in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was charged with offences under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 18 months on each of the charges. On appeal the High Court acquitted him but confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that (i) the sanction is bad as it was not given by an authority competent to remove the appellant from service; (ii) the sanction was invalid because the appointing authority had no power to remove the person concerned from service; and (iii) the sanction being valid in law, the order of dismissal could not be sustained. HELD : (i) The sanction is valid in law. [864 E] (a) The sanction does not confer any right on the appellant to continue in service. It merely gives the authority competent to dismiss or remove him from service. The authority which has passed the order must be held to have been validly appointed. [865 B C] (b) The sanction cannot be said to be bad if it confers no right on the Government servant to continue in office. [866 D] (c) The sanction being valid is not bad. [867 F] (d) The sanction having been issued by an authority other than the appointing authority, the validity of the order of the appointing authority cannot be challenged. [868 A] (e) The sanction was valid in law and the appellant was rightly dismissed. [869 B] (f) The sanction did not confer any title on the appellant. [871 C] (g) The sanction, therefore, was valid in the eye of law. [887 D]
2950: The appellant, a firm of which the respondent was the Managing Partner, had issued policies and printed pamphlets and handbills for the sale of certain cycles. The appellant purchased three Policies from the respondent for Rs. 5,50 each. The respondent paid Rs. 5 to the appellant but the appellant did not pay the amount. The respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 420 I.P.C. before the Magistrate. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and committed the case to the Sessions Court. The appellant contended that the respondent had no right to sell the policy and the respondent could not be prosecuted for cheating. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondent 's defence was not tenable. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to get back his money as he had received the original amount of Rs. 5 in full immediately after the sale of three Polices. HELD: (1) The scheme as aforesaid is a complete code and the respondent cannot claim any benefit out of it. [128D] (2) The scheme is a complete Code and the respondent has no right to ask for its cancellation or refund. The scheme is only an administrative one and does not confer any right upon the respondent. It is not open to the respondent to contend that the scheme is void because the respondent has obtained the benefit of the scheme. [129F] (3) The scheme being a complete code, the respondent cannot take advantage of it. If the scheme is valid, the respondent can claim the benefit of it. But if the scheme is invalid, the respondent would have no right to complain. [130B]
1429: The appellant company was a small scale industry in the Delhi region. It had a large number of chemical works and it was running a large number in the same area. In the year 1959, the company was divided into two units, one for the manufacture of chemical products and another for the manufacture and sale of chemicals. The appellant company claimed that the chemical works should be treated on par with the textile mills run by the company and the claim of the respondents that the chemical work should be treated as an independent unit was untenable. The respondents contended that the chemical Works was one unit of a large number and each unit had to be considered on its own, and the wage structure etc. fixed accordingly; in particular it was pointed out that there were differences in wage structure etc., between the various units which were controlled and owned by the Company and which were all situate in the same areas in Delhi and that those differences should be eliminated and all the enterprises in Delhi controlled by the Company should be treated On the other band the contention of the appellant was that though the chemical works was one unit, some of which were situate in the area in Delhi, the various units were separate and distinct from the industry in Delhi ; and that the wage structure and dearness allowance fixed on the basis of the financial position of each unit must be taken into account in fixing the wage structure, etc. The Tribunal held that in the circumstances of the case the chemical works could not be treated as independent units and that the workers employed in the canteen should be treated only on the same footing as the workers employed by the company. The Tribunal also found that the respondents ' claim that the chemicalworks should be treated at par with the industry in the same manner as the workers in the factory was not correct. The Tribunal further found that the appellant company had been maintaining separate accounts for the different units and that they were doing the same work as the other units in the factory. The Tribunal therefore directed the appellant to pay to the respondents the minimum wages prescribed by the Government under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has given good reasons for coming to the conclusion that the chemical worked in the factory should be treated to be an independent unit. [550 C] (ii)The Tribunal

3051: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a lease of certain flats in the building known as Himalaya House. The lease was for a period of 10 years and the period expired on June 30, 1959. The appellant sought to obtain special leave against the decision in question. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant 's right of occupation in the building was not an absolute right but only a right to occupy the building and that the consideration mentioned in the document was the consideration for the assignment of the right of occupation. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The consideration mentioned in a document is the consideration for assignment of the lease. The consideration is the consideration which the lessee has to pay to the lessor for the use and occupation of the property. [887 E] 2. The consideration for assignment is the consideration paid by the lessee to the lessor in respect of the property assigned. The consideration given is the consideration mentioned by the lessee in the document. The consideration stated in the document is the amount of consideration payable to the lessor. [888 F G] 3. The consideration specified in the document does not include any consideration for the transfer of the right to occupy a particular premises or any part thereof. The consideration referred to in the document includes all rights, liabilities and obligations of the parties thereto. [890 A B] 4. The consideration described in the document represents the consideration for transfer of the property and the consideration mentioned is the consideration towards the transfer of possession of the property or any part of it. The consideration set out in the document cannot be said to be the consideration for grant of the right or interest in the property. The consideration contemplated in the document must be the consideration mentioned therein. [889 D E] 5. The consideration stipulated in the document can be said to have been the consideration for assigning the right or interests in the property to the person who had acquired the property from the original owner. The consideration provided in the document may be different from the consideration mentioned earlier in the document itself. [891 C D] 6. The consideration indicated in the document would be the consideration which a person had to pay to his lessor for the purpose of getting the lease executed.

The respondent company was also merged with HPC Ltd. on May 5,1978. The respondent was given the benefit of the revised scales of pay of Rs. 825-1200 from January 1,1973. The respondent challenged the said order before the Company Law Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the respondent 's claim. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the respondent. 1187: The petitioners, who were the sons of Abdul Hai and his six children, were allotted certain shares in certain shares. They went to Pakistan but the time when they did so did not appear. They came back to India and settled there. Thereafter they migrated to Pakistan. On their death the wives and children of Abdul Hafi and his six minor children by their respective wives and daughters were held entitled to the properties left by them in Pakistan. The order of August 14, 1952, was made under section 11 of the Act vesting the entire property in the Custodian. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it was a nullity as the notice under section 7 of the Act on which it was based was bad for the reason that it was issued to Abdul Hafiz who was admittedly not an evacuee. Held, that the order of August 4, 1952, is valid and the petitioners cannot be said to have been deprived of their property except by recourse to the provisions of section 9 of the Act. The order does not affect the rights of the petitioners. The order merely declares that the properties are evacuee property. The order is not a mere direction to the Custodian to determine the property in question or any interest therein. It only provides that the order shall contain the particulars specified in sub sections (1) and (2) of section 8. The order therefore does not affect any right of the petitioners to hold the property in dispute.
862: The respondents were the Apollo Mills, Ltd., and other companies owning cotton textile mills specified in the annexure to the Special Leave Petition and the Mill Owners Association, Bombay, representing the cotton textile mills. The dispute related to the compensation which the workers claimed for loss of wages and dearness allowances due to the short working or closure of the Textile Mills on certain days during the period between November 1, 1951, and July 13, 1952. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Court by the Bombay Government under section 73 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The award made by the Tribunal was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Industrial Court had jurisdiction to decide the dispute as it was covered by the Standing Orders framed under section 26 of the Bombay Electricity (Special Powers) Act, 1946; (ii) the view taken by the Bombay High Court in Digambar Ramachandra 's case (1) was erroneous and (iii) the award was not binding on the parties. HELD : (i) The decision of the Bombay High court in Digambaram Ramachandra vs Khandesh Mills (I) was overruled by the decision of this Court in Digamber Ramachandra v Khandesh Mills, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 709. The decision of this court in Digambeer Singh vs The State of Punjab, [1961] 3 S.C R. 650, followed. (ii) The decision in Digambar Ramachandra was not correct. It was a decision given in the context of the provisions of the Bombay Act and the Bombay Act. The decision in the Bombay Act was not applicable to the present case because the Bombay Act did not apply to the present dispute. [303 D E] (iii) The decision was rendered in the context in which it was given. The Bombay Act was enacted in order to provide for the better protection of the workmen employed in certain undertakings. The Bombay Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act, 1953, introduced section 2(b) in the Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which provided that "the Act shall be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of October, 1952". 3771: The respondents, Indian Railway Co., were importers of goods for home consumption. The Port Trust filed a suit against the appellants for recovery of demurrage charges on the ground that the Port Trust was in law entitled to collect the demurrage levied on the respondents and that as they failed to pay the demurreer, the Port Trust is not entitled to recover any demurrage from the Port Trust. The Port Trusts contended that the Ports are not entitled to collect demurrage under section 43B (IA) and that the Port trust is not entitled under section 43 B(1)(a). The Port Trust contested the suit contending that the Port was in law not entitled to demand demurrage. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Port had no right to demand demursrage. On appeal by the Port Trust, the High Court held that the Port could not be called upon to pay demurrage unless the Port Trust had taken action under section 43 A (IA) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Port authorities were not entitled to charge demurrage when there was no actual delay in the clearance of the goods. HELD: The Port Trust cannot be said to have acted mala fide or with ulterior motives. It has been established by the evidence that the Port Authorities had taken action in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Port Trust did not want to take action against the Port Trust for the period during which the goods were detained. [639 E] The Port Trust is a statutory body constituted by the Bombay Port Trust Act, 1879 and is a body corporate. It has powers to levy and collect demurrages. Under section 43B(2), the Port Trust may, after giving reasonable notice to the person concerned, impose such conditions as it thinks fit, requiring him to deposit within such time as may be specified the demurraises due to any default committed by him.
